MISS LOLLIPOP'S HOUSEKEEPING. Little Miss Lollipop thought she must help To wash up the dishes, and wipe up the shelf, To brush off the table, and sweep up the floor, And clean off the stains from the paint on the door. She put on her apron and pulled up her sleeve— She didn't want work that was only make-believe; e• 4 " For muzzers who've dot little chillens," said she, "Must have yittle housekeepers; dat's what I'll be." Little Miss Lollipop went through the room, Whisked the dust high with the edge of the broom, Broke the poor cup which she dropped on the floor, Left the paint twenty times worse than before. Spattered and splashed—but oh! how could I chide The little heart swelling with sweet, helpful pride? " For how would my rnuzzer be able." said she, "To get frso her work if she didn't have me ?" *. Dearer the love in the sunny blue eyes. it Than the dust she is raising, which fades as it flies; a Better to miss the best cup on the shelf, Than chill the dear heart which is giving itzelf. Dear Little Lollipop! we are, like you, Spoiling the work we are trying to do— But surely the Father who loves us will heed And take in His kindness the will for the deed !

A Bridgeport man &lye his wife is only halt like a tele- scope. He can draw her out, but he can't shut her up. The motto which went wita a rich lumberman's coat of arms was a puzzle to his Michigan neighbours, but he him' stlf knew that Vidi is the Latin equivalent of "I saw." A Missouri newspaper claims that the bogs of that State are so fat that in order to find out where their heads are it is necessary to make theca squeal, and then judge by the sound. The proprieter of a forge, not remarkable for correctness of language, but wl- o by bonest industry had realised a com- fortable independsoce, eeing called on at a social meeting for a toast, gave, n Sa:cess to forgery." Instructor in Latin: "Of whet was Ceres the goddess'?" ' Miss: "She was the goddess of marrisee." Instructor: "Oh, no; of agriculture." Miss B. (Lsoking perplexed): " Why, I am sure my boek says she is the goduess of husbandry." A FISHY STREAM.—P,,z-ttor (who has firmly hooked a fine root) : "Now, bey. gently dies it! We'll have him our, if I stay here a weee."—Boy : " Ah, he'll be a prize, sir. There's bony been one fleh, caught in this 'era stream for folve year, and he's stuffed and put in tue Red Lion as a curiosity. (Piscator does not remain a week )—l' an. A lady with a young infant was recently presented with a handsome basket besting on its lining the words " Wel- come, Little Stranger." The basket was greatly admired, especially the painted letters in green and gold, but the nurse, an Irish woman, pat in a veto against the salutation, For sure that was wrong, e„fon,the baby is not a stranger, but one of the family." Curran once said to Father Leary, " I wish, reverend father, that you were Sr. Peter;:and had the keys of heaven, because then you could let men." The shrewd and witty ell, priest saw the sarcaem, en' turned its sharp edge on the sceptic by rep'ying," By my honour and conscience, sir, it wou'd be better for you that I hod the keys of the other place, for then I could let you out." A RAT IN PRISON.—An incident which cc tarred a few Sundays ago in the city prison goes towards proving that there are phases of womanly timidity which can not be eradicatel even by the most violent vicissitudes. The Beene was the chapel in which the women prisoners were as- sembled for the usual religious service. The women who are lodged in the Tombs do not exemplify all that is gentle and womanly. Indeed, they are as a class quite as hardened as the men prisoners—as fond of whisky or a free fight, and as ready to take the desperate chances incidental to criminal life. But when on the Sunday in question an affrighted rat made his appearance in one corner of the room, that which is common to all women asserted itself in the hardened assamblage, and the heroines of gin-mill brawls, street fights, and criminal exploits shrieked frantically, and began as- sending the furniture. Composure was not restored till the rat was dead. FOSSILS UNITING THE CEARACIERS OF PIGS AND OF MONKEYS.--Soale time ago M. P. Gereaie discovered in Upper Eocene strata, near Apt, in France, a portion of an upper jaw with teeth, which exhibited an analogy to those of certain omnivorous pachyderms allied to the Saida , and yet res-m`eed in other respects those of the monkeys. For this fteesil he suggested the appropriate name of Ceborherus. In studying the mammalian remains found in the phosphorite deposits of Qtercy, IL M. Fithol detected several specimens of C-hocherus, which enabled him more fully to deectibe the dentition, our knowledge of which was previously very imperfect. Bat he also discovered other somewhat similar remains, r.,whieh approached yet more nearly to the monkeys, and A° these he gave the generic name of Doliocherus. Quite lately he has obtained an al- most complete bead, with lower jaw in place. This unique fossil he described beforejthe A.cadernie des Sciences at their meeting on May 1. It is, therefore, now proved beyond all doubt that there existed durieg the late Eocene period a group of roanimals (Pachysindan;), which united many of the characteristics of the pigs on tne one hand with those . of the monkeys on the other—an association of characters which naturally gives to these fossils a peculiar interest to the student of evolution. LONGFELLOW AND Ms Wiez.—Longfellovs had enjoyed a favourite share of fortune. All his plans had prospered. He was the one person in Cambridge whom every one knew and Isved. A quiet and studious scholar, he outranked all Governors, Congressmen, and other dignitaries. Living In a university town where nearly every resident was the centre of some learned circle, he was, like Goethe at Weimar, the one man famous by divine right and by the universal suffrage of hearty. If ever man had " honour, love, obedi- eace, troops of friends"—everything to fill the mind with serene happiness—that man was Longfellow. Bat the inner feelings of his soul and the sacred remembrances of love • were lacked and guarded from every eye. The public have never known the inexpressible agony, followed by a chastened but perpetual grief, which he suffered in the loss of his wife. It is imoessible to exaggerate his devoted love for this noble woman, the mother of his children, who had made his home little less than paradise. On the 4th of July, 1861, she was berned to death in hie presence. She was dressed in ample' flowing muslin, and by some mischance her garments took fire from a lighted match. The flame spread almost with a flteh ; the etartled husband, seeing no other means at hard, seezei a large rug or mat and at- tempted to roll it about her to extinguish it, but in vain. e In a moment she received injuries which were mortal. His heeds were severely burned in the sharp struggle. Nothing WAS left but the undying sense of his irreparable lose, and the image of a glorious soul to be treasured for ever. There Is not, so far as Can he ascertained, a single reference to this terrible event in his published poems.— Henry Wads- worth Longfellow: A Biographical Sicetch.—By Francis H.' Under wood. TAPE es As AVIARY.—The only requirement redly ne- cessary is that you do sit quietly, when it matters not if you have a nest within a foot of your-elbow, or even built on the back of your chair; things will go on just as uncon- cernedly in your presence as in your absence. On one branch may be noticed two birds going through a few pre- liminary evolutions—advancing, retiring, chattering, and finishing up with a quarrel on the ine amantium principle. Ciesterve, also, what a complete master of his art is this de- scendant of the shipwrecked unfortunate at Elba. He has in his veins the same hot blood, and has no equal at " delntherin," unless it may be the goldfinch on the other side, bowing and scraping and spreading out his coat tails like the dandy he is, while he talks treason to that demure little hen, which we have mason to think is already affianced to one of her own race. Under cover of the bush in the corner sit another couple, whispering the molt affectionate soft nothings, and talking over the eligibility of one or two building sites at their disposel. Immediately above them another pair is hard at work putting the finishing touchee ottage ornije of which the foundations were laid only yesterday, and which must be completed without delay; it is a cage of emergency, and dne " in the course of a fewh will' be required in the morn- ing. Within reach of the han_ dourriits a hen on five eggs, ; and while we watch .Ipe bright eye and admire the canstancy with which she has attended to the first part of her matronly duties, her mate flies up to make anxious inquiries and give 'her a mouthful of food. Perched on a piece of root, in a position from which it seems as if a breath would dislodge the entire fabric. is another nest, above the top of which are - visible half a dozen gapin meuthe, which the are filling with dainty morsels pricfr ti, tbeAr bet ° PUntlte t joked in for an boar's nap. .111 a here are four el,orewhich, tiough hatched only t'uree weeks ago, are 2,titreost as large as Vieir parents, anti fit into their warm bed like the pieces in a Chirtese puzzle. Look which way we will we continually find somethirtg fresh to attract the attention and interest the mind, and the aviary is voted the best room in the house.— ° Canaries and Cage Birds" for Jane. . div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, Sze.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. The posthumous collection of Longfellow's poems, now in the ores, is 'entitled "In the Harbour." While excavating for drainage purposes in Berlin the workmen employed have found a remarkable quantity o amber in the Genthiuer Strasse. Several hundred pieces were found. The inhabitants of Ragatz have been much alarmed at the fatting off of their warm springs. Only one spring yet flows to the baths, and the water, which has usually a tem- perature. of 27 or 28 deg. Reaumnr, shows now only 21 deg. R.; but it shows some signs of ,aoain rising. The Atheneum says that Mr. Wilkie Collins is engaged in writing a new serial story, in which the question of vivi- section is placed in a new point of view by tracing the effect of the habitual practice of cruelty on human character. The story will be translated into the French, German, Italian, Dutch, and Swedish languages, by special arrangement with the author. A correspondent of iVature, writing in reference to Pro- fessor Riley's question as to tho iltilisation of ants in horti- culture by the Chinese, states that an attempt was made to introduce them into Ceylon to check the ravages of the coffee bug, but the red ants sometimes attacked the naked limbs of the Malay coolies so fiercely that the experiment was given up. The British ffredical Journal says that Dr. Riembanit, in a communication made to the Paris Academy of Ma dicine, statsss that he has made a series of researches with reference to "miner's armmia," and he believes that this affection is due to the presence of a worm of the filarta species, and not to that of the anlcylostomum duodenale, as asserted by M. Perroncito, of Turin. . Mr. Mann Valentine, of Richmond. in Virginia, has brought to England a remarkable collection of figures carved in micaceous schist, in steatite, and in sandstone. To what people these sculptures may he attributed is at present an anthropological puzzle, but they are probably not all of the same age. One of the animals is thought to represent the mastodon, hut one of the men evidently carries a gun. The collection was exhibited at the last meeting of the An- thropological Institute. There is yet much to be desired in our knowledge of the poisons employed by savages for their weapons. Dr. Sheuhe, in his monograph on the Aims. speaking of their fashion of shooting deer and bear with poisoned arrows, the effects of which are certainly fatal within a few hours of the skin's abrasion, says that when the quarry is obtained the flesh around the mortal wound is cut away. while the remainder of the carcase is employed for food without any bad effects upon the consumer. Mr. Paul Gibier has informed the Academy of Sciences that he has succeeded in infecting with charbon frogs that have been kept under the influence of a high temperature. They were kept in warm water before the innoculation, and, out of twenty, five showed characteristic bacteria in the blool. Rabbits innoculated from theni reproduced the symp- toms of charbon. M. Vnlpian in the course of discussion, observed that frogs kept in laboratories are often subject spentaneously to bacterian infection, but that, in this caee. the virus taken from them has no affect upon warm-blooded animals.

The harvest prospects in France are said to be most favourable. Indeed, I read in a French agricultural journal that, should present prospects be fulfilled, for the first time for four years France will not require to import food from abroad.—Land. A farmer named Johnson, in the neighbourhood of Wis• beach, has 88 ewe, of ovtlich 23 had triplets, and the 23 ewes with their 69 lambs are now to be seen by themselves in a pasture, svhic'a looks very strangely stocked. The ewes are balf-breds. It is et oted that Sir J. B. Lawes has found by experiment that sheep well fed under cover will consume about 70 pounds of roots, 41 pounds of hay, and 4/ pounds of oilcake Der head per week for every 100 pounds of their live weight, increasing in weight weekly about two per cent. A convention of dairymen has recently been held at Geneva, Wit3COOSIP, and the room was hung round with mottoes, one of which is worth copying. It runs thus:— " The moking of butter and cheese is no profitable calling for an unthinking man—it demands brains." English local authorities might with advantage take a lesson from the French Department of Public Works. From a recent report of this body, I learn that more than 14,000,000 motrea of high roads inTrance are planted with trees. Considerably over two and a half million trees cast their welcome shade upon these roads. Comparatively speaking, there are but a few miles of tree-planted roads throughout all England.—La,d. THE SKIM MILK DIFFICULTY IN NEW YORK has given rise to a bill which is now before the New York Legislature, and, as the Senate has left it, it provides that all milk which has had the cream token off must be sold from vessels marked in durable letters of one inch in length "skimmed milk." An exception is made on Lthis 'point in counties where the milk is produced. The penalty is a fine of 50 dollars and costs, one•half of which goes to the prosecutor, who may be "any person or persons," and the "remainder to the overseer of the poor for the use of the poor of the town in which the offence was committed." In default of pay- ment defendant may be sent to gaol "for a period of not less than one day for each dollar of the amount of judg- na. nt."

At this show the r 'nehmen from the western plains could also learn what peirts were most needed in the true beef animal. These lessons were learned net only from the live animals as they stood in the stills and rings, hut when slaughtered and hung side by side in the Expositi n building. Thoroughbred bulls likely to reproduce in their get those points decided upon at the fat stock sh )ws are being picked up and taken far back upon the Plains, and in every cross an improvement is made. This takes time, but the work is going on at a rapid rate. To make the improvements more rapid among the western herds, heifers are bought from the stock-breeders east of the Mississippi to be bred to the fall-blooded bulls. In this way in a few years the home supnly will be mostly provided for. Another way is of late being adopted to more thoroughly and rapidly eliminate the native breeds, which is the practice of buying no delves of any aee under a year old, got by thoroughbred bulls on high-bred cows. I will state the course adopted by a beginner of: stock breeding in this county. Last fall he purchased an imported Hereford bull and six females. His own herd being so small, he has eng sired cows of his near neighbours at a charge of £2 for eervice, with the privilege for the owner of the cow to de- liver him the coif, either male or female, at four months old for £4, the calf to have new milk at least during the first month, and to-he well fed and cared for during the four months. At these terms he has alaree number of cows now engaged, and more are ready to accept the same terms. To meet the demand he has lately bought] another imported Hereford bull, and one hundred cows or more in one neigh- bourhood, mostly of high grade Shorthorns, are to be put to breeding, for the buildrng no of herds west of the Missis- sippi by these graded Herefords. Even among the cows engaged, quite a good many are full-blood Shorthorns. When a car-load or more of calves is ready, the western ianchm in or his agent comes for his young stock and takes them to their new home. In this way year by year the native blood disappears upon the Plains. As they mature for market in the form of beef, the large corn cribs of Eastern Kansas. Nebraska. and lowa will afford them a abort stooping place for those whose age and form are such that a little grain feeding is necessary to fit them for direct shipment to the eastern cities and to England." The Athenatorn says that a treasure of Singular apposite- ness has just turnPd up in the form of a preface, suppressed bv the publishers as being too outspoken. written by Thackeray for the second edition of his "'lrish Setch Book." This preface, which forms a long essay on the political situation in Ireland, will shortly be printed in the Century Magazine. In it Thackeray strongly supports not merely the dise4tablishment of the Established Church, which, be says, will no more grow in Ireland "than a palm tree in St Paul's Churchyard," but even the repeal of the Union. He goes so far as to venture on a prophecy that the latter concession will be wrung from Sir Robert Peel i„ 1848. 4) i

The North China Herald mentions a novelty in the way of applied science which is said to exist among thieves in China. They prepare a composition of some medicated in- gredient, supposed to be aconite, and, li.thting it, blow it into the room to be nabbed by means of a tube through a hnle previously made (not a difficnit thing in Chinese houses with paper windows and doors.) The inmates are thus aumsthetisised or at least deprived of the power of speech and llcomntioe, and the thieves enter and do their work. In vain does the proprietor being robbed see the burglars. He cannot move limb or tongue. It is said that water absnrbs this poison, and so for this purpose it is not uncommon for wealthy people to sleep with a basin of water at their heads. It is celled mea lesiang or lesion hsiang —to suffocate or asphyxiate with incense. In the Numismatic Chronicle, Dr. John Evans describes a board of early Anglo-Saxon coins found at Delgany, in Wicklow, in 1874. It included some very rare Kentish coins, and was indeed "the most essentially Kentish hoard of which we have any record." The latest in date of these coins are those of Beornvulf, from 820 to 824. It is note- worthy that neither in Sweden nor Denmark are such coins found of earlier date than 830. Hence Dr. Evans suggests that the inroads of the Danes into Smthern Britain during the first half of the ninth century were made, not by the Eastern Dines of the Continent, bat by the Western Danes from their settlements in Ireland. He thinks that this board is part of the spoil which fell to the invaders in 832, when " the heathen men ravaged Sheppey."

THE JEANETTE EXPEDITION.—DisCOVERY OF DEAD BODIES or Tam EXPLORERS.—The following telegram bas been received by way of Irkutsk, at the London office of the New York Herald, from Mr. W. H. Gilder, one of the spe- cial correspondents of the Herald in Siberia :—" Lena Delta, April 12th (246). 1882. Melville found bodies De Lone's party, March 23rd; they were in two places 500 and 1,009,i yards from wreck of scow. First started from supply dept to follow Nindemann'a route from Ueterday to Marvay, afterward from Marvay back toward Usterday, looking for wreck. Found wreck, and following along hank, Came upon rifle barrel hung upon four sticks supporting • bridge poised of snow hank; set natives digging each side of poles, who soon came upon two bodies under eigbt feet of snow. Whilel natives digging towards east Melvills went on hank 20,t. ' I-above river to find place to take bearings; saw camp kettle land remains of fire about thousand yards from tent place, and approaching nearly stumbled upon De Long's hand sticking out of snow about thirty feet from edge of bank. Here, under about a foot of snow, found bodies De Long and Ambler about three feet apart, and Ah Long lying at ' their feet, all partially covered by pieces of taunt and few ;.pieces of blanket; all others, except Alexv, found at tent place. Loe and Knack close by. In cleft in bank towards west two boxes records with medicine chest and flag on staff at tent place; none of dead had boots, feet covered with rage tied on. In Dockets of all were pieces of burnt skin clothing they had been eating ; hands of all more or less burnt, and looked as if when dying had crawled into fire. Boyd lying over fire and clothing burnt through to skin, which was not ' burnt. Collins's face covered with cloth. All bodies carried to top of bill three hundred feet high, about forty versts south-west from where found, and interred in mausoleum constructed of wood from scow, built form of pyramid, 22 feet long, seven- high, surmounted by cross 22 feet high and foot square, hewn out of drift wood, conspicuous at distance of 20 versts. Mausoleum covered with stones, and to be sodded in spring, cross inscribed with record and names of dead cut in by search party in their house at night. After eempteting tomb,*narty separated to search delta, for traces of Chinos' people ; Melville north-west part of delta, and west as far as Olenck River, Nindemann centre. and Bartlett north east. Nindemann and Bartlett found nothing. Mel- ville not yet returned ; search to be extended to Cape Bor- chova and hay. Expect to finish in time to reach Jalcatik or Werchojansic before rivers break up ; If not, will bare to retreat to foot of hills and mountains with natives until w Aar falls, as whole delta covered with water in spring four feet deep, though now bank some places 20 feet above level of river' otherwise would have buried dead where found. Letters with map and diagrams by maII.—GILDER."

Oats are particularly good. As we proceed a little further west and get upon dry soil the prospects brighten in almost all kinds of crops. The quantity of ryegrass and clover which is cut is much greater proceeding from Cuddington, I and cutting was going on. Old meadow grass is mainly ready for cutting or thereabouts. In this district I node( d a small field of oats shot. Turnips are nicely up, and so far I as I could see, are Gee of the fly. In the neighbourhood I of Tarvin a large quantity of splendid clover is down, but I could not see a single field that had been cleared. It will be very serious for this cnop if the weather should continue 1 as humid as it has been for some time past. There is a ; large quantity of grass down about Mickle Talfford. All along the route cattle and sheep are looking very well. Proceeding from Chester in the direction of Warring- ' ton there is not much haymaking to be seen except about Mickle Trafford, but on approaching Helsby the hay har- vest has commenced in good earnest. Here and about Frodsham there is a great quantity of heavy grass down, but none housed. Several fields are in big cock, and two or three successive fine days would see a cansiderable area c7eared. In this neighbourhood are several wheat fields which have a rusty look, but not a great deal is yet in the ear. The potato crop looks promising. After leaving War- rington, all along to Timperley, the grass shows a fine breast, and having been quickly grown is tender. Much of it would have been better in rick or barn a week ago. The grain crops with a few exceptions in the district referred to are looking very well, but there is less wheat shot than I expected to find. A few fields wear a rusty look. Taking the round, there is a great difference observable in potatoes as to forwardness, there being a number of fields on heavy sole which have only just broken through the crest of the drills. This has been caused by the rain having retarded planting. Should the ssether take a desirable turn what with the increased price of cattle and sheep and the field prospects at the present time the British farmer may take fresh courage. From what I have heard harvest wages are likely to be a little lower this year."

their side the falchion of battle. He, a tribune of the pe:„. carries likewise the falchion of other battles—the falchion of eloquence, more redoubtable than the sword." Lord Jef- fry, a professional critic, declared that all other speeches in the House seemed to him only talking schoolboy talk after he had heard O'Connell. Roebuck declared he was the greatest orator he had ever heard in the House. Charles Dickens, when a reporter in the Gallery of the House of Commons, once pat down hi pencil when engaged in reporting a speech of O'Connell's on one of the tithe riots in Ireland, and declared that he could not take notes of a speech, so moved was he by its pathos. It was, however, in his own land and before his own countrymen that O'Connell appeared at his best. Possessed of an herculean frame, a stately pre• l fiance, a face capable of expressing easily and effectively the most rapid alternations of mood, and a voice almost unri- valled _ for strength and sweetness, he could make whole _ _ _

masses bend before his matchless sway. Justin M`Carthy says:—" He could send his lightest word thrilling to the extreme of the vast concourse of people whom he desired to move. He swayed them with magic of an absolute control. He understood all the moods of his people. He made them roar with laughter. He made them weep. He made them thrill with indignation. As the shadow runs over the field, so the impression of his varying eloquence ran over the assemblage. He commanded the emotion of his hearers as a consummate:conductor sways the energies of his orchestra." And this power he employed in the advocacy of legitimate means. He at all times preached the doctrine of constitu- tional agitation strictly, and declared that "no political amelioration was worth one drop of blood." He exhausted all his eloquence in contrasting the advantages of constitu- tional agitation with the horrors of war, and exhibited at all times, both in public and in ;.-;rivate conversation, an almost Quaker detestation of force. Of the Irish rebels of 'PB he spoke with as savage an intolerance as the narrowest English Tory could show in speaking of himself. The Tones, the Emmets, the Fitzgeralds, whom se many of the Irish people admired. were, in O'Connell's eyes and in his words "a gang of miscreants." It was mainly by his influ- ence that the Irish people could not be induced to follow the revolutionary movement of 1848. He infused into them a touching faith in the power of peaceful agitation which un- happily did not survive his death. They are by no means the disciples of O'Connell who sing Give me the sword and dynamite, Or worse, if man or heaven can give, The lightning in its thundering flight I would direct her foe to rive. f et. Yes: in my heart such hatred dwells For England and the Saxon race, I'd grasp the fire of thousand hells And hurl it blazing in their face. No! No! Daniel O'Connell was the great apostle of that sect whose first doctrine was that no political change was worth the shedding of a drop of blood, and that all might be ' obtained by the irresistable might of moral force, and he looked forward to a "good time coming" when, in all political struggles the might of public opinion would prove invariably triumphant. Yet it cannot be denied that often his eloquence was marred by considerable defects. He indulged in scurrilous personalities and intemperate abuse—eloquent Billing•%ate in short—unworthy of his great powers. He celled the Duke Of Wellington "a stunted corporal." One might as well have called Mont Blanc a mole-hill. He called the Times "an obscure rag." We all know whom he called "a lineal descendent of the impenitent thief." Not only did he nickname Sir Robert Peel as Orange Peel," but he de• scribed him as" a raw youth, squeezed out of the workings of I know not what factory in England." "A foolish and fading gentleman" was his descriptive phrase he applied to Sir Francis Burdett. When the Dublin reporters wrote against him he called them "a parcel of nibbling mice." "Do you call me a mouse ?" demanded the renegade Eb- rington. " No," retorted the ever ready Dan, "If I called you anything I should call you a rat." For indulgence of such slang we have no apology to offer. Clearly our hero is _here open to rebuke and censure. The truth is that though his heart was warm and good-natured, and his die. position jovial and genial, his temper was irritable, and this led him into language coarse and unbecoming. And the language he habitually employed towards opponents gave a bitterness to political controversy in Ireland which it had never before attained, and which has been productive of baneful results.

To no Irishman, however, can the wonderful life of O'Connell fail to be impressive—from the day when, a fiery and thoughtful boy, be sought the cloisters of St. Omer's for the education which penal laws denied him in his own land, on through the manifold struggles and 'victories of his earlier career as he broke and dung off with a kind of haughty impatience link after link oi the social and political chain that six hundred years of British policy had woven around every limb and muscle of his country, down to that supreme moment of the blackness of darkness for himself and for Ireland when he laid down his burden "entered the eternities and rested upon his arms there." For ourselves we say with Lecky—" The more we dwell upon the subject, the more are we convinced of the splendour and originalitly of the genius and of the sterling character of the patriotism of O'Connell in spite of the calumnies that surround his memory and greiyous faults that obscure his life."

THE STATE OF IRELAND. The deith is announced of Mr. W. Bence Jones, whose letters as an Irish landlord and relations with his tenants in county Cork have recently attracted a considerable amount of attention.

Two incendiary fires occurred on Monday in the vicinity of Mallow. The farmhouses and barns of two farmers named Daniel Creedon and Daniel Hanlon were set on fire and partially destroyed whilst the owners and their families were attending special service at the parish church.

A gentleman resident in Dublin recently had an invitat;on to an entertainment at the Viceregal Pahce. On the card were not only the usual letters, "R.S.V P.," but the fotlo w- ing in addition, " P.P.G." Being somewhat at sea as to the meaning of " P.P.G.," he made enquiry at the proper quarter, and learned that the mysterious letters signified Police Protection Guaranteed." A man named Patrick Runne, tenant of Mr. Anthony Ormsby, of Ballinamore House, was fired at as he was return- ing home from Claretnorris fair _on Saturday. He was struck on the shoulder, thigh, and ear, but the wounds were not serious. The' cause assigned is that Runne was about to take possession of a farm known as the Land League farm. The police are scouring the country, but no capture has as yet been made. An outrage of an extraordinary character was committed on Monday morning at Rowels, County Longford, at the house of Mr. John M'Carthy, rent-warner and bailiff to Mr. Langford, J.P. In the absence of the family four men entered the house, where M'Carthy's daughter, aged twenty, was alone, and seizing her, cut off all her hair. They then fired the building and decamped. The house and contents were destroyed, but Miss M'Carthy escaped with a severe shock. '

MR. PARNELL AND Mn. DILLON.—It has been definitely arranged that Mr. Parnell, M.P., and Mr. Dillon, M.P., will formally receive the freedom of the city of Dublin, which was voted to them durinc, their incarceration in Kilmainham by the Corporation, on the occasion of the festivities to com- mence on the 15th of August next in celebration of the movei!ing of the O'Connell statue and the opening of the exhibition of Irish manufactures and products. At the service on Sunday in the chapel at Enniskillen, the Rev. Father Quigley, who was officiating, read the pastoral of the United Hierarchy, which has been recently published, and afterwards, referring to its contents in an explanatory manner, remarked that neither the Land nor the Ladies' League was a secret society. The County Court judge here- upon withdrew from the ehapel, a circumstance which at- tracted a great deal of atien;.i&a. WI has been much com- mented upon siace. On Monday, a bady of disguised men entered the residence ' of captain Uostello, of Edmundstown, Boyle, and ransacked the premises in search of arms. They shot a bull dog which attacked them in the parlour, and tied the servants with 1 ropes, leaving them powerless to interfere. Captain Costello was absent, and they carried off a stand of arms which he had for protection. Two policemen were attracted by the noise of the escaping marauders, and fired after then at long range. The shot was returned. Six arrests were made at Callow in the evening in connection with this daring outrage. _

As—an illustration of the state of the country, it is worthy of notice that the county cess of the barony of Eliogartv, , county Tipperary, which was in arrelr at the spring assizes, is still unpaid with the exception of a sum of is. 10.:1. Au affidavit of this fact having been made by the eess collector, it was resolved by the Grand Jury to call a meeting of magistrates to appoint a barony constable to collect the money. The meeting was called and candidates were in- vited, but no one was found to undertake the post. The total amount due is £2,62G, and the Grand Jury have now issued an advertisement inviting "tenders" for the situation of collector as in the case of a contract.

OIITRAGE Il4r MEATH.—Near Athboy, county Meath, on Sunday, a pensioner named Magahy was shot. He hag served 20 years in the police, and is now in the employment of Mr. Flood, an extensive farmer. He was in the habit of giving dances in his house, which were largely resorted to, and he appeared to be not on the best terms with the police, but had probably incurred suspicion of gaining information by his dance assemblies and communicating with the authorities. He was sitting in the lodge on Sunday, reading the newspapers, with his two daughters and two young men, visitors, when three disguised men were seen to cross the road and come to the door. He went to meet them,. whereupon one of them fired a shot, wounding him danger- ously in the right shoulder. The three men decamped as they had come. I. The revival of outrage in Ireland within the last three days is matter for a regretful article in the Freeman's IJournal. The Freeman, the most advanccd of the respect- able portion of the Irish papers, remarks that these outrages are simply ruinous to he Irish cause. "Every crime com- mitted tends to paralyse the hands of the Irish party, to strengthen their opponents, and to defeat the strenuous efforts now being made to cut down some of the worst pro- visions of an oppressive measure. These dreadful open-day attacks, in which persons in a humble station of life are dragged tram their homes and maimed or tortured are a peril to the national prosperity and a disgrace to the national honour. No man's life is safe from the midnight tribunal which—on we know not what charge, supported by we know not what evidence—dooms poor human beings to mutilation or death. What we want is peace—not ally craven surrender, not any cessation from lawful agitation, but social peace and absence of outrages." AGITATION AMONG THE FARM LABOURERS OF IRELAND. —There is a revival in Ireland of the demand of the labourers for a Land Act for their benefit. A meeting called by the Labour League was held at Longford on Sunday,

_ the following resolutions were passed That we, the labourers of Longford, do now call on the farmers of the county to look to our interests by applying to the Govern- ment for a loan to build suitable cottages, together with half an acre of land of suitable quality." "That we now call on the Government to advance the loans for the building of cottages on the security of landlord and labourer, and to extend the time of payment at least over forty years, there- by making it easier for the occupier to pay." Similar reso- lutions were passed at meetinga held at Bruff, in Limerick, and at Ballivasloe. The selfishness of the farmers was warmly denounced, dnd the words of one of the speakers that "the farmer who does not give half an acre of land " —were interrupted by the shout " He's a dead man," a threat which elicited a "hear, hear."

_ AN IRISII LAND CORPORATION.—The Land Corporation of Ireland, Limited, having its offices at Westminster, has issued an appeal for capital7-£7so,ooo—which is accom- panied by a long statement on the conditicn of the country, and the remedy therefor, signed by Arthur Kavanagh, who proposes "that a Co-operative Association or Joint-stock Company should be formed for the purpose of dealing with farms from which tenants have been evicted, on account of their refusal to pay rents' at the instigation of the Land League, and which farms have been left waste or derelict by the action of the same body, and to enable the landlords, without loss to the company or association, to realise some return from them, and thus to hold out long enough to break down that illegal conspiracy." The Freeman's Journal (Dublin) regaris this new movement as an evinence that" we are on the eve of witnessing the appearance in the theatre of this distracted land of a new element of dis- order, danger, and dissension." The design is that the com- pany is to get possession of large tracts of land, to demand the old impossible rents, to clear out the people unable to pay these rents, and to stock the land with farmers from other countries. The scheme must, says the Freeman, fill with misgiving every lover of peace. We find among the subscribers to the company's capital Mr. Evelyn Ashley, M.P., the Mai quis of Bath, Mr. Maxwell Close, M.P., the Marquis of Ely, Earl Fitzwilliam, Earl Fortescue, the Maiquis of Headfort, Sir J. APG. Hogg, M.P., Lord Har- warden, the Marquis of Lansdowne, the Earl of Bosse, Mr. A. H. Smith-Barry, the Marquis of Waterford, and Sir Richard Wallace. The guaranteed capital, says a later statement, has been increased by £B,OOO, of which the Duke or Devonshire has subscribed £2,000 and the Duke of Aber- corn £l,OOO. The total now subscribed amounts to £128,000, and the original capital will probably be increased to £1,000,000. AN AGENT AND A BAILIFF SHOT DEAD.

An atrocious double murder of an agrarian nature was committed on Thursday morning about half a mile from Long!area, the victims being Mr. J. H. Blake, ,of Rathville, Kiltulla, Athenry, agent to the Marquis of Clauricarde, and his steward, Thady Keen. They were returning together with Mrs. Blake:on a ear from Naas, and when they reached the spot mentioned they were fired at from behind a wall, which had been loopholed for the purpose. Mr. Blake and Keen were both shot dead, but Mrs. Blake appears to have escaped unhurt. The murder had evidently been most care- fully planned, the circumstances attendiog it being similar to those which characterised the murder of Mr. Burke and the dragoon Wallace at Ardrahan. In eaah case a will had been loopholed to afford cover for the murderers, as the victiais in both cases were riding on a car. The police are stated to be in pursuit of the murderers. THE OPPOSITION TO MR. Davirr IN AMERICA. A New York afternoon paper reports that Michael Davitt said on Friday:—" I intend to answer once for all the charges brought against me. If repeated, I shall resign my position in the Land League and return to Ireland." Mr. Davitt, declared that he had worked in the interest of harmony, and was not promoting discord and disunion. He declared that Mr. O'Connor Power, M.P., was a traitor to the cause of Ireland. There was- no split or dissention in the League in Ireland, and no difference between Mr. Parnell and himself. The charges against him was false, and due to conspiracy. He once more threatened to resign if again called upon to defend himself against these false charges. With reference to the foregoing the Press Association is informed by Mr. O'Connor Power that he entirely repudiates any action justifying the language of Mr. Davitt, with whom he declines to enter into any controversy. He regrets that if Mr. Davitt had any charges to make against him they were not made before he left England, but adds that this is not the first time Mr. Davitt has attacked him from a distance. AGRARIAN MURDER NEAR TR ALEE. On Tuesday night a caretaker named Patrick Cahill, who was in charge of a boycotted farm at Ashilf, near Tralee, was shot dead, his body being found in a field early on Wed- nesday morning by a man named Nnis White. Deceased was over GG years of age. The scene of the murder is about five miles from Tralee, on the side of a barren mountain. The deceased was engaged in taking care of a farm from. which the tenant had been evicted, and which belongs to Mr. Sylvester Poff. The deceased's house is situate about a mile further up tha mountain, and it was while returning from the farm he was attacked. Four bullet wounds were found on his body. One was on the head, another in the back (the bullea passing the abdomen), a third in the chest, and a fourth was on the thumb of the left hand. Brosnan has been arrested. About -ten or twelve days ago deceased reported that he had baen fired at by Brosnan, who discharged three or four shots at him and then pursued him. Cahill afterwards refused to prosecute Brosnan, and it was thought that the story of the shooting was an inventien. The assas- sins made morecertain of their work this time.

div.head: ILLUSTRIOUS ' IRISIIIHN.
div.p: ILLUSTRIOUS ' IRISIIIHN.
BY WILLIAM FRANCIS.

XXVI.—DAN IE L O'CONN ELL. "So much I feel my genial spirits droop. My hopes all flat, Nature within me seems In all her functions weary of herself. My race of glory run, not race of shame, And I shall shortly be with those that rest." Milton's Agonistes. We have alreedy seen that from the beginning to the end of his career O'Connell had three great objects in view. He desired to emancipate his co-religionists of the Catholic faith and also the dissenting Protestants from the civil dis- abilities that oppressed and degraded them. In other words ha sought to win religious liberty for the vast majority of the Irish people and even for the minority of the English and Scetch. Ho aimed at uniting Irishmen of all races and religions into ore strong nation. But his greatest and noblest ambition was to regain the legislative independence of his country, to make Ireland a free naticn once azain. He succeeded in accomplishing the first of these objects, and this he did not by resorting to arms and overthrowing his opponents on the field, but by assembling his fellow countrymen in vast public meetings and bringing an im- mense pressure of public opinion td bear on the hostile Go- vernment and legislature. He met with but partial success Ire his endeavours to unite all the various jarring elements of the Irish nation. Bat in his efferts to achieve the third he failed completely. After a vast and imposing display of nenular gatherings and all the marvellous dominion which his transcendant abilities had given him over the popular mind the seeming might of the repeal movement gradually dwindled away, and at last the whole organisation dissolved Into thin air, while the aged chieftain broken alike in health and heart and power retired to a foreign land to die. The year 1846 found Ireland sitting under a black shadow. The potato crop, for the second time, had failed. Famine and pestilence were walking in the darkness and wasting at noonday. O'Connell's jests and familiar speech were for ever at an end. The most jovial of men now at length bowed his head in Conciliation Hall and wept. He was powerless in Dublin. He was powerless in London, His people died in thousands and in myriads, and numbers were buried without coffins. —Lord Brougham, in his high flown elassical way, deecribed the horrors of the famine "as sur- passing anything in the page of Thucvdidee, on the canvas of Pnassin, in the dismal chant of Dante." The "nn- crowned• king" became weak in body, and his buoyant spirits deserted him. In 1847 and amidst the deepest gloom and horror of the famine O'Connell, old, sick, and heavy Fallen, left Ireland, and left it for ever. He ctme to London. Weak and prostrate in health, he attended for the last time that Legislature which he bad so triumphantly entered. In a speech of simple and touching eloquence, entirely free from every tinge of his ancient violence, he showed the fearful magnitnde of the calamity impending over the coun- try, suggested his remedies, and with a solemn and heart- felt pathos implored the generous aid of Parliament, but his voice was so faint that but few could catch his words. The fearful change impressed all who saw him. Old rancour , and party spirit were forgotten in so great a sorrow. He ' was listened to with almost reverential silence. His old , antagonist, Disraeli, in his "Life of Lord George Bentinck," has given us a touching picture of this, the Liberator's last appearance in the Meese of Commons. Physicians in Lon- don recommended a journey to the South of Europe, and O'Connell himself desired to see the Pope before he died, and to breathe out his soul at Rome in the choicest odour of sanctity. By slow and painful stages he proceeded towards! the city of the Pontiff. As be passed through Paris he ! received a visit from the illustrious advocate Berryer, to ; whom he said: "I cannot refuse myself the pleasure of pressing your hand." But he was unable to converse. To ; a Catholic eociety, headed by Montalambert, the talented ; author of "The Monks of the West," he said in French: "Sickness and emotion close my lips. I should require the eloquence of your President to express to you all my grati- tude." He pissed on to Lyons, where he was much wow. " He seemed," said one who visited him there, "to be a con- I tinual °rev to sad reflections His face had grown thin, and his lock proclaimed inexpressible sadness; his head hung noon the breast, and the entire person of the invalid, formerly so imposing, was greatly weighed down." One more stage and his strength failed him. His wanderings , ceased at "Genoa the Proud." At three o'clock in the after- noon of the 15th of May, 1847, he called his valet and thanked him for his faithful services. That evening he breathed his last in the seventy-second year of his age. He ' had vainly desired to live until he could reach Rome and! redeive the Pontiff's blessing. The Eternal City is the capital, the shrine, the Mecca of the Church to which, O'Connell was undoubtedly devoted with all his heart, and , he desired to close his stormy career there. He had longed to lie down in the shadow of the dome of St. Peter's and rest there, arid there die. But it was not to be. However, while he bequeathed his body to Ireland, he bequeathed his heart to Rome. The former rests in the Cemetery of Gies- nevin, in the vicinity of Dublin, and the spot is marked by a round tower which was ereeted in his memory; the latter near the tomb of Lascaris, in the Ctturch of Sr. Agatha, at Rome.

During his lifetime O'Connell declared that he was "the best abused man in Britain," and even after his death he has I Ibeen the object of unnecessary and malignant attack. The historian has magnified his defects and minimised his merits. One is somewhat startled in reading the strictures of liar-Jet Martineau upon O'Connell. No one can deny to ; Miss Martineau the possession of broad and liberal views, yet her strictures upon cur hero are bated upon what a humorous writer has called the "fiend in human shape theory." The lady not merely assumes that O'Connell was absolutely insincere and untrustworthy, but discourses of him on the assumption that he was knowingly and purposely a villain. Not cle's she hold that the Reel Agita- tion wee An unqualified evil for his country, and that Repeal, !! galnei, would have been the curse of it, but she insists that O'Connell himself was thoroughly convinced. of the fncts. She holds that with O'Connell it wee simply a ques- tion of pounds, shillings, and pence—that he enriched him- self at the expense of the poor and foolish people, who almost worshipped him. "He never," says this lady critic, "kept his eye off the money boxes which supplied his an- nual income from the scrapings of the earnings of the poor." Now, there could be no reasonable objection to O'Connell being supported by his country. There was every reason why he should be and why he should not. He had a large family, and was sure to rise to great eminence in his profes- sion if he had devoted himself to it as professional men necally do. If, because he was the man to redeem the Irish cause, he was withdrawn from his profession and its emolu- ments, it was merely just that he should be compensated by I the Irish people. And it is a matter of fact that be gave ; up a splendid practice at the bar to carry on the agitation ; that he lost by the agitation, pecuniarly, far more than he ' ever got by it; and that he died poor, leaving his sons poor. On one occasion, at the residence of Sir Robert Peel, an• animated discussion took place between George Stephenson ; and Dr. BaCklarui. on one of Stephenson's favourite theories as to the formation of COal. But the 'result ; Was that Dr. Buckland, a much greater master of tonene- fence than Mr. Stephenson, cumpley. silenced fiinid Next morning, before breakfast! when Stephenson was walking in the grounfle, deeply pondering, Sir Wil- Ham Foliet eadie up and asked what he WU thinking' about. "Why, Sir William, lam thinking over that arga- ' went I had with litickland last night. I know I am right, and that if Only I had the command of words which he has I'd have beaten him." "Let me know all about it," said Sir " and I'll see what rcan do for you." The two sat 'down in an arbour, and the attutri lawyer made himself thoroughly acquainted with the points of the case, entering , Into it with all the zeal of an advocate about to plead the dearest interest of his client. After he had mastered the ; subject, Sir William rose up, rubbing his hands with glee, and said, "Now lam ready for him." Sir Robert Peel was made acquainted with the fact, and adroitly introduced the subject of the controversy after dinner. The result was that in the argument which followed the man of science was overcome by the man of law, and Sir William Follet had at all points the mastery over Dr. Buckland. "What do you say now, Mr. Stephenson," asked Sir Robert laughing. "Why," said he "I will only say that all the powers above and under the earth, there seems to be no power so great as the gz.ft of the gab." And that is one of the conclusions we arrive at as we study the life and work of O'Connell. O'Connell's power lay in his tongue. It was by that instrument he accom- plished his noblest achievements. " Never,"saye an eloquent French writer, " in any age or: country, has any man ob- tained over his nation an empire so sovereign, so absolute, so entire. Ireland impersonates herself in O'Connell. He is in some sort, himself alone, her army, her Parliament, her ambassador, her prince, her liberator, her apostle, her god. His ancestors, descendants of the Kings of Ireland, wore at

div.head: SEIZURE OF ARMS IN CLERKENWELL.
div.p: THE SEIZURE OF ARMS IN CLERKENWELL.

EXAMINATION OF THE PRISONER WALSH. On Tuesday, before the usual hour for commencing busi- ness at the Clerkenwell Police Court, a large number of persons assembled in front of the court anxious to gain ad- mission to hear the proceedings in the case of Thomas Walsh, aged 33, described as a carpet planner, and giving his address at 12, Charles-street, Hatton-garden. They, I however, were doomed to be disappointed, for late on Mon- day night tte Home Secretary decided that, as the case was. lone of so much importance, it should be heard by the chief magistrate, Sir James Ingham, at Bow-street, where the prisoner was removed in the ordinary course from her Majesty's House of Detention, Clerkenwell. Walsh was subsequently brought up at Bow-street before Sir James Im.,,hatn, the chief magistrate, who took his seat at a quartet-past one. The charge agaittlst the prisoner is for feloniously receiving and fraudulently dealing with certain rifles, bayonets, and other firearms, believed to be the pro- perty of her Majesty's Government, since the 6th of April, 1882, at OD, St. John's-street-road, in the parish of Clerken- well. In consequence of certain threatening letters having I been received, extra constables were placed on duty both inside and outside the court. On the route from the House of Detention special constables were also posted, and six men rode on the van conveyine• the prisoner to the court. Mr. Poland, instructed by 'Mr. Pollard,• solicitor to the Treasury, appeared for the prosecution ; and Mr. S. B. Abrahams, solicitor, appeared for the prisoner. Mr. Abrahams, before the proceedings commenced, corn- plained of the tone which Lad been taken by several of the ;leading journals in reference to the case, and said that as ! the prisoner was only now under examination it was unfair to him to state what societies he might or might not have been coanected with, as, of course, he might have to go on for trirl before a jury. He thcught the information must have been supplied by the police, and hoped that in future such information would not be supplied. Sir James Ingham said he was able to inform the learned advocate that he had not read a single word of the case, and was therefore entirely unprejudiced in the matter. Mr. Poland ten said that he did not think it necessary 1 to make any long opening statement, but he might say that it was his intention to ask the magistrate when the pre- liminary inquiry was concluded to commit the prisoner for trial under the act known as the Treason Felony Act, which included a sentence of transportation for life. He should endeavour to show that the prisoner had been engaged in a conspiracy of a treasonable character, and that he procured arms which it was intended to send secretly to Ireland for , treasonable purposes. The learned counsel then detailed the facts of the case as they have already been related, and added that the prisoner had been known to the police as a man who had previously sent consignments of arms secretly to Ireland. He took a placc at Homerton in October last, saying he was a dealer in lacquer ware, and the same thing went on as at St. John's-street-road until February, when he left. Of course it would not do for him to remain in one place for any lengthened period for fear of causing suspicion, and therefore they should now be able to trace the prisoner at several places. He observed also that he had sent arms secretly to Ireland in the name of a false consignee and a false consigner, the arms being addressed to persons in the counties of Tip- perary and Limerick. Some of the cases were addressed to clergymen and ladies, and they were opened in London and found to contain arms and ammunition. They were for- warded, however, after being resealed, and a great many of them found their way into the hands of the police in Ire- lend, the persons who were actually instructed to call for them fearing to do so. He should be able to prove the pur- chase of arms by prisoner, and be believed the evidence would overwhelmingly prove that the prisoner had sent the arms to Ireland with a treasonable intention. He be- lieved the prisoner had sent arms to Ireland for many years, while the offence with which he was now charged had taken place since 1881, when the Peace Preservation Act came into operation. His charge AM that this man bad been guilty of an overt act, and that his offence was nothing more nor less ' than that of treason-felony.

The evidence of Mr. Schoof, who let the stable at Clerken- well to the prisoner, as given at the last examination, was repeated, and the nature of it has already been published. . The case was ultimately adjourned till next Monday. The police have succeeded in tracing in Ireland some of the arms sent there for distribution by Walsh. They were received by secret societies. Walsh stored the arms at four different places in North London. A patent shell cartridge block has also been found in possession of the plisoner, which, being placed in the breech of the Snider rifle, enables the user of it to discharge small bullets similar to those em- ployed in rook-shooting rifles. The bullets are about the size of an ordinary pea, and are in brass cases containing fulminate. By this means rifle practice can be carried on co as to attract little attention, the sound of the discharge being very slight, although at the same time the bullet is discharged with sufficient force to kill a man at 20 yards distance. The Press Association is informed that some im- portant links.in the evidence against Walsh have been dis- covered in connection with the recent seizure of arms. The inquiries are not yet absolutely complete,but it may be men- tioned that the east end of London is now being very care- fully watched.

A number of-the miscreants who'murdered and outraged Jews and Jewesses at Balta, in Southern Russia, have been found guilty by a district court. One of the gang, who had inflicted " mortal injuries" on a Jew—in plain English, ' murdered him—was sent to prison for 33 months. Another, who had outraged a young girl, was sent to prison for four years. The public, we are told, received these sentences with " much satisfaction," as no doubt also did the crirni- mils, who in any other country would have been hanged or sent to prison for life. The Russian police have ,made a considerable number of important arrests in St. Petersburg, Moscow, Kieff, and Odessa, of persons known to be revolutionists. Sevdral military men are among the prisoners, and it is feared that a considerable leaven of Nihilism exists in the marine forces of the artillery. A Vienna telegram says that immediately after the Imperial Family left Gatschina for Peterhof a mine was discovered under their apartments. It is said to have been dug by the son of one of the palace officials.

The Wrexham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway Bill WAS mad a third time and passed. The Entail (Scotland) Bill was committed pro forma in order that it miglit be printed with the amendments. The Lunacy Districts (Scot- Lind) Bill was read a third tim-! and passed.—ln ply to Lod de L'lsle and Dudley, Earl GRANVILLE said the Government had information of Arabi Pasha having been decorated by the Sultan, but had received no information that he had also received a letter from the Sultan approving his conduct in the crisis in Egypt. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THVIISDLY,

THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.—In the House of Commons Sir C. DILKE stated that it was not thought desirable to publish the substance of Sir E. MALET's telegram suggest- ing the desirability of Turkish co-operation, which had been communicated to the French Government.—Mr. CAMPBELL- BANNERMAN, who was questioned as to the preparations in the dockyards, stated that the Orontes was taking out a strong draft of marines to reinforce the fleet in the Mediter- ranean, but that no additional expenditure had been in- curred.—The UNDER-SECRETARY informed Mr. Gibson that Earl Granville had taken steps to remove the misapprehen- sion under which the French Government appeared to labour with respect to the conversation between the noble Earl and M. Challemel - Lacoun Mr. 11. RICHARD desired to know if, before the Government used force in Egypt, the House would have an opportunity , of considering the subject, to which Mr. GLADSTONE replied I that he did not expect any change from the course hitherto I pursued, hut he could give no pledge, as it might be the duty of the Government to assume responsibility of action for themselves, and to submit their conduct to the judgment of the House afterwards.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON stated that in the interests of the public service he must decline to give any answer to the question whether prepara- tions were in progress in India for bringing Indian troops to Egypt. -SPANISH WINE DUTlES.—Referring to our negotiations with the Spanish Government on the subject of the duties on wines, the PRIME MINISTER stated that the Governm9nt had been compellee:to signify to the Spanish Government that the finance of this country did not admit of any re- duction at the present time, but that they would not be un- willing to approach the question under more favourable conditions of finance.—The House again went into commit- tee on the Prevention of Crime Bill, and considered the com- pensation and retrospective clauses.

CONTINUED FLIGHT OF EUROPEANS. THE CONFERENCE. WAR PREPARATIONS BY ENGLAND. Reports from Alexandria show that large numbers of British subjects have been and are being forwarded to Malta, where they arrive in a state of complete destitution, and completely dependent on the Government. All necessaries have been found for them. Ourabi Pasha has entreated the Europeans not to leave the country, but the value of the protection he is able or willing to afforde,them is shown by an incident related by the Times correspondent. Two years ago Mr. Cotterill, consulting engineer of an irrigation com- pany, was summoned before the international tribunals by three Saidi fellaheen for an alleged debt. The verdict was in favour of the defendant, and the fellaheen were con- demned in costs. The other day they appeared in Alexan- dria, sought out Mr. Cotterill, and demanded payment of their claim, threatening him with death if he refused. They declined to leave his side, even mounting into his carriage. Mr. Cotterill went to the British Con- sulate. Mr. R. T. Bourke, barrister, of Rat,hfarnham, Dublin, has received a letter from his sister relative to the murder cf her husband, Dr. H. P. Ribton, in the recent massacre at Alexandria. Dr. Ribton was the only surviving child of Dr. G. RU don, bton who is brother to the late Sir John and uncle to the present baronet. The letter from the bereaved widow is as follows :—" Alexandria, June 15. They have mur- dered my husband, and I am alone in the world, the only friends we had being killed with him. I know not what to do. All are flying, but where are we to fly to My poor child saw her darling father killed, and was only saved her- self by the mighty arm of God, being carried into a harem, where they kept her till late at night, and then brought her home to me in disguise. May God remember them in the last day. Oh, what my poor child has gone through, and tile blows the brutescgave her! Ido not know how she is alive. I only learned yesterday that my darling was dead. I hoped against hope that he might have been taken to some hospital, and so he was, but thrown naked on the ground and so mutilated that no one could know him. Oh, what will the English Government have to answer for at the last day ! Good bye. This may be the last line you may ever have from me. If I get to a place of safety I will surely Write. Meet me in our Saviour's Kingdom.—Your heart- broken sister, A. R."

The troopships destined to convey re- liefs to Malta will arrive there some time after the greater part of its garrison has left in the ships of the Channel Fleet. They will at once land the reliefs brought. out from home, and will emb irk the remainder of the garri- son, as well as additional material, and will continue their journey to Alexandria. The reason for this shifting of gar- risons, the correspondent points out, is a good and simple one. The men garrisoning Gibraltar and Malta are already seasoned to the climate of the Mediterranean and its heat, while troops fresh from England are not. It is therefore thought advisable to allow the regiments sent from home to become acclimatised at Gibraltar and Malta before moving them a stage further east. Moreover, by this mode of pro- cedure the Government would be enabled to order it force of at least from 12,000 to 15,000 men being landed at Alexan- dria within a fortnight. The correspondent adds that the 3rd battalion of the Grenadier Guards, now quartered at Chelsea Harracks the Ist battalion of the Scots Guards, quartered in Wellington Barracks; and several regiments of the line, besides cavalry and artillery, engineers and comis- sariat, have been detailed for service in the. Mediterranean to relieve the garrisons of Malta and Gibraltar. Sir Evelyn Wood, V.C., has been ordered to hold himself in readiness to proceed to. Egypt, via Brindisi, at a moment's notice. ZULULAND. A correspondent of the Daily News, telegraphing from Maritzhurg, says he has been specially asked to warn the public against exaggerated 'reports with-regard to Zululand. Though the position is critical in Zululand itself, no dis- turbances have taken place within seventy miles of the Natal. frontier, which is perfectly quiet, and no alarm what- ever is felt in the colony itself. The correspondent adds that there is nothing further from the British Resident in Zululand, which, under the circumstances, is favourabld to the prospects of peace. CETYWAYO'S VISIT TO ENGLAND. A Maritzhurg telegram says :—lt is officially announced here from Cape Town that Cetywayo is to proceed to Eng- land at once. Mr. Shepstone leaves here next Saturday for Cape Town to accompany the ex-King. Two chiefs go with him. It is universally believed that this is only a step to- , wtrds the restoration of Cetywayo in Zululand. There is no fresh news from the Zulu country. It is stated that the necessary arrangements for the in- tended visit of Cetewayo to this country have been left entirely in the hands of the South African authorities. It is understood that the Zulu King will sail in the course of a week or two for England. The passage for him will be taken by one of the mail steamers, and he will be accom- panied on the trip by several Zulu chiefs and two or three of his wives. The StandaPd says :—lt is expected that Cetywayo will arrive in England towards the latter part of July. His visit will extend over a month or five weeks, and during his stay he will be placed under the charge of two officers of the English Government. It is now generally understood among the supporters of the Government that he will, on leaving England, be allowed to return to Zululand.

- _ The long-lookeA for "garden party " promoted by the British calico printers was held at the gardens at OM Traff n-d on Satuiday, and was in every respect markedly successful. The dead bodies of Sofia Kopuski, the wife of a Polish Jew, and her child Antonio, aged five, were discovered on Tuesday in a. workshop in . the rear of their residence at Vi'hitechapel, poisoned oy cyanide of potassitrn. Mr. May, solicitor, one of the imprirone I Macclesfiald brib us. resumed his duties on Tuesday as clerk to the Mac- clesfield Guardians. The chairman congratulated him on his release, and expressed a hope that he might long con- tinue in office. A fashionably dressed lady, giving the name of Melia Bankes, "just arrived from France," and sometimes "a countess," was on Saturday committed for trial by the magistrates at Bettws-y-Coed for swindling hotel proprietors at that interesting resort of excursioßists. The experimental operations of the Channel Tunnel at Dover are still progressing, and the total length of the head- ing, it is stated, now exceeds a distance of 2,000 yards, with a very gradual seaward incline. Night and day gangs are , employed, but the boring operations are only conducted I during the day. According to a parliamentary return just issued, there were 302 cases in which flogging formed part of the sen- tence for otTences under the Act 26 and 27 Vict., cap. 44, during the period between the 13th July, 1863, and the end of lastyear. The number of cases in which the same offender has been found guilty of similar offences, and be- come liable to be reflogged was five. 'PANIC IN A. CHURCH AT ORMSKIRK.—During the ser- vice on Sunday in the parish church of Ormskirk, near Liverpool, a thunderstorm broke, and as the vicar was pro- nouncing the benediction a report was heard resembling heavy cannon, axd what seemed to be a ball of fire passed through the edifice. A cry of fire was raised, and a panic ensued, which was with difficulty allayed. Subsequent examination showed that the . stonework of the steeple had been damaged. The House of Keys, the representative branch of the Manx Legislature, met on Tuesday. A report was presented by a committee upon the proposed expenditure at the lunatic asylum. The committee reported adversely to the expenditure recommended by the general committee of the institution. The report was unanimously adopted. Mr. Cowell introduced a bill for the purpose of abolishing the property qualification of members of the Keys. FATAL DYNAMITE EXPLOSION.—A fatal dynamite ex- plosion occurred in the Cam n Brea Mines, near Redruth, on Tuesday morning. The men in charge of the boring machine bad with them in the mine a box containing five packets of dynamite and one packet of caps. From some at present un- explained cause, .the dynamite exploded, killing Albert Cocking, of Leaner, cud Joaaph Jeffrey, a lad, of Mogan, instantaneously. William Paull, of Mogan, and George Jeffrey, brother of the lad killed, were severely injured in the back, legs, and arms. Paull also appears to have sus- tained some internal injuries. Both the injured men were conveyed to the Miners' Hospital, Redruth, where they were attended to by the mines surgeon. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL AND WORKING MEN—On Satur- day evening a numerously-attended meeting of representative working men was held in the lerge room of the St. John's Head Tavern, Soutfiwark-st., London, to discuss the question of the construction of the Channel Tunnel. Mr. Thomas Mottershead (Patriotic Club) moved a resolution to the fol- lowing effect :—" That, the construction of the Channel Tunnel being of the highest importance to the industrial interests both of England and France, and calculated to foster international friendship amongst the workers of both countries, this meeting resolves to do everything in its power in support of the same." The motion was unani- mously adopted. SUICIDE BY HAN9ING IN CARNARVON GAOL.—On Mon- day morning, a hawker, named William Davies, was found dead in a cell attached to the Carnarvon Gaol, deuased having committed suicide by banging himself. It appears that the man was locked up on Saturday night on a charge of having stolen some hens, and was to have been tried this morning at fife Borough Police-court. Dec( ased, it seems, made a knot in his braces and tied one end around his neck, making the other end fast to one of the iron bars in the cell, and in this manner strangled himself. The act was dis- covered by a police-constable, who went to the cell for the purpose of conveying the man to court, but at that time the deceased was quite dead and the body perfectly cold. CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED MURDER NEAR CARLISLE.—A man named Joseph Bell was on Saturday brought before the county magistrates at Carlisle charged with being the person " .n.orna_ mac int o a house at Dals- who threw the Inc ton, near Carlisle, on Tuesday morning, the 20th inst. Ie was arrested at Whitehaven on board a steamer. The Superintendent of police asked for a remand for a week. He said the prisoner was charged with attempting to murder John Bell and Elizabethßell with dynamite or other missile, and the evidence was strong in support of the charge. It will be remembered that the "infernal machine" was thrown into the house of people called Brown, and that one of the inm.toe had the presence of mind to throw it over the stairs before it exploded. The theory of the prosecution is that the prisoner intended to murder John Bell and Elizabeth Bell, and mistook the Browns' house for his brother's, which is next door. The prisonea was remanded. TEE SALVATION Anam—Mr. Wm. Booth, the head of the Salvation Army, writes to say that they have secured the lease of the Eagle Tavern, in City-road, T.ondon, in- cluding the Grecian Theatre, dancing pavilion and grounds, dancing saloan, and assembly rooms, capable of seating in all 10,000 people. Standing amidst a dense working-class population, and with a character far and wide such as makes it unnecessary to describe the scenes nightly to be witnessed there, the building, he adds, will give them rin opportunity far superior to any they have hitherto had of gathering tens of thousands of the worst of the people together to hear about salvation. The Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of London, Earl Cairns, the ex-Lord Mayor, and others of influence have expressed their warm sympathy. The Arch- bishop of Canterbury has also sent a contribution to help them.

The mess of the officers of the 15th Regiment, stationed at Aldershot, was totally destroyed by fire on Wednesday night, cnly the plate being saved. The origin of the fire is unknown. The Three Choirs festival is arranged to take place at Hereford on the 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th September. Mesaames Albani- and Patey, with Mr. Lloyd and Mr. Santley, will be the principal vocalists. The returns of the metropolitan pauperism issued yester- day shows that during the second week in June there were 48,659 indoor and 38,413 outdoor paupers relieved, making a total of 87,070, against 86.645 in the corresponding week of last year, 85,050 in 1880, and 81,492 in 1872. The number of vagrants relieved during the week was 754. Three hundred men and boys were imprisoned on Monday evening at the fence pit of the RothervaleColliery Company, Woodhouse Mill, near Sheffield, owing to the rope attached to the loaded chair snapping and closing up the shaft. Pro- visions were passed down to the men, whose rescue was effected on Tuesday by means of the cupola shaft. No per- sonal injuries were sustained. The Fitiheit is not issued this week, but a printed sheet without an imprint is circulated among its sub§cribers, headed "Our Situation." The article discusses at some length the condition of the extreme section of the Social Democrats, both in this country and elsewhere. It con- cludes:by saying the revolutionists must advance, and that the Freilteit in the future will be bolder and sharper than ever in the death-struggle entered upon between the Proletariat and their foes. THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH: NARROW ESCAPE.—A sen- sational account is given of a narrow escape of the Duke of Edinburgh from death by drowning. When fishing at a place near Corunua he hooked a large fish, and then, slip- ping his foot, fell into the water, and was carried into a weir sixteen feet deep. He disappeared four times under the water, but after half an hour's immersion was .fortunately rescued from his perilous position, and at Once went on board his ship. THE FULHAM MURDER.—At the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, Mr. Besley, who was instructed with Mr. Avery to defend the prisoner Richard Wells, applied to Mr. Justice Denman to postpone the trial to the next sessions. He said the case was of a very complicated character, and it was very important for the prisoner that certain inquiries should be made, and no sufficient time had been allowed for that purpose. Mr. Poland, who was instructed with Mr. Mon- tagu Williams on behalf of the prosecution, said he would not oppose the applicaticn, and the trial consequently stands adjourned to the July sessions. FENIAN ArAnet.—:A letter of a threatening character has recently been communicated to the authorities at the Times office in Printing House Square, London. It is rumoured that the document emanates from an association in connec- tion with the Feniane, and that it contains threats to the effect that the premises will be attacked. There are no armed constables posted inside the Times office, and the police authorities say that if any armed men have been placed in the building to protect the property they have been privately engaged, and do not belong to the regular force. EMBEZZLEMENT.—A painful charge of embezzlement was before Mr. Raffles, stipendiary of Liverpool, on Monday, the accused b&ng Charles Barker Wood, lately superinten dent of the United States Cattle Company in Liverpool, at , a salary of £324 per annum. Evidence was only offered respecting two missing sums of £3O 10s 7d and £64 13s 3d, but it was stated that the total defalcations amounted to £4f1.0. On behalf of the prisoner, it was stated that domestic affliftion was the sole cause of his conduct. Mr. Raffles remarked that it must not go out to the public that he could deal summarily with a case which involved so much money, and Wood was committed to the sessions for trial. SOMETHING Wotan NonerG.—Mr. Perronet Thompson, at the County Court, Liverpool, on Monday, in giving judgment in an action brought by the _Rev. James Kelly against his solicitor, Mr. Quilliam, and a cross action by Mr Quilliam against Mr. Kelly, let fall a remark which all persons having dealings with solicitors should be cognisant of. Mr. Kelly sued Mr. Quilliam for damages for neglect and for retaining a document which Mr. Kelly wished to have himself, but he failed to make out his case, and Mr. Thompson, in giving judgment,remarked that Mr. Quilliam was simply doing his duty in retaining possession of the deed until his bill was paid, adding that, as a solicitor, he had a right to keep any papers which came into his posses- sion in the course of his employment. This, no doubt, was news for Mr. Kelly, as it will be for many others besides. . RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR PETERBOROUGH.—A serious accident occurred on Monday night a few miles to the north , of Peterborough to the Great Northern Scotch express as it was passing Werrington Junction at about 50 miles an honr. The tve rod of the engine broke, throwing the whole train off the line. Several carriages were thrown down the embankment, while the engine parted company, and was not palled up for some distance down the line.
