div.head: TORPEDOS IN THE SUEZ CANAL.
div.p: TORPEDOS IN THE SUEZ CANAL.

The Suez Canal officials are taking great precautions to guard against tampering with the Canal, as there are rumours of torpedoes having been laid down, but no proof is forthcoming. Still it is very difficult to protect the whole length, ninety-nine statute miles. There are some suspicious- looking native craft at Ismailia, which are being watched day and night. 30,000 ARABS STARVING. A Daily News Alexandria telegram says :—The Presi- dent of the Council is very anxious about the large number of foodless Arabs, already estimated at 30,000, in Alexan- dria. A special Council of Ministers has beed called to consider their case. .

div.head: TURKISEI HOSTILITY TO THE CONFERENCE.
div.p: TURKISEI HOSTILITY TO THE CONFERENCE.

A telegram from Constantinople on Thursday, says The Ambassadors of the Powers are still endeavouritag to make the Porte understand that the principal object of their mission is to treat with the Ottoman Government upon the measures to be adopted for the re-establishment of order and security in Egypt. If the Porte persists in its refusal to negotiate, the Ambassadors will be under the necessity of recommending their respective Governments to come to an understanding between themselves concerning the measures to be taken.

div.p: The anniversary of the Queen's coronation was celebrated at Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Wednesdly, with much rejoic- ing,.

sBarnnel Ashby, who plehdcd guilty on a former occasion to writing a threatening letter to the Mayor of Lewes, was sentenced at the 0!(1 BAiley, on Thursday, to six months' im prison ni-u t. ' At the Central Ciiminal Court, on Thursday, Timothy Sullivan was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for the manslaUghter of his wife in East London, by throwing a piece of iron at her.
At a meeting I=eld at Beighton, on Wednesday night, it was decided to prosecute the Lancet for libel in an article alleg- ing unhealthiness at Brighton. A guarantee fund of £4,000 was subscribed.

On Thursday morning the Preston Town Council ap- pointed Dr.Pilkington, of Pr, ston, medical officer of health for the lin-ough at a salary of £450 per annum, he to devote the whole of his time to the duties. There is a probability of penny tram stages being ob- tained in Oldham, not only on the proposed new:line from Rochdale but on the line teasel by the Manchester aarriage Company. The question is to come-befmre the CorporAion, and it is believed the concession as to advertisements will be made, and that thus penny stages will be secured. John M'Cayseland, a small farmer of Ballyclare and a cooper of Belfast, was murdered on Wednesday night at Ballynashee. He was attacked by two men who split his skull with a scythe. His servant was severely injured... 7' A farmer named M'Gury has been arrested. On Wednesday night, as a portion of the Salvation Army was marching down George-street, Oldham, from the Parish - Church, it was set upon by a gang of roughs, who threw stones and broke the ranks. A man named Jackson was struck on the shoulder with a brick. Miss Jackson, the captain, was also hit rather severely, and another had his. face cut. The attack seemed to have been organised. At Accrington on Thursday morning, John Whittaker, a ' • militaman, was committed to prison for three months with hard labour for neglecting his wife and family. The reliev- ing officer stated that the wife had been shamefullv • ne,r_4lected about the time of her confinement, and in all probability would have died but for the kindness of the neighbours.
rt..l

On Thursday afternoon an inquest was held at Darlastop respccting the death of a boy named Joseph Johnson. who was drowned whilst bathing. It was shown that deco was seized with cramp, and sunk to the bottom. Two "...t boys, aged thirteen, who witnessed the occurrence, jumped into the 'eater to save him, but they had a narrow escape. Johnson was drowned. The jury returned a verdict of acei- dental death. On Wednesday night, Lance-Corporal Madden, of the' - Bth (Liverpool) hegiment, was drowned while bathing with several companions in the sea rear Fleetwood. Two officers f•-j of the 103rd (Dublin Fusiliers) swam to the drowning man's ; ',- assistance, but owing to the strength of the current they failed to rescue him, and the body was found by a regimen- tal search party on Thursday morning. tr At the Wednesbury Police Court, on Thursday. Edr ard umpage, a notorious prize-fighter, was charged with - violently assaulting a police-constable. -The prisoner was wanted for committing a felony, and at midnight a police- man named Patton met the accused, and upon taking him into custody the prisoner att,nripted to strangle the officer.' ;a A desperate struggle followed, and the policeman and prisoner weee badly injured. The prisoner, who was taken to the police station by civilians, was sentenced to sx months' .imprisonment. _

On Thursday, John Sidney Pugh, manager for Messrs. Ovenden Brothers and Co., tobicco brokers, of Liverpool and London, was comitted for trial, charged with stealing 1 200Ibs. of toh3cco, a cheque for .£215, and .£77 in cash. The cheque was sent by Messrs. Hibblethwatte, Leeds, in payment of a:count, and the cash was taken from the office, in the absence of the cashier. The tob,mcn was sold and not accounted for. The prisoner said 1 e lost the money at Chester Races.

At the Bury Police Court, on Thursday, Thomas Greeri halgh was charged with steadin. £2OO from his father. The prisoner took thq money in bank notes from a box and went to Liverpool. He was apprehended on board the City of Montreal in the Mersey. He ha el £lBO upon him; tlit • remainer be had spent in passage money to America and outfit and in horse riding at New Brighten. He was eomrn mitted for trial.

AGITATION TO REMOVE A COUNTY COURT JUDGE.—TII6 decisions of Judge Woodforde, of the Derbyshire County Court, have given so much dissatisfaction to tradesmen and others interested that a petition has ben presented to the • e Lord Chancellor prayin.e for his removal. It is twenty-six yards long, and contains 10,000 signatures of tradesmen in .`• Nottingham, Sheffield, Derby, Chesterfield, Burton, Relpers,o Ilkeston, Wirksworth, Ash bourne, Alfraon, Clay Cross, Chaper-en-le-Frith, and other districts A list of cases in which his honour=ss decisions are impugned accompanies thte petit ion. Tern PARCELS Pos-r —The terms arranged between the postal authorities and railway companies for the new system of parcels post are as follows :—Parcels not exceeding 11b., 3d.; not exceeding 311)5., ; not exceeding slbs., 95: not exceeding 711)8., is. The division will be 55 per cent, to railway companies and 45 per cent. to the Post Office. The Post Office is to take the whole of the receipts on parcels not conveyed by railway, receipts for the present book par- cels to be included. It is proposed that the agreement shall continue for a p eriod of not less than twenty-one years., These terms now only await the confirmation of the ' Treasury. At Birmingham, on Thursday, a sailor named Rainbow was charged -with cau,ing the death of William Saviger, eight years of age. On Wednesday night the prisoner in- duced the deceased to go into the canal by promising to teach bim swimming, and carried him into the middle upon his back. The prisoner then pretended he could not swim himself, and throwing the youngster off got across to the uppocille bank. The boy immediately sank, and although the crowd near the spot called upon the sailor to save him he declined to do so. baviger satire tne tnirra time without any effort being made to get him out, and his body has not yet been recovered. His companions set upon the prisoner for his cowardice, knocked him down, and kicked him, while a constable was being fetched, when they gave him into , custody. The prisoner was remanded. FOURTEEN PEnsoNs DROWNED.—A Berwick-upon-Tweed correspondent telegraphs that on Thursday afternoon a message was received by the coastguard stating that the steam tug Alice, from Newcastle, with a number of excur- sionists on board,struck OR the Bondicar Rocks, near Amble, 30 miles south of Berwick, and seeeral passengers were drowned.—A Newcastle correspondent says it appears that 14 lives have been lost by the foundering of the Alice which left the Tyne for Workworth yesterday morning with over .. 100 passengers. The steamer struck on the rock about a quarter of a mile to the south of Coquet Island. Immediately ehe showed signs of foundering the lifeboat was seized, and by an accident one of the ropes was cut, the result being that the passengers were thrown into the sea and 14 were drowned, the remainder being rescued by a local boat. The Alice drifted and grounded on the roclzs. THE BAXTERLEY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—The coroner's , inquiry into the terrible accident at the Baxterley Colliery, in Warwickshire—an explosion resulting from a fire among the coal—was concluded on Thursday. The persons re- see, specting whom this inquiry was heel formed an exploring ' party which descended the pit to t-y and extr3cate nine or ten men from whem the fire had cut off all means of escape, and whose bodies are still in tee workings. The evidence was very remarkable. It appeared that the coal - caught fire soon after a pumping engine was placed in the , pit, which was 10 days before the explosion. The end of s the-funnel attached to the engine was not more than 2ft. from the coal, and one witness had "seen the flames from - . the funnel playing on the coal." "'1 he coal was red-hot . when the engine was playing !" The engine-driver said the coal was on fire the first time he went to the engine. The ~ consulting engineerat the colliery had advised the placing e of brickwork around the engine, but the manager (one of : the deceased) had not carried out the suggestion. The fate .se of the exploring party was not a natural result of the fire, e and the jury could not attach any criminal responsibility to anyone in respect to these aeaths. They passed some cen- ereel sure, however, on some of the pit arrangements. TILE CAREER OF AN ADVENTURESS. At Devon quarter sessions at Exeter, on Wednesday, Annie Hastings Snell, aged 39, alias • Annie Cheetham, was indicted on several exi.. charges of fraud. This was the case in which the prisoner answered the advertisement of a e ;dower at Torquay for a aese housekeeper, and by representing herself as havingcome into see property worth several thousands, induced Snell, the .s widower, to marry her, and akerwards contracted debts to the amount of £7OO, ran away, and left the husband to "7 pay them. At the trial she was foiled guilty of having borrowed Ll from a gardener et Newton (near Torquay) in 1880 under false pretences. She was then indicted for obtaining by false taretences from Thomas Joyce three dresses and other articles, value EL She told Mr. Joyce she had bought Bellrise House, a house of considerable value in Torquay, and she had altered the name of the house to Glen Iris, in memory of her estates in Treland. It afterwards turned out that she had not bought Bellrise. On being arrested, she said that she had no estates in Ireland, but that they were in Melbourne. The prieoner . was found guilty, and it was stated that he had bees convicted at P-lymouth in 1877 and at She Surrey ses- tit sions in 1874. The Court sentenced her, -on the first count, to three days' imprisonment and on the second to five years' penal servitede. TITE CONSERVATIVE LEADERS AND THE GOVEP.N•MENT. public rneetingo at all at such a crisis (you see he is evi- dently in doubt about the wisdom of the course pursued), and if the policy to be advocated at those meetings is a truly popular and national policy, let them be mass meet- ings at Blackheath or in Hyde Park, or in any other locality which can conveniently contain large and freely admitted audience'; and, in the second place, if the leaders of the Tory party see cause for pronouncing censure on the Go- vernment, let them move votes of censure in the House of Lords and in the House of Commons, where debates can take place on which an instructed public can finally give judgment." Few Liberals at any rate will be found to dis- agree with the hon. member's sentiments in this respect. The House of Commons is doubtless the place in which to censure the Government, but I hope the contemplated debate will be deferred until the noble lord has recuperated him- self, so that the House may not be deprived of his trans- cendent eloquence, his profound erudition, and his scathing denunciation of all the actions—good and bid alike—of a Liberal Government. A Liberal Government will, however, survive all the member for Woodstock may have to say. Lord• Salisbury has recently been dabbling in figures, but he has not been very happy in his effort. Speaking at a meeting at Stratford, the leader of the Opposition in the Peers said that at the last election so close were the contests in a great number of constituencies theta little more than 2,000 men turned the scale in Greatßritain. The statement having been challenged, the noble marquis gave a list of 63 seats, in which the total actual Liberal majority ranging from one to 185 amounted to 4,042. Then the marquis adds : " These 63 seats would count 126 on a division if transferred from one side to the other. The Liberal majority in Great Britain after the general election was 125. The seats were won by an aggregate majority of 4,042. Of course they would have been lost if a majority of this majority, i e., 2,021, had voted the other way, or, allowing for casting votes in those constituencies where the majority was an even number, the number of electors whose votes actually turned the scale in the whole election for Great Britain was 2,064." It is all very well to say what would have happened if those Liberal victories gained by majorities of less than 200 had been won by the Tories, but his lordship overlooks the fact, a correspondent points out, that 60 seats were also won by his own party by majorities not exceeding 200. The aggre- gate Conservative majority in these 60 constituencies was 5,110. If, to use Lord Salisbury's own words, "a majority of this majority," i.e., 2,555 "had voted the other way," the Tory minority in the House of Commons would have lost some of its most prominent members (amongst others Lord Randolph Churchhill, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Mr. Warton, Mr. Gorst, Mr. Burke, and Mr. Cavendish Bentinck), and nearly a quarter of its voting power, while the Liberal majority instead of being 125, would have been 275. A very different result is therefore obtained by applying his lord- ship's reasoning in the manner shown above. Perhaps his lordship will, in his leisure time, offer some comments on how it came about that the net Liberal majority in ten constituencies was no less than 75,219 at the last general election. But if the noble marquis's principles of computation be applied to the election of 1874, the following, as another correspondent shows, will be the result :—Lord Beaconsfield's majority in Great Britain was 86. So that a different result in forty-four c‘nstituencies, each seat counting two on a division, would have "trans- ferred the majority from one side to the other." he aggre- gate Conservative majority in 44 constituencies was 3,098, and "if a majority of this majority, 2". e., 1,549 had voted the other way," the seats would have been lost, and the Con- servative party instead of being in power would have been in a minority in Parliament. But goings step further than this, it is found that no fewer than 10 Conservative M.P.'s did not represent majorities of any kind, either small ,or large, but were returned by minorities owing to Liberal divisions, The deductions of these, each counting two on a division, leaves the Comervative majority in Parliament at 66, based on majoritiea voting in 4 conatiEuencies. The aggregate majority is thus diminished to 1,773 votes, The correspondent alluded to therefore concludes by commend- ing to Lord Salisbury's notice the following result 2---" The number of electors whose votes turned the scale in the elec- tion of 1874, and enabled Lord Salisbury to engage in the Constantinople Conference, the Schouvaloff Memorandum, and the Berlin Congress, was fewer than 1,000, or to be pre- cise, 887. Mr. Gladstone's majority looks respectable after this." Lard Salisbury, who is an adept in the art of con- veying the suggestio falsi by means of the suppressio yen, has not returned to the charge, and if he has pet used the correspondence I do not think he is likely to. These facts ',Toy show the wisdom of a proposal such as Mr. Ashtou
Difke's, that no member of Parliament shall be returned who
_ does not succeed in gaining at least a majority of the votes actually cast at the poll for his constituency. FL A CC US.

SOCIETY.—Mr, John Rough having resiguv... secretary to this society, the committee have appointed Mr. Richard Whiteside, of Victoria-road, Widnep, to suc- ceed him.

RAILWAY SERVANTS' ORPHANAGE.—On Saturday morning a trip from Liverpool to Llandudno, in aid of this charity, passed through Runcorn. We are sorry to state, however, that neither the attractions of the charming watering-place nor the claims of the orphanage, induced many persons to undertake the journey. Only seven persons booked at Run- corn, and the trip altogetLer did not receive that support which it deserved.

THUNDERSTORM AT RUNCORN A HOUSE DAMAGED.— A thunderstorm of about half an hour's duration broke over Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon. Hailstones of unusual size descended, and the lightning was very vivid. The electric fluid in entering the house occupied by Mr. 'Thomas Houghton, in Trentham-street, made a hole in the roof, and damaged the woodwork of the window. A large quantity of soot was displaced in the chimney, but the furniture sus- tained no damage ; while the inmates escaped unhurt, being, however, slightly alarmed at the occurrence.

tacom Vormrrgas Conrs.—For the first time for a number of years the F. and G. Companies (Runcorn•of the Earl of Chester's Rifle Volunteers attended divine -service at Halton Parish church on Sunday morning. There were about 90 men on parade, under the command of Captain Hazlehurst, and their bearing as they went through the town was very creditable. The Vicar, the Rev. J. Lock- wood, preached a sermon appropriate to the occasion. On Wednesday evening about 100 men from the Rtrncorn corps journeyed by train to Chester, to take part in the ordinary battalion drill. Captain Hazehurst was in command. We understand that on the 19th inst., when another drill will be held at Chester, a prize cf considerable ,value will be awarded to the best drilled company in the battalion, each company to be under the command of its own officers. THEFT OF A. COAT: AN INGENIOUS DEFENCE.—At the Widnes police court on 'Wednesday, before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn, F. H. Gossage, and Holbrook .G.askell, jun , a labourer. named James Connolley, was brought up in custody charged with stealing a black coat, worth 13s. 6d., the property of James Cookson, pawnbroker, Woolton.r— William McWaters, manager for the prosecutor, stated that he hung the coat in his master's shop on .the afternoon of Tuesday, the 20th ult. At 7 o'clock the-came day the coat was missed.—Mary Johnson, a well dressed woman, said the prisoner was her brother. Between 6 and'? o'clock on the day in question the pr;soner went to her house wearing the coat produced, and mt his request she ,pawned it. The money, 7s. ed., which she recived by so doing, she gave the prisoner.—ln defence the prisoner had an-ingenious story to tell. Whilst walking to Wavertree he was overtaken by a man who inquired the way- to Warrington. He directed him. The man then asked if he would buy a coat, and at length he gave hisnlis., and the coat he was wearing, for it, He (prisoner) was drunk at the time, and after his sister had pawned the coat he got more liquor.—The Bench com- mitted the prisoner to gaol for a month. DAMAGING A. PUBLIC.HOUSE AT 'WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., James Heath, a man whose dress waa very ragged, was brought up in custody charged with doing wilful damage to the Golden Ball public-house, West Bank, kept by Alice Lightfoot. Robert Lightfoot, the manager of the house, said on Saturday night the prisoner entered the bar about eight o'clock. He was in a state of intoxication, and took from the counter a pint cup, which he smashed on the floor. He (witness) requested him to leave, but was obliged to forcibly eject him. The prisoner then imme- diately turned round, and, with his fiet, deliberately smashed a stained and lettered plate glass window. The nett cost of the window was £5 55., but it would entail an expense of £6 to replace it. The prisoner was very violent in the street, and a policeman was sent for, but on the arrival of P.C. Snowdon the prisoner had departed. The officer, however, followed the prisoner to his lodgings, 5, Moss Bank-road. His landlady asked the officer to turn the 'prisoner out, as she was afraid of her life ; and the landlord alleged that he had assaulted him. With aosistance the witness got him outside, and his conduct was then so violent that he was taken into custody. He wae afterwards charged with breaking the window. Prisoner said, "I have nothing to say; I know 1 broke them." The prisoner was committed to the sessions for trial. LANCASHIRE INDEPENDENT COLLEGE.—The eessional anniversary of the Lancashire Independent Coltege was held on Thursday, at the College. The Chairman (the Rev. J. Maefadyen) presided at the business meeting, and congratulated the friends on the circumstances under which they had aesembled. The building was now free fromadebt. It must not be supposed, however, that the Committee had a lot of mouey in hand that they did' not know what to do with, Having paid the debt, they were at the beginning of the important work which they had set before themselvea for ten or twelve years. The preparatory class had been closed, and so far they had redeemed thc pledge to make the College a purely theological institution ; but to accom- plish that it would be absolutely necessary that they should enlarge the professorial staff. The Rev. E. R. Conder, Leeds, delivered the annual address. A resolution was passed expressing the satisfaction of the meeting at the re- moval of the debt. A further resolution expressed the gratitude of the friends for the munificent bequest of £lO,OOO from Mr. Asa Lees. A garden party was held in the even- ing, to celebrate the extinction of the debt.

RUNCORN LAWN TENNIS CLUJ:I.—The adherents of the now popular game of lawn tennis in Runcorn, have lately formed themselves into a club, and the inaugural game WAS played on Saturday last. A field 60 by 40 yards his been •-•A T-livber Runcorn, adjoining the Volunteer rifle • - Alit for the game in

fleCUrtu _ butts, and it has been excellently three terraces. It is enclosed by wire and scantling, ana is held on a threa years' lease. Already the club numbers about 60 or 70 members, and the list of its officers contains the names of some of the mott prominent ladies and gentle- men in the locality. The officers are as follow: President, Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A.; hon. treasurer, Mrs. G. S. Hazlehurst ; hon. secretary, Mr. Fred. A. FOUND DEAD AT RUNCORN.—At the Navigation Inn, Runcorn, on Tuesday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquiry respecting the death of Ellis Williams, whose body was found in the canal on Sunday morning last, under the following circumstances :—William Williams, boiler fire- man, Spring Gardens, identified the body as that of his brother. Deceased lived at Spring Gardens, and was a carpenter, 64 years of age. He was a single man. Witness last saw him alive at home on Saturday evening last, about eight o'clock. He was then und6r the influence of drink, and left the house. Witness had seen the body, and had no reason to believe that deceased bad met with foul play.— Lot Hurst, shopkeeper, 16, Bridge-street, raid he knew the deceased very well. About 10 minutes to 12 last Saturday night, the deceased and three young men came to his shop. Deceased seemed as though he had had some drink. He ordered three bottles of ginger beer, which the young men drank. Deceased did not pay for the ginger beer. They stayed in the shop about ten minutes, and then went out together. Deceased turned to his left its the direction of his 'home, and the young men turned to the right towards their homes. He stood at the door and watched them co away. Deceased seemed able to take care of himself.—James Limb, 66, Nelson-street. said he wascaptain of the boat Alice. On Sunday morning last, ; about half-past ten o'clock, 'he was on the Bridgewater Canal in his boat. A steamer passed him near Mr. Abbott's yard, and he saw the fan of the steamer turn up something-; and when the steamer had passed he pushed his boat across the canal, and picked up the body of the deceased. The police came sip just as be got the body out of the water, and the afterwards conveyed it home. He saw the body searched, but there was nothing in deceased's pockets.—There was no evidenne to show how deceased got into the canal, and the jury returned a verdict of 'Found dead." DESPBRATE ASSAULT ON A WIFB AT WIDNI3B.-AtWid- nee Police Court, yesterdaybefore Mr. Holbrook Waken cunr., a ,railway labourer, nettled Edward Carney, .was jharged with committing an aggravated assault on his vaife Ellen. The prisoner pleaded not guilty. The prosecutris said on Wednesday evening the ,prisoner locked her out of the house and she went round to the back door. She effec- ted an entrant(' there, but no sooner had she "put her foot inside" than the prisoner knockedher to the ground. Whilst she lay therehe placed his knee on her breast, and clasped , his band round her throat to choke her. Releasing her from this position he savagely kicked her, and bruised her foot in a terrible manner. In answer to questions, the prosecu- trix said she gave prisoner no provocation. She asked him if he "paid for his brother's ale" and he replied that he "could do as he liked with his own money ". She was "blowing him up," and then be "thumped her in the face." —The Clerk (Mr. Lewin): What is that mark on your fore- head? That was done by a knife he had in his hand, but I don't think he meant to use it. He did not make any blow at me with the knife. When I was on the ground I put my hand up to protect myself, and got this cut. (Cat shown.) —The prisoner asked his wife if she had any dinner ready for him when he came home from St. Helens Junction on Tuesday, and she replied there was a "ham bone" ready for him. She did not want to send him to gaol • only to bind 41im over to keep the peace.—P.C. 804 was called, and stated the prosecutrix was a drunken woman, and he had fre- quently heard her quarrelling with her husband.—Mr. Gasket! (to prisoner): Your wife may be a drunken woman, but that doesn't give you any right to knock her about in this way. I don't want to send you to prison,•and you will be bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, yourself in a.O and two sureties in £lO eacb, In default you will have logo to gaol for 14 days.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday, Colonel J. Black- burne presented apetition from the inhabitants of Widnes in favour of the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts. THE STAR OV WIDNES LODGE 1.0.G.T. held a weekly session on Wednesday evening. Mr. Hufton, W.C.T., occupied the chair. Bro. Wendt and Sisters Wendt and Dodd sang several duets, and recitations were given by Bros. ; Wendt and Kenyon. Sisters E. and M. Goff also rendered good service.

I HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—Tb e 1 Rev. George Hack, preached a special sermon to children in the above place of worship on Sunday last. A large number of young people were present. SERMONS AT WESTON WESLEYAN SCHOOL.-011 Suniay the Rev. Thomas Rippon, of Warrington, preached the anniversary sermons of Weston Wesleyan school, to good congregations. The Rev. John Nowell, also preached a sermon on Monday evening. The collections amounted to £l5.

PAVILION THEATRE, WIDNES.—Mr. Russell has had a most successful run this week; the "Old Tall House," and "Ingomar," which have been placed upon the boards, pro- viding very attractive pieces. To-day (Saturday) "Gipsy King" will be performed, to be concluded with the drama, "Knights of the road." ACCIDENT AT DITTON STATION.—An engine called "The Runcorn Dodger," when leaving Ditton Station, on Satur- day last, was turned into a siding and ran into the stop block. Fortunately no damage was done, and no person sustained any injury. PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT ROCK SAVAGE. The new chapel at Rock Savage, the foundation stone of which was laid about two months ago, is drawing near completion, and is expected to be opened at the latter end of this month. We have previously stated it was the intention of the Pri- mitive Methodists at that place to build a school at some future day, but a quantity of material being left from the erection of the chapel, it has been decided to at once pro- ceed with that work.

GARSTON AND WIDNES PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.—At the annual meeting of this society, held in the Central Chambers, Widnes, on Monday, a dividend of five per cent for the past year was declared. The balance sheet was read and passed.. The retiring directors, Messrs. Matthews and Leith, were re-elected, and the secretary, Mr. W. Tracey, senr., was re-appointed. THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS FOR BUNOORN.—Wednes- day was the last day to receive nominations for the extra- ordinary election of three Guardians allowed by special order of the Local Government Board. The three gentlemen who prev:ously filled the vacanciss—Messrs. W. Handley, Wm. Fisher, and Wm. Whittaker, are the only persons nomina- ted, and will constquently be elected without opposition. We are pleased to notice that at the National Competition at South Kensington, Mr. Arthur I'. Nowell, son of the Rev. J. Nowell, superintendent Wesleyan minister, Runcorn, has gained the gold meth' for Antique drawing. At this exhi- bition some six or eight i'iawings are usually forwarded from each of the principal Schools of Art in the country, and the distinction cbtained by Mr. Nowell is consequently a very important one.

HALTON PAROCHIAL SCHOOLS.—The scholars attending these schools dispersed for their midsummer holidays oil Thursday last. Miss Louisa Woodier and Miss Eliza Ann :Rows have concluded their apprenticeshipsas pupil teachers

and the Vidat, on behalf of the managers, teachers, and scholars, presented each lady with a handsome morocco. bound album. The album bears an inscription testifying to the esteem and regard in which the recipients are held, and expressing good wishes for their future welfare. Miss Woodier, we understand, has accepted the assistant mistress- ship of Norley National School, near Frodsharn.
TRIP FROX WIDNES TO BLACKPOOL—The work- men employed by Messrs. Gossage and Co., at Widnes, bad
their annual trip to Blackpool on Saturday. With the friends of the workmen, the excursionists numbered about n Ch. The

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIELY. .—The usual monthly meeting was held on Monday evening, in the Free Library; the president (Mr. S. J. Capper) in the chair. Messrs. H. Pedder and H. Williams were elected members of the society. After the transaction of the ordinary business the Rev. S. Fletcher Williams read a paper on " Darwin and Darwinism," which was listened to with great interest. The meeting terminated with votes of thanks to the reader of the paper and to the visitors, who were numerous, and included several ladies. During the conversations Mr. B. Cooke exhibited insects collected during Whitsuntide excursion to Sherwood Forest, which included the rare mordellzstena abdominalis; Mr. Von Sobbe, a box of European lepidoptera ; Mr. W. Gardner, a box of coleoptera from North Wales; and the hon. secre- tary (Dr. Ellis), a smoky variety of abraxas ulmata captured at Ince Blundell. DEATH OP THIS Ray. DR. MASSINOHAM, FORMERLY OP WARRINGTON.—The death is announced of the Rev. Dr. Massingham, a clergyman who twenty years ago played a very prominent part in Lancashire in controversial matters. He died at Chelsea, in the fifty-sixth year of his age. The Rev. John Deacon Massingham was at the time of his decease Vicar of St. Paul's, Longport, Burslem, which is in the patronage of the Rector of Berslem. Mr. Massingham was of Trinity College, Dublin, B.A. 1851, M.A. 1854, LL.B. and LL.D. 1867, B.D. and D.D. 1869. He was admitted to deacon's orders in 1851, and was ordained priest in 1852 by the Bishop of Lichfield. His first curacy was that of All Saints', Derby; he then became successively Vicar of St. Paul's. Derby, Vicar of St. Paul's. Warrington, chaplain of the Warrington Union, and lecturer for the Church Defence Association, London. He was the author of numerous tracts, published sermons, and pamphlets. WYCLIFFE BAND OF HOPE Pie-NIC TO FRODSIIAM —Ol2 Tuesday afternoon last the 'workers and friends of the above society held their first annual pic-nic. The party which numbered over a hundred persons left the school about two o'clock in five large conveyances supplied by Mr. Ed. Con- nor, of Sankey-street. The drive to Frodsham was most enjoyable the weather being beautifully fine. Upon arriv- ing at their destination the party proceeded to ascend the bill in order to reach Mersey View, the place selected for the afternoon's enjoyment. It now being about four o'clock preparations were at once made for tea, which all were quite ready for and to which full justice was done. After tea amusements consisting of bowls, cricket, donkey races, swings. were indulged in. The return journey was started at eight o'clock, Warringtou being reached about ten o'clock. The whole arrangements of the day were in the bands of Mr. Wm. Roberts, the secretary of the society, and everything passed off in a most agreeable and happy manner, everyone being delighted with the treat thus afforded them. THE AFFAIRS or G. D. WENHAM.—In the matter of George David Wenham, bookseller, 18, Brown-street Manchester, and of Wilson Patten-street, Warrington. an application has been made by Mr. Johnson atthe Manchester County Court for the registration of the resolution passed by the majority of the creditors. The resolution was for liquidation by arrangement, and the appointment of a trustee. The matter came before the Court because a reso- lution had been passed by the creditors dispensing with the attendance of the debtor at the meeting.—Mr. Addleshaw supported the application on behalf of the trustee, and Mr. Edgar (Boote and Edgar) also supported the application on behalf of the bulk of the creditors, who were of opinion that the arrangement was a desirable one. The debtor did not get his discharge, and the creditors were placed in possession of the estate immediately.—The Registrar, whilst of opinion that the resolution dispensing with the attendance of the debtor did not go far enough, as it did not state cause had be:? shown for the absence, at the same time made the order applied tue, fte there was no opposition.
• Blit-rer, CONDUCT 01? A SON-IN-LAW.-At the Warrington Police Court, psterday, 'Mom CaptAin Reynolds and Mr.

Z. Armitage, William Cross, a yothig Mat, Was summoned for assaulting his father-in-law, John Cotton, on Friday last. The complainant stated that the defendant was his son-in- law. For two years past he (witness) had paid his rent, but had never had any comfort with him. On Friday last he threw him against a mangle, and severely injured his arm. The defendant said it was Walking Day, and he got a little drink. If they would excuse him this time he would never do it again. Chief Constable Hunt said the complainant had repeatedly complained to him of the conduct of the de- fend:int. The defendant was a man who lived on a very in- dustrious wife and a mother of children. He had brooght a lot ' of children into the world, and would not now provide for them. The Complainant: My daughter will be very glad if she can get a Protection Order. He is no good to her—he is more a hindrance than anything else. The defendant said if the Bench would let him off this time he would not do it again; he would sign teetotal. The Chairman re- marked that there was no excuse for him. He had been before thent previously, and would be committed to prison for two months with hard labour. He deserved more. He would not have him about the house if he was his wife.
ANOTHER BOY DROWNED AT WIREINGTON.—The distrist coroner (Mr. C. E. Priffield) held an inquest at the 77--.1-Rtreet, en Thursday morning. touching

Oin tdrow, the death of Charles Henry Rotherham, 8 years Di of George Rotherham, boiler maker, 12, Trafalgar-place, Church-street, who was drowned about half-past five on Tuesday evening, in one of Mr. Edward Bolton's brick pits in Orford lane. It appeared that the deceased with two companions took off their boots and stockings and commenced to wade.for the purpose of catching "jacksl;arps;" but in a short time deceased appeared to slip and then sank under the water. He rose to the surface and his companions called out for assistance. Hearing their shouts, George Brooks, of the Hawthorn beerhouse, ran to the pit and was just in time to see deceased sinking. Being a good swim- mer, he at once plunged into the pit with his clothes on, and mataged to grip deceased with one hand as he went down, and but for a young man who 'jumped in close by trim' and who caused him to loose his hold, he b.dieved he touldhave saved the deceased. He then returned home tor, a grapple, and without taking his wet clothes off he agair proceeded to the pit, and in about 20 minutes recovered ate body of the deceased, which was taken home. Witness 'said the pit was a very dangerous one, and was 16 feet deep about the place where deceased was drowned. He remembered five other persons being drowned in the same p?t, and he bad on a previous occasion, saved a person from &owning there. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned," and recommended that steps bt taken te prevent access to the premises by child:Yr) and others. ne coroner thought the conEuct of Brookes was highly commendable.

ROBBERY OF NITRO-GLYCERINE.

Yesterday morning the inhabitants of Runcorn awakened somewhat surprised to discover there had been, according to the daily papers, a Fenian scare in the neighbourhood. Naturally this statement created a little " talk," but even then there was no scare, or even an approach to it. The circumstances which had given rise to the announcement, were that a navvy, employed at the Mersey Salt and Brine Works, near Runcorn, had suddenly disappeared, taking with him 10Ibs. of nitro-glycerine 51bs. compressed powder, and five rings of patent fuse used for exploding purposes. These facts given, it needed little imagination to represent that the police believed him to have a connection with the Fenians, and were in hot pursuit. So far from the occur- rence being viewed with alarm, however, it is regarded by the police as a common felony. It is true a man named John Hemberton absconded with the amount of explosives stated on Tuesday morning, but in addition to these materials, be also carried away a num- ber of picks, spades, candles, and other articles. But his disappearance and the robbery are capable of an easy ex- planation. Hemberton was not a common navvy as sated, but what is termed a sub-contractor, and in that capacity employed a number of men. For a consiuerable time he has been employed in the work of making the tunnel under Bea- Hill'fur the Brine Company, and was thus constantly using explosives. On Saturday night, we are informed by Mr. Supt. Williamson, liemberton, who was very fond of drink, was in Runcorn with a woman, and it is supposed that he there got robbed. Having then no money with which to pay his men's wages, it is probable he decided to leave the neighbourhood unknown to the men; and as be would not be able to get work without tools god material, he robbed the company of the articles enumerated. It is even alleged that he was in a state of intoxication when he committed the theft. By no manner of reasoning can the thief be connected with the Fenians. In the first place he was an Englishman, born in Staffordshire, and in the second the articles he took were such as he required for his daily avocation, while had he wished to obtain ex- plosives for the Fenians, he could have taken large quantities on the day he &sill- menced at the salt works. The police are of opinion he will be found at work on the Liverpool Water Scheme in Wales, but the Mersey Brine Company are not very desirous of prosecuting. The delinquent, it may be well to state, is a man of about 50 years of age, sft. Bin. in height, with brown mark on the left side of the face, sparely built, wearing a blue monkey jacket and brown cap.

A SAD PHASE OF DOMESTIC LIFE. At the Warrington Police Court yesterday, before Cap- tain Reynolds (in the chair), and Mr. Z. Armitage, Samuel Jackson, 19. a labourer, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Harriet Jackson, on the 25th ult.—The Complainant deposed that the defendant came home from his work and wanted her to get. his clothes out of pawn. She had no money to do so, and went to try acd borrow some. She could not do so, whereupon be commenced to ill-use her. He struck her on the mouth, the back of the head, and many other places. He was sober at the time. Not only on that occasion had he assaulted her—he had done it previously.— The Deputy Clerk: How long have you been married? The Complainant: We have been married five weeks last Mon- day. He has done it many times during the five weeks.— In reply to the Bench she further stated that he had dragged her out of bed and bruised her arm—The Defendant said that his wife would not mend his clothing, and on the morn- ing in question she was "using her lip," and struck him with a knife. He then struck her back.—The Complainant: No, I did not strike him —The Chairman: You are speaking about Friday morning, what about Thursday night? The Defendant: I gave her 225. and asked her to get my clothes out of pawn. She said she had got her's out and I could get mine. I earn 225. per week, and have given her money every week.—The Wife: He gave me 12s. the first, 14s. the secohd, and on the Ahird week he offered , 103., but I would not have it. He kept it three days in his pocket, and kept me without food, sending out foraNhat he wanted himself—The Chairman (to defendant) : How old are you ? The Defendant: 19.—The Chairman : What do you do—what is your labour ? lam a labourer at Whiteeross. She has run about £3 in debt, and we have only been married five weeks.—The Complainant: You must not believe him.—The Defendant : I have the bills in my pocket.—The Complainant: He has never given me a proper week's wage since I had him. Out of the 20s. be gave me, he knew Bs. went to the pawnshop.—The Defen- dant : When I went in the house on Sunday night, and asked her where the bed clothes had been removed to, she said if I wanted them I could get them.—The Complainant: I had as much right to them as you. He very nearly broke my jaw bone on Sunday night for nothing.—The Chair- man : I should fancy after your experience during the last five weeks it would be better for you to live apart as you did before.—The Complainant: I have never drunk his money away.—The Defendant: No, she has got , it.—The Chairman : I think we have heard enough of these domestic quarrels.—The Defendant: I have been on "slack time" at my work, and did not make a full week.—The Complainant: It was not like as if we got iNnarried on a clear bottom; there was so much owing to the - - .•••/• nn trust.—The Chairman (to de- . Pc en shop. They sofa Us

fendant): You will b—e biund over in one surety v, keep the peace for six months. I think be has been aggravated.—The Complainant: No, sir, he has not.—The Defendant: I have been aggravated, sir.—The Chairman: I think there has been aggravation, and it is better for you to live apart than live that sort of a life.—Mr. Armitage (to the complainant): You have given us a sample of what you can do in the way of talking.—Chief Constable Hunt: She happens to be four or five yeara older than he, and she thinks she has a right to talk. DEATH OF MR. G. ARTINGSTALL, Waatingtonians were startled an *Puesday by the news that Mr. 'George Artingstall, J.P., bad died at his residence, Latchford Route, at an early hour that morning. The event was totally unexpected, inasmuch as it was eot even known that the deceased gentleman was at all intisposed, and its alarming suEdenness gave greater forceto the sad intelli- gence. Mr. Artingstall occupied his accustomed Beaton the 'Bench at the last sitting of the Warrington County Petty 'Sessions eaVednesday, the 21st June„ when he appeared to be in his usual health, and as he was wont he pointed out to therinebriates how expensive it was to be brought before the court and advised them to join the 'Bite Ribbon Army. We understand, however, that Mr. /Wingatell has sufferednor some months, and on Friday fortnigtit he con- sulted•a'Liverpool medital gentleman whom he saw again on the following Thursday. On this return be became worse, and on Saturday last sent forAtr. T. Starkey Smith, who found'him suffering from acute inflammation of the bladder. Mr. Smith was in constant attendance, but Mr. Artingstall rapidly sank under his inoet painful malady, and expired at 3-25 on Tuesday morning, aged '73 years. Of his early history very little is known, except that he was born during the troublous times at the beginning of the present century at Swinton, near Manchester, which place he left with a determination to make his way in the world, and his subse- quent career proves what .can be done with energy and perseverance. At the age of 19 Mr. Artingstall came to Warrington and entered the service of Mr. Samuel Edelsten, nin manufacturer, as traveller; He afterwards went into partnership with Mr. William Boaumont,wireworker, Wilderepool-road, and on the dissolu- tion of the partnership he commenced business on his own account on the site of the present works. He was joined -several years later by Mr. W. R. Dell, but -since that gentle- man left him, 26 years ago, he has ,carried on a success- fill business alone. The deceased gentleman was acquainted with several continental languages, which he put to practical use in his travels over Europe.; and as a business man, it is stated, he has left few behind him his equals. He was formerly a member of the Town Coencil, but latterly has not prominently identified himself with local politics, although he occupied several important positions in connection with local institutions. As already stated be was a county magistrate, and was most regular in his attendance; he was also a trustee of the Warrington Blue Coat School, and of the Warrington Savings Bank, a governor of the Warrington Grammar •School, and of the Royal Albert Lunatic Asylum; and a Commissioner of Taxes. He was a member of, and teok great interest in, the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, of which he was e x-president. Mr. Artingstall was a libera •Supporter of the local charities; but his philanthropy wasl not confined to Warrington, as he was also a subscriber to ,charitable institutions in Manchester and Liverpool. In religion, the deceased gentleman was a Churchman, and was a member of St. James's Church, Latchford ; while in politics he was a staunch ConservatiO, and heartily sup- ported the" Fair Trade" movement about which so much was beard sometime ago. Since the sad event became known the sags at the fowl] Hall and St. James's Church have been atkalf mast.

THE PROPOSED MILITARY INTERVENTION.

In consequence of a telegram from the War Office the artificers of the Royal Carriage Department of Woolwich Arsenal commenced work at day's.); eak yesterday morning, preparing for the issue of a light siege train, which has to be reidy within 48 hours. The siege train comprises a very formidable armament including 10 forty pounder and ten twenty-five pounler siege gums, six seven pounder guns, 10 six-and-a-half inch howitzers, tegether with the neces- sary carriages, ammunition, waggons, siege platforns, etc. A. special barge was dispatched from the Boyal Arsenal yesterday with four of the latest pattern machine guns to complete the armament of H.M.S. Orion. At Rye dock- yard, Woodwich, operations have been commenced to get ready the whole of a field hospital transport, including the pharmacy and surgical waggon. The field telegraph is also being got out. The transport corps at Woolwich were yesterday also actively engaged in moving war stores from the dockyard to the arsenal in order to complete equip-

A ra:is telegram of yt-serday's date says :—A telegram from Constantinople received here announces that the Con- ference yesterday exitnined the proposal submitted by Lord Dufferin for a Turkish military intervention in Egypt. The desire was expressed to subject this intervention to such conditions as would in any case prevent it from becoming a Turkish occupation, and from restricting the liberties and independence of Egypt. The Press Association is in a position to state that the Government have received no confirmation of the report that the Conference now sitting at Constantinople "regards a speedy armed intervention as necessary."

THE AGRARIAN MURDERS IN IRELAND. A Loughrea correspondent, telegraphing later particulars resp.cting the murders near that place, says the murderers of Mr. Blake and his servant appear to have laid their plans well, and it is believed that their number was the same as those who recently wrought the murder of Mr. Burke. The wall had bees loopholed on each side of the road, and three shots were fired as the car was rattling by. M. Blake and his man fell at once into the roadway, but Mrs. Wake, who was sitting on the opposite side from which the shots came, was uninjured. The horse drawing the car with the affrighted lady walked into Loughrea, where there was a crowded market attendance, and whore the sound of the firing had been heard. Mrs. Blake was greatly agitated, and could not give any account of the number of the assas- sins. Mr. Blake had refused police protection, but at the time of the murder his conveyance was being followed at some little distance by a guard of police. Mr. Blake was well connected.

Another correspondent telegraphs that the deceased were driving from Rathville to Loughrea to attend a landlords' meeting, when they were fired at from behind a loopholed wall. Mr. Blake and Keane fell dead instantly, and directly the news was made known the police went in every direc- tion, but up to the present tNey have failed to make any arrests. Mr. Blake was over 70 years of ago, and had but recently been married. He has had the reputation of being a fair man towards the tenantry, with whom he was not un- popular, but several evictions had recently taken place on the estate, which is a very extensive one. In the recent issue of a weekly paper published in the locality where the late Mr. Blake resided, the strongest language was made use of towards the unfortunate gentle- man. He was denounced as "The agent of Lord Clanrack- rent, and as having driven hundreds of the unfortunate tenants into the workhouse." Three arrests have been made on suspicion of complici.y in the murder. Mrs. Blake still lies at the hotel in Loughrea. She does not yet know that her husband ie dead, tier only brother is a surgeon on board H.M.S. Bacchante with the Royal PriPoee.

THE COLLIERY DISASTER IN WARWICKSHIRE. ANOTHER DEATH.

There is yet another to be added to the heavy list of deaths from the effects of the recent disaster a* the Baxterley Colliery, the latest victim being Charles Archer. Thin makes the total number of deaths 32, Archer br.ing the twenty-third person who has succumbed front the injuries received in a gallant though unsuccessful attempt to rescue the nine men still entombed. TERRIBLE LEAP DOWN A PIT SHAH'. Archimedes Muff, 04, farmer, East Therley, Bradford, flung himsel down a coalpit at Hunswcrth, 03 Thursday, and was dashed to pieces. The distance from the top of the shaft to the bottom is 100 yards. His son followed him to mouth of the pit, and a terrible struggle ensued: The father, however, tore himself away from his son's grasp, and hurled' himself down the shaft. Business matters had preyed upon his mind for some time. BRUTAL WIFE ASSAULT. At the Sheffiel4 Quarter Sessions yesterday, Aaron Lee 4., ham, who was recently apprehended on a charge of being implicated in the murder near Rotherham 26 years ago, was indicted for a brutal assault on his wife. He was separated from her, but he visited her house one night, alliging that a man was there. He then threw her on the bed, knelt upen her, smashing three of her ribs and inflicting other injuriet He was sentenced to five months' imprisonment. DESTRUCTIVE THUNDERSTORM. During a violent storm of thunder aud lightning on. Thursday night a house at Crofthead, Lanai kshire, was struck by lightning. Two children were slightly burned, and the stone work of the house was damaged. At Carl uke the rainfall was very heavy, and several houses were flooded. The lowlying parts of Hamilton were also flooded, and the darkness was so great while the storm lasted that gas had to be lighted. Yesterday the heat was intense. FOUR GROOMS CHARGED WITH MANSLA.UGHTER. John Hodgson, groom to the Stand Stud Company, Whitefield, Manchester; John Kelly, groom to Mr. Garbutt, of Marton Grange, near Darlington; Wm. Fox, groom to Mr. Martin, of Scoreby Grange, Great Helmsley; and Wm. Barks, groom to Mr. Letts, Camps,ton, near York, are in custody charged with causing the death of John Leo, farmer, of High Ellers, Doncaster. It is stated that a pub`ic- house quarrel occurred between the men on Thursday nigh, and Les was afterwards kicked to death. THIEVES SENTENCED TO THE CAT. At Wolverhampton Quarter Sessions yesterday morning tli-e following cases were disposed of :—William Tuustall (54), sailor, and Arthur Gibbs, alias Gibson (18), brass-fitter, both from Birmingham, were indicted as incorrigible rogues, being reputed thieves. They were found in Wolverhamp- ton with intent to commit felony in May last. Inspector , I Black, of the Birmingham detective department, said he had ' known the:elder prisoner for seven years as a professional travelling pickpocket, and during that time he had been *convicted of robberies or attempted robberies at the race meetings at Newton, Newcastle, Worcester, an other places. The younger man had for three or four years constantly been in company and under the tuitioa of the older one. Tunstall was sentenced to six months' hard labour and 12 strokes with the cat o' nine tails, and Gibbs to three months' hard labour and eight crokes.—Francis Roberts, an ex- policeman, for committing an indescribable and disgusting outrage on four little girls, was sentencod to 18 months' hard labour,

FIRE AT A MIDDLETON MILL. Shortly before ten on Thursday morning a fire broke out at the Suffield-street Spinning Mill, Middleton, occnpie.! br Messrs. T. B. Wood and Son. The workpeopie were all QII the premises, but were got out in safety. The mill is for- tunately close by the fire engine-station of the Middleton Commissioners, and help being immediately on the spot, the fire was put out before any considerable damage was done. The damage is chiefly caused by water. POLICE APPOINTMENT AT BLACKBURN. Inspector Lewis, of the Old Swan. Liverpool, was on Wednesday afternoon appointed superintendent of the Blackburn borough police force, in place of Superintenilent Wald, who has been made chief constable. Mr. Lewis was only appointed inspector a few months ago, having been a sergeant in the Blackburn county police force for mmy years. Earlier in the day he was presented with a £25 gold watch by the Blackburn county magistrates, in recognition of his faithful service.

MYSTERIOUS MURDER IN LONDON. On Thursday evening some lightermen at Ilorsleydown Stairs, London, picked up the body of a man who was found to have been stabbed about the face and body. It appears that the deceased was a master builder named John /3nø, residing at Maidstone. A fortnight ago he went to London on business, and has never been heard of by his friends since. It is stated that there had been a disagreement with a person, whose name is known, about some money, and that the latter has been for some days dogging the deceased. W. Girten, of Horsleydown Stairs, examined the body directly after it was picked up, and is of opinion that a murder has taken place. The lightermen believe that the body was brought to the surface by the concussion caused by the guns at the Tower, which were fired on Thursday in honour ot the Queen's coronation.

The Lord-Lieutenant witnessed the evolution of the troops et the field day in Phoenix Park, Dublin, yesterday morning, under General Sir Thomas Steele. The Lord- Lieutenant subsequently rode to Dublin Castle with the usual escort. He had an interview with Mr. Hamilton, the under secretary, Colonel Brackenburv, of the crime depart- ment, the Inspector-General of Constabulary, and other heads of departments.

ANOTHER BARRACKS MYSTERY. Yesterday morsing Lieut. Tothill, of the 64th Regiment, stationed in Athlone, was found dead in the castle adjoining the military barracks' with wounds on his head, caused evidently by bullets from a revolver lying beside him. It is doubtful whether deceased committed suicide or the occurrence was accidental. BREAKING A MAN'S ARM. At the Liverpool Police Court, yesterday, Edward Haines was charged with savagely assaulting a corporate official named Thwaites. The latter went to the house where Haines lodged to demand the payment of the balance of rates due. The landlord being out Haines opened the door, and Thwaites having stated his business Haines without any further parley seized him and threw him down five steps. Thwaites's arm was broken, and he suffered other injuries. The prisoner was committed for trial.

EXPLOSION AT A BURNLEY COLLIERY. On Tnursday night an explosion occurred at the Alice Pit, Townley Colliery, Burnley, resulting in the death of William Lord, 21 years of age, who lived in Mosley-street, Burnley. The deceased went to work in No. 5 district about half-past two in the afternoon, and it appears that he must have taken the top of his lamp off and worked with the naked light. Four or five hours afterwards an exolosion was heaid in the pit. The men then working in the pit were summoned to the pit's eye by the fireman and were got out. The deceased being missing, search was made and the body was recovered. The gas is supl i iosed to have originated nan old working near to which deceasei was engaged.

div.head: Teter to Mr ditor.
div.p: Teter to Mr ditor.

"THE TIMID ANIMAL."—ANOTHER CORRUPTION. Sir,—Your Newton and Earlestown correspondent, in re- ferring in your issue of June 17th to my letter anent the , establishment of a hare-breeding and coursing farm in New- ton-le-Willows, published in your issue of June 10th, says: —" The old cookery books begin by saying, 'First catch your hare,' and then 'proceed to show how to cook it. The word "catch " is a corruption for which there is every reason to believe the " paper-stainers " are respensible, as Mrs. Glasse, whose name is usually mentioned in connection with the "mythical phrase," in all the editions of her book I have seen, uses the word "cast," i.e., to skin. I have not any glossaries by ma as I write, but the corrupted saying attri- buted to Dr. Kitchener, the author of "The Cook's Oracle,"— (but which is probably far older than his time),—is most ' likely a play upon an ancient word still in use in Norfolk and Siitoik. Mr. Eliezer Edwards says:—" In those coun- tries, where the word skatcli means to skin and dress an j anined for cooking, the direction First sketch your hare,' ' might be easily mistaken for the mythical phrase, First catch your hare,'L--a saying which has been productive of so MICA merriment, it seems a pity to disturb it." There is, agaia, another theory, which is that the word originally used was "case," one meaning of which was formerly, according to Johnson, "to strip off the covering; to take off the skin." Shakespeare uses the word in "All's well that ends welt," where he makes one of the lords attendant on the King, in speaking of Paroll'es, say, "We'll make you some spert with the fox ere we case him." The direction in the old,cookery books would probably therefore bo, "First case (or eleatc) your hare,"—that is first skin it. And in his "Anatomy of Melancholy" alluding to the genus, Burton says,—" Generally, as with rich-furr'd conies their cases are far better than their bodies." In connection with folk-lore, it was formerly a belief amongst country people that hares annually changed their sex. Fletcher, in The Faithful Shepherd," has Snakes that east their coats for new, Chameleons that alter hue. • Hares that yearly sexes change." And Butler; in" Hudibras," says "When wives their sexes change, like hares." Your correspOndent is correct in stating that the practice of hunting the hare is ancient. Zenophon took great delight in it; and it is a curious fact that whereas he, in his day, re- commended the flesh from the hind-legs of goats, as the best meat to feed tthe. dogs upon that were used in the hunt, so in many parts of England at the present day legs of mutton are used as food" for "trained greyhounds." Ido not know what the price of mntton is in Ne vton-le-Willows, but I sincerely hope that a too evident love of coursing on the part of some of ft.,: inhabitants will not result in juicy cuts of the flesh Charles the Second is credited with having been so fond of, passing the bairns to go to the dogs. Nor mast it be for- gotten that though' the hare is as a rule a timid animal, in- stances have bt burred where it has turned upon its pursuer or oppressor with considerable fury. Your correspondent concludes by stating that it will be interesting to me to know that in Newton they have "legal and illegal betting, and that many are so hare-brained as to indulge in both." Ido not doubt the statement. A glance through your in- terceing columns has convinced me that Newton has got its fair =hare of peculiar people. I only wonder that he has not recorded the fact more satirically or pungently by say- that whereas Whittington gained fame, riches, and conferred a benefit on a rodent-pasted country by "selling the cat," some Newtonians indulge in the foolish and unprofitable habit of "buying the rabbit." Ido not quite catch what he means by "a thousand a year certain and percentages on the take; " but if he alludes to the assumed profits of the new venture, I would remind him of what Burns said anent the "best-laid schemes o' mice and men." It' I recollect rightly the poem (on the subject of the ligature dropped by the fair 'Jaen, Countess of Salisbury, and which was picked up and so gallantly refastened by Edward 111., an incident which. is credited with being the cause of " Hcni soit qui mal v pense " appearing on the royal arras) commenced by a worthy Newtonian in 1851, has never yet seen the light ; and so it may come to pass that the Newton hares will not turn out profitable to their breeders and hunters as the latter suppose and expect. Meanwhile I 'thank your correspon• dent for his good opinion, and yourself far your courtesy in inserting my"letter.—l am, sir, etc., Newington, London, S.E. ANGLO-SCOTUS.

div.head: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
TbPse Sessions were opened on Monday at Chester before

Mr. Horatio Lloyd, deputy chairman, who, in addressing the Grand Jury, said that the number of prisoners whose cases would be presented to them was rather in excess of that with which they had to deal at the corresponding pori3d of last year, there being eighteen prisoners now, as against nine on that occasion. A satisfactory feature of the calendar was that there was no juvenile offenders. Mr. IV. TURNER moved—" That the Court proceed to the consideration of a statement laid before the Court at the last Quarter Sessions by Justices who are of opinion that the several townships of Over, Marton; Weaver, Darnhall, and. Wettenball, now forming part of the petty sessional division of Eddisbury, and the township of Wharton, now forming part of the petty sessional division of Middlewich, would form together a convenient and proper division, within and for which special sessions should henceforth be held and that an order be made accordingly." Mr. FORSTER. seconded the adoption of the recommenda- tion.

Mr. G. W. LATIUM said ha was perfectly well aware of the inconvenience experienced by persons going from Over to the Abbey Arms, a distance of six miles, to attend the hearing, of a_ case, and he thought it was a very great hard- ship to business men who had to appear in school attend- ance cases, that they should lose their time in going that journey backwards and forwards. But at the same time he had a strong objection ta a small petty sessional division. It was, in his opinion, open to the same objection as that of a small district from which juries might be selected. Local feeling was more likely to be imported than if the magis- trates were selected from a wider arca. At present, in the Northwich Petty Sessional Division. with which he was connected, they had petty sessions in three different places, and had a meeting of magistrates once in three weeks. As to Wharton, which it was proposed to include in the division,
the inconvenience of the people there was not so great as was

. . supposed. Even those who lived on the banks of the river had only to go three miles to the petty sessions court and as it was impossible to bring justice to everybody's front door, he did not think the people of Wharton had any more reason to complain than the people of Alsager Cr Odd Rode As soon as the new court-house at Over was built he would suggest that the Eddisbury magistrates should hold occa- sional seszions there. Then the convenience mud safety of the public would be insured. He would suggest that the motion be withdrawn. The CHAIRMAN thought the proposition of,Mr. Latham was a very reasonable xne. He could not conceal from him- self the technical objection that might arise out of the ap- portionment of mlgistrates, and the difficulty of getting additional magistrates to leave their district and hold petty sessions for the limited district. He thought the proper suggestion would be to withdraw the motion. If any diffi- culty might hereafter arise, then the matter might be brought forward again. In reply to the Chairman, Mr. W. TURNER said he was nite willing to withdraw the motion. The motion was then withdrawn. _

Mr. T. W. TA.TTQN moved a resolution to the effect that it was expedient to rearrange and increase the number of poll- ing districts and polling places in the parliamentary division of East Cheshire and that the revising barrister should hold! a court at each of the new polling places.—A discussion took place on the motion, and it was ultimately agreed that the number of pollin_r places should be increased from eight ' to fifteen, and that revision courts should be held at Bol- line-ton and Cheadle. The CHIEF CONSTABLE (Major Hammersley) submitted a return of crims for the quarter ending on the 31st May, which showed that the total number of persons apprehended and summoned was 2,353, of whom 61 were committed for trial, 1,989 summarily convicted, and 303 discharged. In comparison with the corresponding period of last year there was a decrease of two apprehended and summoned. During the quarter ended on the 31st May 600 males and 78 females were proceeded against for drunkenness, showing an increase of 97 males and 15 females on the corresponding period of last year. During the past quarter 10 persoes had been proceeded against under the Adulteration of Food and Drugs Act, 1875, eight of whom were convicted and two dis- charged.t.The Chief Constable stated thatoplcuro-pneurnonia had been _reported at the following places :—Maniev 21 attacked, 12 killed, eight buried, One died ; Bridge Trafford, one attacked,"one killed and bunco; Kelm'', one attacked and one killed for food. One fresh case of foot-and-mouth disease had been reported at Eaton, near Macclesfield. Seven cattle and six swine remained-under treatment on the 16th May, 19 had been killed, and five swine recovered. Swine fever had appeared on two fresh farms, two animals having been attacked and having died. The county had been free from sheep scab.
