div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the meeting held on Wednesday last there were pre- sent :—Mr. G. Blackhurst (chairman), 'Major Cartwright, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Darbyshire, Appleton, Kilshall Marsh, Hall, Wallington, Longshaw, Runt, Brown, Cooper, Burn, Taylor, Greening,Woolfall, Greenall, Bonnell, Bat- harry, Gibson, Owen, Houghton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

div.head: TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.

The CLERK read the following letter from the Local Government Board, dated 15th June :—" Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 7th inst. submitting a resolution passed by the Guardians of the Poor of the Warrington Union as to the desirability of elections of Guardians taking place triennially instead of annually as at present; and stating that the Guardians are of opinion that the law should be so changed as to provide for triennial elections without resort to a poll of o.vners and ratepayers thereon., I am directed to state that the suggestions of the Guardians will receive the Board's consideration."

div.head: BOARD AND THE RATEPAYERS.
div.p: THE BOARD AND THE RATEPAYERS.

The CLERK read the minutes of the House Committee, which stated that the committee recommended that the Stedolph bedsteads should be purchased for the use of the new schools if required; and also that the expense incurred by the children on Walking Day be paid from :the Interest Fund. _ _

- Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and Mr. APPLETON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. BROWN, referring to the first recommendation, said he thought the Board had better wait until they got into the new schools before they purchased bedsteads. He opposed the recommendation,and moved that the minutes be con- firm.d with the exception of the recommendation referring to the bedsteads. Mr. BURN said he had made it his business to enquire into the origin of the resolution passed at the ratepayers' meet- ing. He was anxious to know what it was, because he in- tended as far as he was concerned that everything should be fair and above beard. He suppased the resolution had refer ence to bedsteads, but if the tradesmen of Warring- ton asked exorbitant prices for their goods, it was only likely the Guardians would go out of town for the goods they required. He was very glad. however, that Mr. Brown had referred to the recommendation on the minutes, and he seconded the amendment. Major CARTWELIGIIT had a vivid re-collection that the committee had new bedsteads when they went to the Barracks and he had a very strong opinion that there was no neces- sity either to purchase bedsteads or bedclothing at present. The chairman would remember he opposed the expenditure, without the sanction of the Board, of £BOO for furniture, the principal portion of which had already been purchased for the schools and he defied them to put more into the new schools in their present state than they had got down at the Barracks. They had got at the Barracks nearly 200 children, but what had they at the workhouse? Why they had far more patients and inmates there, and yet less officers than there were down at the Barracks. Therefore, independent of the expenditure, he thought the Board were acting very much in favour of one committee and against the other. He maintained that every committee ought to be treated in the same manner, and that no committee should go to an ex- penditure over £5 without the sanction of the Board. He thought every ratepayer in the Union who could supply the Board with goods eqeal in quality and at as fair a price as an outsider ought to have the order. (Hear, hear.) He supported the amendment. The CLERK: Major Cartwright is under an entire misap- prehension. We cannot spend £5 without coming before the Board for sanction. .

Major CARTWRIGHT: I will venture to say if this is passed it 11 give the committee unlimited power. The CLERK: No, sir; not at all. Before you spoke, Major, the committee had agreed to the amendment. The £BOO is being borrowed by the Guardians and not by the committee. The committee cannot spend a penny of it. The CHAIRMAN: It was distinctly stated at this Board that there would be no expenditure incurred by the Barracks Committee without the sanction of the Board. Major CARTWRIGHT : When was it? The CHAIRMAN: About a fortnight ago. Major CARTWRIGHT : Did it appear on the minutes? The t LERIC: It is the law. Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in reply, said they had not given orders for the bedsteads nor did they intend to do so until they knew the price and until they saw whether they were required. . If they were, and they could purchase the bedsteads cheaper from the tradesmen in town they/would do so. The committee were always glad to give tradesmen in town the benefit of any commission they might get and which the Guardians could not obtain from their orders. As to what fell from Major Cartwright he could assure him it was not the intention of the Barracks Com- mittee to spend any money without the clnsent of the Board. [Mr. APPLETON : We can't]. The £BOO referred to was an approximate amount of what they might require and was given t) enable them to obtain the consent of the Local Government Board to borrow money to purchase the furni- tura. He was not apprehensive that that amount would be required. A vote was then taken on the amendment and the minutes, and the latter were carried by three votes.

div.head: FIRE EXTINGUISHING APPARATUS.
div.p: THE FIRE EXTINGUISHING APPARATUS.

The Hous. Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing :—The Matron reported that she was unable, with the present staff, to do the washing for the Barracks at present, having between 400 or 500 blankets to wash at this season of tbs year. Major CARTWRIGIIT moved the confirmation of the minutes.

Mr. BURN said a fortnight ago he called attention to the state of the pipes for extinguishing fire. Major Cartwright said he was sorry Mr. Burn had not had the same experience at Warrington as he had had at York. He thought it was hardly fair that he should have it thrown in his teeth at that Board because he had been ri—guardian at York he had not had the same experience here. There was a laugh, but he did not want to be laughed at. The Major then went on to say" He did not seem to know that a short time ago they spent £125 in attaching hose for the express purpose of putting out any fire which might occur. Had Mr. Burn asked him for information he would have given it Lim." He did not ask for information, but on Friday he asked the engineer to put on the hose. He did so, and was going away when he asked " Where are you going to ?" The engineer said, "Oh, lam going to put the pump on." He said "What about the tank ;" and he replied "There is no connection whatever with the tank. The tank might be full of water now and if a fire was to break out you ceuld not use a spoonful !" That was after the Major had stated there was rr impediment in the way of putting out a fire if they could only keep the tank full. He contended Major Cartwright ought not to have turned round to him and made the remark he did. They ought to have pipes laid and hydrants fixed in different parts so that if a fire broke out it could be speedily extinguished. If a fire broke out that night there was no means of putting it out ; (hear hear)—but at his old home—York—they had a fire lately and they bad it out directly. Major CARTWRIGHT : That is a friendly attack. Mr. DARBYSHIRE : You are out of order.
Major Cartwright appealed to the Chairman, who allowed him t ) proceed, Mr. Darbyshire still remarking that he was out of order.

Major CARTWRIGHT : I have the right of reply. Here's a dictator who wants to be chairman, who wants to be clerk, and wants to domineer over everybody here. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE : Well, lam under your training! You do it. You are out of order, I say. Major CARTWRIGHT went on to observe that when he said Mr. Burn had not had the experience at that Board as he had at York, he thought every member of the Board would quite agree with him. He was at York ten years, but he 'had not been here two months. Bet the very fact that he had been a member of the Board of Guardians at York gave Mr. Burn a locus stawli here. if he lived to have ten years experience here he would gain far more-experience than he had at York. kLaughter.) Referring to the fire hose, he said he must confess he did not know but what it was really attached to the tank. As to the old veteran ',vial his roseate face and pleasant looks, he really could not get vexed at what he said. He was not at all vexed at Mr. Burn's remarks, and the only objection he had was that he did not go to the House Committee and explain his views. The CLERK then called attention to the minute.

The CHAIRMAN remarked that the subject had been re- ferred to the House Committee, who had power to give Mrs. Mackey all the aid she rf quired. The CLERK stid it was open to any gentleman to move that assistance be obtained.

-Major CARTWRIGHT: We are of opinion it is not the matron's duty to do it. The CLERK That is not on the minutes. The reason is not that it is not her duty, but that with her present staff she cannot do the work ; and the reasonable outcome is that you should enable her to get a staff to do the work. The minutes were agreed to. Mr. BURN then moved that a committee be appointed to assist the House Committee in seeing after the fire ap- paratus, that an architect be employed, and thai the expense he paid out of the Nemo Fund. Mr. BONN= seconded, and asked the Board to take this matter into consideration at once, as it was a very serious matter indeed. He feared if a fire took place a great sacri- fice of life would be the result, for they could not put a fire out with the present apparatus. The CHAIRMAN did not see why the resolution should be parsed. If 20 members were not sufficient to take the matter in hand he was sorry for the committee.

Mr. DARBYSHIRE sympathised with Mr. Burn in heipg compelled to ask the assistance of the Board, because he knew there were some members of the committee who were not pleasant gentlemen to work with, and he had no doubt Mr. Burn had found that out. lie had been in the same position, and had been compelled to quit the field. They were not, however, in a worse position than any other house, because if a fire occurred they could call in the Corporation fire engine. Nevertheless, he agreed with the proposition. Mr BURN withdrew his motion, but observed if the com- mittee did not take the matter up at once he would bring it before the Board again. ASSISTANCE FOR THE MATRON. Mr. DArtnYsurrtE proposed, and Mr. BALHARRY seconded, that the matron be permitted to obtain what assistance she required. _

Major CARTSVMOUT opposed the proposition, and said the il•lrracks' staff should wash their own dirty linen. The )lac 3 was supposed to be perfection. They had room enough, they had a sufficient stiff: and make them do their duty, anti they need not call upon Mrs. Mackey to do a single thing. _The motion was carried by seven votes. Ma for CARTWRIGHT : We three protest.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 1, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 1, 1882.
Mr. DARBTSHIRE : It is not the washerwomen we have to deal with, Major; it is you. We can manage a few washer- women.
MRS. MACKEY ON HER DEFENCE.

A letter was read from Mrs. Mackey acknowledging the receipt of a copy of the resolution of the Barracks Commit- tee, at which she expressed her surprise, and after remark- ing that she thought the Board in justice might have , granted'a personal interview to one who had served them faithfully during the last 15 years, said the clothes were ' returned simply because having received na message or re- ply to her note. She naturally felt sure that they had been sent without the knowledge of the committee, and before they had time to give their decision of the matter. As to not having sufficient staff or apparatus to do the washing at the Barracks she pointed out that the Board had increased the staff since she had charge there and had further re- lieved them of all the younger children. The appliances at the Barracks were the same as she had when all the washing was done there, and if she had charge there she would do it all again. Whatever might be said about the Barracks staff relieving her of a portion of the washing it should not be forgotten they had also taken away the assistance she had for doing it, and at the Barracks they had over double the staff she bad for all the children when they were at the Workhouse. As to any violation of an understanding about the work, she stated there was none on her part—in fact she was never asked. The work was put on her in viola- tion of the rules and regulations laid down by the Local Government Board, and approved by the Guardians, which stated among other things that the matron appointed at the Barracks was "to superintend and give the necessary direc- tions concerning the washing and getting up of the linen, stockings, and blankets, for the schools, and although she (Mrs. Mackey) superintended everything there in addition to her ordinary duties at the house until they got into a way of working—extra work, which, according to the law, was clearly the duty of another—yet she had never had any recognition for these extraordinary services. In conclusion she expressed her regret, after having done her duty satis- factory for so long a period, that she found it necessary to answer a charge.of this character.,
as he had always told the Board. There was no disputing what Major Cartwright said, that this interest belonged to the common fund.

Mr. DARBYsmirE had listened attentively to the report, and he proposed that the bills be paid out of the Nemo Fund. He also moved the following "that the clerk be ordered now to hand over to the Guardians their private bank books, and if asked for SAM by the auditor he is to say the Guardians will consider any communication the Local Government Board may make to him and will deal with the account as may be lawful, according to the result of the cor- spondence. Mr. HALL seconded, and remarked that be thought the best policy was to keep from the auditor, who he supposed was very wide awake, the books which contained an account of the interest. He thought the Local Government Board were acting very properly in seizing interest funds, and he contended the Board ought not to lay rates to extract money from the ratepayers' pockets so that these funds could be created. He thought the best course was to make use of the fund and reduce it to a small amount so that nothing more would be heard of it.

Mr. OWEN asked if the Board ever authorised Major Cartwright to attend the audit and explain the interest fund. He was very near proposing a vote of censure on the Major for going before the auditor when he had not been deputed to attend.
Mr. BURN asked if the accounts had been paid out of the Nemo Fund before.

The CHAIRMAN: No. There was a trip fund, and the surplus was invariably used to give the children a treat on Walking Day. Mr. BURN : I understand you have £2O in hand now? Mr. BROWN : I believe last year there was a deficiency, and therefore the Schools Committee are anxious not to weaken their present position. Mr. BURN pointed out that Major Cartwright or any other ratepayer had a right to go before the auditor. Major CARTWRIGHT observed that any gentleman not only had Power to go before the auditor if he found there was anything to which he could object, but to communicate with the Local Government Board. He had always gone before the auditor when he had an opportunity, and he advised every gentleman to act in a similar manner if he found there was a cause of complaint. He had a cause of com- plaint. He objected not because he did not partake of these particular Assessment Committee feasts, but for another reason. It was nut he would not sit down with the gentle- men, for it was well known to members of that Board, who had asked him again and again to join them, he had said he would be very glad to do so, but there was an obstacle in the way. __ _

Mr. OWEN had never heard Major Cartwright object to the Nemo Fund before he attended the audit; and he con- tended the Major should have communicated to the Board his intention of speaking to the auditor on this subject. The CHAIRMAN was very sorry this question had been raised from time to time. It had become obnoxious to him, and he was inclined to wish the auditor would take it into his own hands and add it to the common fund—(hear, hear,) —and thus stop all this squabbling. He did not think they were gaining anything by the discussion. Mr. COOPER hoped the Board would unanimously support Mr. Derbyshire's motion. They were entirely indebted to Mr. Dun's generosity and kindness in allowing them the interest; and he thought it very hard when gentlemen had to leave their business—and very important business too— and give their valuable time to the Union, especially in visit- ing asylums and conferences, that the Local Government Board woull not allow anything for money out of pocket. While they had a difficulty with the interest fund they ought to take care to keep the books away from the auditor, and he thought it a very wise motion that the books be taken out of the hands of the Clerk. Major CARTWRIGHT : I object to it because it is sanctioning what I believe to be illegal. The resolution was carried.

At a later stage, Major CARTIVRIIIHT said he was exced- ingly sorry Mr. Darbyshire did not retract the personal allusion to him, which he considered amounted to a libel, and unless 'there was something done that day he should certainly take another course, which he should not mention. He should be very sorry to take that course, but it was a personal, very offensive, and totally untrue remark; and he should be compelled to take such a course as would compel him to withdraw what he considered an attack upon him. The CHAIRMAN: of course the matter is entirely in Mr. Darby9hire's own hands, but I do not consider that he very much overstepped others.

If he had made remarks of that character to any gentleman he should have been the first to apologise, and said be was sorry to have made ued of the remark. He would not have his character attacked as it once was.

Mr. DARBYSRIRR said Major Cartwright had not repeated what he stated. Instead of retracting, his dispositioli was to add to what he had said. because he could say a great deal more. What Major Cartwright said previously was the reason why he said what he did. He was calling the mem- bers of the Assessment Committee—the country members— for coming to feast there as if he had nothtn., to eat, but he said again Major Cartwright had had as tune% as any other member of the Board. With regard to him only dining once, he had seen the Major eating not once, twice, or .thrice, but he had seen a cut taken out of the joint before it came to the Committee, who had had to dine of what he had left.—[Major CARTWRIGRT : It is totally untrue. As to his character, if the Major would go in the neighbourhood where he lived and -enquire, he would find everyone speaking well of him. Mr. DARRYSHIRE willingly withdrew everything he had said that was offensive. He was sorry the remarks had been occasioned, as it would no doubt have been better if they had not been used. ALLEGED POCKET-PICBING.--Wm. Moran was charged on Saturday with stealing a watch from the person of Thos. Abbott on the racecourse at Newton. The prosecutor had been to see the races, and while coming off one of the stands with his wife he felt a tug at his watch guard. Ho missed hi q watch at once, and turning round saw the prisoner close beside him. He seized hold of him, but the watch was not found on him.—The Bench dismissed the case for want of evidence.

BETTING MEN IN Thountm—William Ashton, John Langles, and Thomas Marsh, all belonging to St. Helens, were charged on Saturday with stealing a satchel containing £7 68. fid.from Joseph Knight, a betting man, of Sheffield.— Superintendent Jackson stated that Knight and his partner had been on the course on Wednesday at Newton, and shortly after the race was run a number of men came up, one of whom presented a ticket belonging to another firm and asked for £ts, which he alleged he had won on Prud- homme at Chester. This Knight, of course, refused to give, and he was seized and pulled off his stool, the satchel taken away, and the money it contained. He identified the three men as having been concerned in the row.—Mr. Swift, who defended, pleaded an alibi, and the Bench dismissed the case.

An account was presented of the expenses incurred by the children on Walking Day, and it was recommended that it be paid out of the Nemo Fund. Major CARTWRIGHT objected to the amount being paid out of this fund.
Mr. OWEN asked on what ground the Major wished tho fund to be done away with. .Could it be applied to a better Ise than that of providing refreshment for the coun- try Guardians?

The MAJOR declined to give his opinion. Mr. DARBYSHIRE : I should think there is no one eats more at the Workhouse than you do. Major CARTWRIGHT was sorry to hear from that gentle- man, whose education he was sorry to say must have been grossly neglected, such an observation. He begged to tell him he did not get any food—(hear, hear)— Mr. DARBYSHIRE : I have seen you eat food, drink drink, and smoke 'bacca. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: I think you are out of order in discus- sing this. Major CARTWRIGHT bad no doubt of that. It was only in unison with the ungentlemanly observations made at the Board, and he set it down to his total ignerance and want of gentlemanly conduct. (Laughter.) If man who ought to be above that, a man who aspired to be, and had been Chairman of the Board—although at the same time an usurper—(laugliter)—a man who had figured as Chairman of the School Committee, a man who was nominally Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, a man who was followed and supported, be was very sorry to say, by friends behind bim to make such remarks was condemned entirely from filling any position of note. He had his name at present im- mortalised, but at whose expense? The ratepayers. Not that Mr. Darbyshire subccribed very much—he only repre- sented 59 persons. He was sorry—well, lie was not sorry to say he happened to be a ratepayer in the small township which he represented, but he came there to dictate and make use of very coarse language. He begged Mr. Darbyshire to understand that he had not eaten and drunk, with the ex- ception, he verily believed, of one committee meeting, at the expense of that Board. He defied Mr. Darbyshire or anyone else to say he ate more at the expense of that Board than anyone else. He was unworthy of a seat on that Board, and he called upon the Chairman to call upon _Mr, Darby- shire to retract the remarks. If he was to be upheld as Chairman, it was his duty to protect other gentlemen from rude and ungentlemanly attacks. The CHAIRMAN: You cannot condemn in another what you do youriell. Major CARTWIGHT : It is for you to call upon him to retract those words. I don't want to be insulted by any member of this Board in the manner in which I have been insulted,—personally insulted and accused, and my char- acter, which will bear investigation— Mr. HUNT : I think the remarks were not made in that light..

—Major CARTWRTGHT : It Was personal. The CHAIRMAN: I do not think any gentleman indulges nidt•e in personalities than Major Cartwright—(Major Cart- wright: They are legitimate)—and when attacked he is the • very first to Cry out. If a gentleman is so very sensitive he should be very careful of other people's feelings. But, un- fortunately, he never is, and never has been. Ido not feel I bound to call upon Mr. Darbyshire to withdraw any remarks he has made. Ido not consider he made any remarks in- tended as an insult. I took them as jocular remarks, and therefore I do not think I ought to ask him to withdraw. Major CARTWRIGHT : It is Only what I expected. The CHAIRMA.N : There you are again. The CLERK then read the following report : Mr. Efatehurst, district auditor, is now engage!, upon the audit of the accounts of your Union for the half year ended at March last The Board will recollect proceedings before Mr. Knott upon his audit of accounts for the September half year, 1881, relative to your bank accounts. I have hitherto been without instruction from your Board with regard to them, and It is desirable you direct me on the course to pursue if the pass- books are applied for. div.head: SCHOOL TREAT.
div.p: THE SCHOOL TREAT.

Mr. MINES had pleasure in reporting that the festivities in connection with Walking Day so far as the schools were concerned had passed off satisfaCtorily. He was indebted to his fellow °Ricers for their hearty co-operation in the work of preparation, and for their earnest endeavours to enhance the children's pleasure throughout the day. He had also (on behalf of thd children) to thank Mrs. Carleton for her present of a quantity of sweets. He added that the whole of the new clothing worn by the children on this occasion was made at the schools.

div.head: NEW SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE NEW SCHOOLS.

The CLERK reported at considerable length on his attend- ance upon the Local Government Board at Whitehall last week on various subjects pending as to the new schools at Padgate, and the borrowing of money for the purchase of land, erection of new buildings, furniture, tfic. Mr. Sutton explained his interviews with several heads of departments, the result of which in each case was satisfactory. 'He also explained proceedings taken by him for the loan. The Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, from whom the Board bad been in the habit of borrowing money, in the first instance offered £4,000 at 4 per cent., which was per cent. less than the £lO,OOO borrowed from them two years ago. He found, however, he could borrow from money agents at 4 per cent., but they would require commission on the money obtained, and there were Aber reasons why it had always been considered very more satisfactory to trade with the Insurance Company .direct. He called upon Mr. Pearson, auditor to the Metropolitan Life Insurance Com- pany, and it was agreed that they would advance the money at 4 per cent., repayable in half-yearly instalments of prin- cipal and interest within 25 years. With reference to a letter which bad been received from Mr. Robert Garnett, the Clerk explained the material difference existing between the mode in which poor law guardians could only borrow money, and that prevailing with Corporations and similar public bodies. The Board considered the steps taken by the Clerk, to have been very satisfactory. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

The silence which reigned last week at most of the public works in this neighbourhood was on Monday broken by the sound of the cheerful " buzz" and hum of industry.. But this silence favoured the deign of some depredator, who first took a small toy obelisk from a grave in Wargrave Church- yard, leaving the glass shade which covered it, because it had an inscription with the name of, the donor on it, and returning on Sunday night to fetch another shade from another grave presumably to complete his collection of This contemptible thief could hardly have been a native, or he would have seen the command, "Thou shalt not steal," in large letters over the chancel in the same church. The churchyard' gates are locked every night so that the thief must have come like the typical thief to pur- loin these tokens of affection from the graves. It is ex- cessively annoying to think that a place of public resort every day in the week, and especially on Sunday, will liencaforth have to be watched to prevent these petty larcenies. If he must have an obelisk let him, come and fetch that one on the market place which is .neither orna- mental nor useful, a sort of white elephant, and along with it that ugly unmentionable, and it would cot be taken amiss if all of the same make and name were removed from the fronts of the public-houses here, those that remain are an offenc,3 to decency, and publican 3 who have any regard for these t'inga have bad them removed to their back pre-

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

In musical circles it is generally anticipated that Mr. Walter Parratt, the well-known organist of Magdalen College, Oxford, and formerly of Wigan, will succeed Sir George Elvey as organist of the Chapel Royal, Windsor. THE TRAMWAYS TO INCE AND HINDLEY. —On Monday morning the first sod of the new line of tramway to Ince and Hindley was cut in King-street. The line is about two miles and a half in length, and the company are desirous of having the rails laid in as short a period as possible in order to secure the heavy passenger traffic which passes along the route. Messrs. Phillips and Co., the well-known contractors, have been entrusted with the laying of the rails and the equipment of the route.

a TEE BUILDING TRADE.—At a meeting of the Wigan Master Builders' Association,' held at the Clarence Hotel, Wigan, on Saturday evening last, it was unanimously de- cided that a general holiday be held this year for three days, viz., Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, August 7th, Bth, and 9th. A proposition to extend it to a full week was submitted, but in consequence of the slackness which has been experienced in the trade for the last twelve months, it was thought adVisable to let it stand at three days. Other matters relating to the trade were discussed, and a vote of thanks to Mr. Pilling, the president, and Councillor John Johnson, vice-president, concluded the meeting. NEW POST OFFICE FOR WIGAN.—From information received, we ( Wigan Observer) believe we are correct in stating that a site has at length been determined upon for a new building for post office and telegraph business in Wigan and that, as soon as the preliminary arrangements are com- plete and the plane determined upon, the work will be forthwith commenced. We are glad to add that the site selected, immediately opposite Messrs. Meek's establishment in the Wallgate, will command almost universal approval as the most eligible and central for the duties of the office, and the most convenient for the bulk of the community who have to transact postal, telegraph, or money order business. The new office, being so near the old one and immediately adjacent to three of the four banks in the borough and the bulk of the attorney's offices, including the town clerk's and corporation offices, the offices of the clerks to the borough and county magistrates, and the two railway stations, ensured for it from the first a decided approva! on the part of the postal authorities, and when some littWifficulties had been successfully encountered and others cheerfully removed, the site was unhesitatingly selected. The duties of the Post Office are increasing so rapidly, bags being sent or received by most of the railway trains—four mails with heavy des- patches and receipts being attended to every night in all weathers and seasons—it was of the first importance that the new office should be fixed" as near as ..possible to both stations, and in this respect the authorities have cause for congratulation on their success, as they have also in its proximity to the mills and other large works in the town and neighbourhood. We trust that a building will be erected which will not only be useful in every respect, but an ornament to that part of the borough,

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Local Government Board have assented to the pro- posal of the Northwich Guardians to unite the two divisions into which the Weaverham district was divided for the purposes of the administration of medical relief to the sick poor.

The quarterly meeting of the United Methodist Free Churches belonging to the Northwich circuit was held in Witton-street Chapel, Northwich, on Monday. The annual dinner of the members of the Monday. Vic- toria Football Club took place on Monday, when about 90 sat down to an excellent repast at the Crown and Anchor Hotel, Northwich.

Mr. Enoch Ellson, of Hough, near Nantwich, died on the 25th ult. Mr. Ellson was formerly a builder, and the owner of a row of houses in London-road. He was brother-in-law to Mr. Cooper, Chairman of the Nantwich Local Board. The deceased had suffered for many years from heart disease, to which cause his death is attributed.

A resolution was passed at the last meeting of the North- wich Guardians to the effect that the re.lief for each of the three•districts in the Union be administered by a corn- itteo consisting of the Guardians of each district. The first statutory meeting of the creditors of George Henry Martin, of Middlewich, draper and grocer, as held at Crewe, on Saturday. The statement of affairs presented showed liabilities, £776 ; and assets, les. referential claims, £2BB. Liquidation was resolved upon, and Mr. G. Hayes, of Hanley, and a trade creditor were appointed joint trustees. The principal creditors were represented by Messrs. Asthury and Eckersley, accountants ; Mr. F. Walmsley, assistant secretary of the Creditors' Association; and Mr. H. J. Shoolhred, accountant, of Manchester.

The course for this race was from the Royal Mersey Yacht Club Slip, Tranmere, round flagboat off the Dingle, round South Powder Magazine back to flagboat, Dingle, round South Powder Magazine and again back tollagboat, Dingle, finishing off Royal Mersey Yacht Club Slip, Tranmere, passing between same and flagship, leaving the latter on the starboard had. The boats kept well together all the way, there not hem..' more than two minutes difference -between them. Both crews showed seamanship, as they rounded the magazine, and at the close the Lily came in first at seven minutes and two seconds past six, the gun for both races having been fired at 35 minutes past three. The Sea Star was second, having arrived at the flagboat at nine minutes and fourteen seconds after six. The- second and only other race was for second- class yachts of not exceeding six tons, for prizes of £7 and £3 respectively. With the exception of the Sheila, a 3-ton yawl (owner, Mr. F. G. Fowles), all the beats kept in close proximity to each other, taking the same course as the other yachts. The Elaine, 4-ton cutter (owner, Mr. John Bonet)), came in first at 44 minutes past five ; the Zazel, five tons (Mr. D. C. Baynes), second, at 46 minutes and 30 seconds past five; and the Tyro, three tons (Mr. G. 11. Willmer), at 46 minutes and 30 seconds past the hour. The Tyro lost by four seconds, having to make an allowance to the winner of 2 minutes and 25 seconds, owing to her tonnage.

div.head: OUTRAGE ON A GIRL AT WIDNES PUBLIC BATHS.
div.p: OUTRAGE ON A GIRL AT WIDNES PUBLIC BATHS.

A case which excited considerable interest and feeling was heard at the Widnes Police Court on Monday after- noon, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. The court was well filled, and during the hearing of the case, a crowd col- lected in the streets outside. The prisoner was a man named Wm. Woolstencroft, employed as a foreman fitter at the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co., and he was charged with committing an indecent assault upon a girl named Annie Maguire, at Widnes Baths, on the previous Saturday. The prisoner was unrepresented. The complainant said she was a single woman, 17 years of age, residing with her parents at 4, Eleanor-street, Widnes. About 11 o'clock on Saturday night last she, with a companion named Elizabeth Keatings, went to the Baths in Victoria-road, and they saw the attendant standing in the doorway. He took hold of the right arm of the com- plainant, and said "Come in and look at the baths." He pulled her and her companion inside, and fastening the out- side door he pushed them through the curtains, saying, "These are the public baths. Come along, I will show you the ladies private baths." Both girls went with him to the wash-house. They had only been there a few minutes when a knock was heard at the side door, which the attendant opened, and allowed the prisoner to enter, who accosted them with " Good night." The complainant replied "Good night," and remarked that they (herself and companion) "must be going." " Come and look at my drying house," then said the attendant. Keatings prepared to follow him, standing on the top step; complainant behind her; and the prisoner was behind the complainant. The prisonerithen pushed the attendant and Keatings into the drying heuse, fastening the door behind them. The prisoner and com- plainant were then alone, and the prisoner suddenly threw the complainant down. She implored him to allow her to leave, promising that if he would do so she would "say nothing about it." Inspector Barnett: How did he knock you down? He put his foot behind me and tripped me down. He also knocked her down a second time after she had risen; and on this occasion she screamed. The complainant then described in detail the assault which the prisoner committed upon her. Before, however, he could accomplish his pur- pose, the door opened, and the prisoner jumped hastily to his feet. Previous to this occurring the eomplainant had screamed wildly, and the prisoner to prevent her had placed his hand over her mouth. A constable had heard her cries, but when the door opened the first person she saw was Elizabeth Keatings, who exclaimed, "Oh, Annie; what has he done ?" Complainant replied, "I will let him see what he has done ;" and she then left the baths. Standing at the door wm the attend Ant who asked her not to say any- to g about it. She at once, however, went to the police- station and reported what had occurred. She had never given the prisoner any encouragement to behave in the man- ner he had,

Elizabeth Keatin.gs, residing with her parents at 26, Eleanor-street, Widnes, deposed that she accompanied the last witness to the baths on Saturday night. The attendant pulled them inside and locked the door. He invited them to see tha washhouse, where the prisoner joined them. Subsequently he pushed herself and the attendant into the* drying room. Whilst there she heard, the complainant scream, " Lizzie " and "0, mother." Witness knocked at the door to gain admittance, and she asked the attendant to open it. He replied that he could not as the door opehed from the other side ; but, eventually, by pushing, she, with the help of the attendant, opened the door. She could not say Whether or not it might have been unlatched on the other side. When the door opened she was first in the room and saw the complainant lying on her back on the washhouse floor. She immediately arose when the attendant said, " Don't say anything about it or I shall lose my shop." She knew the prisoner by sight, but had never spoken to 'him in her life. That night she had been in the company of the complainant about three hours. They had had noth- ing to drink during that time. The time they were in the baths would not be longer than a quarter of an hour. Joseph Cheynoweth was next called, and stated he was the attendant at the baths, and resided in . Carey-street, Widnes. At 10-40 on Saturday night the complainant and the last witness went to. him when standing at the door of the establishment. Keating asked him to allow her to "have a look" at the wash-house, and the three went to do so. They were there joined by the prisoner. The door between the wash-house and the drying-house was fastened by a catch. As near as be could guess, he and Keating.. were not in the drying-house more than two minutes. At the expira- tion of that time the door was opened and he entered the wash-house. Woolstencroft was standing, and near him was the complainant, also standing. She complained that she had been insulted, and threatened that she was going to fetch a policeman. By the Clerk He saw nothing wrong in the wash-house. Inspector. Barnett And though this girl had been as- saulted you saw nothing wrong? No, sir. Witness, how- ever, admitted asking the girl to say nothing about it, as he might get discharged, and he told them it was "all a lark."

FURTHER CHARGES OF ASSA.ULT AGAINST CHESHIRE CONSTABLES.—At the Chester County Police Court, on Saturday, two members of the Cheshire Constabulary named Morgan and Pearson—the former being a sergeant—were charged with having violently assaulted a labourer named John Basnett, residing at Aldfoad, who was formerlya mem- ber of the force. There were cross-summonses against the prosecutor. The assault was alleged to have been committed at the anniversary celebrations of a local club, held at Singleton. It appeared that a disturbance arose in the even- ing through the perversity of the complainant's brother, who was drunk, and that the police were called upon to quell it. A struggle took place between a constable named Lee ana the drunken man, and the complainant alleged that whilst this was proceeding he was deliberately struck in the eye by sergeant Morgan and knocked down. Witnesses for the ! defence held that the policemen were set upon by the Idrunken man and others, including the complainant, and that thev did not use more violent means than were neces- sary. Tbe case was dismissed, as also were the cross summonses. In reply to further questions by 'lnspector Barnett, the witness said there was nothing on the rules against admit- ting females into the baths at that late hour ; but the baths were then closed and he had cons,quently no right to allow the public to enter. The prisoner at that time Was in charge of the boilers in the baths for the night. He and the prisoner were neither friends nor companions. P.S. Robinson said*from information received on Saturday night, he apprehended the prisoner in Gaskell and Co.'s works on Sunday morning, and charged him With assault- ing Maguire. He replied "It is a lie." He afterwards made the statement that he " had been dragged into it ;" remark- ing, subsequently, "Joe gave me the wiak and I went in." The case for the prosecution being now completed, the usual questions were put to the prisoner. He replied "I am not guilty. I never attempted to committ the assault in the way she has made oat. I have no wish to do anybody harm."
The prisoner was then formally committed for trial, bail being refused.
