div.head: WIDNES SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.
div.p: WIDNES SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.

INAUGURAL MEETING. For some 1.3 w months there has been a movement on foot among the different Nonconformist Sunday schools in Widnes to feria a union. A committee consisting of repre- sentatives frem several of the schools was formed, with the object of establishing such an organisation, and eventually, receiving promising indications of success, they fully matured tho plan. On Wednecday evening the inaugural meeting of the union, which is termed "Widnes Sunday school Union," was held in Lacey-street Wesleyan School- room, Widnee.under the presidency of Mr. Benjamin Brown. The ruleset forth that the union is composed of Evangelical schools. The object of its formation is to promote the extension and improvement of the Sunday school system; to cultivate a feeling of sympathy and Christian union between the churches of all Evangelical denominations; and to stimulate and encourage teachers in the prosecution of their work. The methods enumerated to accomplish this end are numerous, amongst ethers being the holding of public meetings of the union and of the scholars at stated periods. It is also intended to hold Scripture examinations for the scholars connected with the schools included in the, anion. Not the least important devise, and one likely to be of great here& to those engaged in Sunday school work, is the intended quarterly conference of teachers, at which subjects "appertaining to the practical work and spiritual well-being" of the schools will be discussed. A training class, to be attended by the younger teichers, and the elder scholars, with a view to their becomeig teachers, is also included in the project, but the establishment of this depends upon the decision of the committee. Each school joining the union will be called upon to pay a subscription of 2s. per annum per 100 scholars ; the maximum, however, being fixed at ss. The union is to be affiliated with the Sunday School Union, 56, Old Bailey, to the funds of which a guinea will be annually con- tributed. The attendance at the meeting mentioned above was far from numerous, probably to be accounted for, in some measure, by insufficient advertising. Amongst those present were the Revs. T. Peters and J. H. Cummings, Messrs. S. Drought, T. Swale, F. Lawrinsor, H. G. Siddon, T. -T. Peters, and J. Peate. There were .150 a number of ladies present. Prayer having been offered by Mr. S. Drought, The Cseinaneer said most of those present would be acquainted with the object of that meeting, which was the inauguration of the Sunday School Union in Widnes. It was late in the day now to make any attempt to justify Sunday schools; and it, was needless for him to place any figures before them to prove their advantage. His observa- tions brought him to the conclusion that if ever it was important that Sunday schools should be conducted in the most efficient manner, that time was the present. When they remembered the great advances education of a non- religious character had made, and was making outside the Sunday schools, it behoved them, as those who professed to believe religion of the highest importance, to conduct their Sunday schools in the manner which would best supplement the education given in the day schools, by sound religious principles. With these feelings it had been considered advisable to establish that anion of the schools in Widnes, which by the interchange of thoughts among the teachers and officers connected with it, and visitations to various schools, would conduce to their more efficient working, and result in a higher standard of teaching in all their schools. Describing how the union had been projected, the speaker said the following schools had joined :—Lacey-street and Albert-road, Wesleyan"; Hutchinson-street and Simms Cross, Primitive Methodist; Zion Methodist Free Church; and Milton and the Welsh Congregational Churches. If be could do anything which would advance the usefulness of Sunday schools in Widnes, be should be glad to do so; but the usefulness of the union would depend very largely on the earnestness of each school, and the use which was made of the advantages to be gained from it. (Hear, hear.) It was one thing to have a scheme and a system; it was another thing to carry out the scheme, and develope the system; and while he believed the idea of the union very praiseworthy and that they would find the rules very applicable and easily worked, the benefits to be gained would depend upon the way in which they entered into the work which it would open before them. He trusted the union would be of great benefit to each school, and that it wculd be a success. Let them try to discover what was good in each other, and profit by it; and he felt sure that the combining of their various schools and their teachers would be productive of good. Mr. S. Demmer (Primitive Methodist, Simms Cross), after a reference to the absence of Mr. Fogg, moved the fol- lowing resolution :—‘ That this meeting, feeling the great importance of Sunday schools, and believing that their im- proeement, extension, and permanency will be best secured by mutual co-operation and assistance, is pleased to learn that a Sunday School Union has been formed in Widnes, and pledges Reel( to give its hearty support." He was sorry the announcement of the meeting had not met with a greater response; but that did not alter the importance of Sunday schools. (Hear, hear.) As the Chairman had remarked, they were all agreed on the importance of Sunday schools being carried on efficiently and effectually. Sunday schools were intended to train the youeg and rising generation,upon whom in these times there were many influences of a degra- ding and demoralising character brought to bear, and ren- dered it all the more necessary that religious principles should be inculcated in those who were advancing in life. (Hear, hear.) It might be that some people did not fully estimate the importance of the work of Sabbath schools; bat he did not V- ink there were many teachers who devoted their time, energy, and talent to the furtherance of Sunday schools were likely to make that error. Many parents, he feared, and those who took a deeper interest in the spiritual- weil-being of the rising generation, undervalued the import- ance of Sunday school work. He thought it second to none, save the preaching of the Gospel to the masses of the people —(hear, bear,)—and he did not know whether it was second to that or not. (Hear, hear.) They had the same end, but he censidered the training of the young children demanded more attention from those who ministered in holy and divine things from the sacred desk Sabbath after Sabbeth. The Sunday school teachers aimed at the heart and mind of individuals when they were just devel- oping into life, and he held that that was the right time in an individual's history when spiritual truths, and religious principles, should be instilled. It was important, too, because they were carrying out the great commandant of the Master himself, when, speaking with reference to little children, he said "Suffer them to come to me, and forbid them not for of such is the kingdom of Heaven." He learned with pleasure of the union being formed, because the Sab- bath school with which he was connected was the weakest, and it would be one of the purposes of the Union that it should not remain so. The Union would take hold of any- thing that was put within its reach to further the great , work they had in hand, and he trusted the schools would look at the matter in this light, and they would thus mutu- ally benefit each other by their connection. The Rev. THOMAS Payees (Simms Cross Congregational Church), in seconding the resolution, remarked that their friend had introduced the subject with very beautiful feel- ing, and he trusted they were in a measure under the senti- ments which he would have them adopt. He could remember being led to Sunday school mere than 50 years ago, and his attachment to it was ever increasing. It was one of the grand means that God had used so graciously and powerfully to lead souls heavenward. In the present day they had to consider the influence of the school upon the church—not one section nor another, but the whole church. Consequently there was a fitness and a beauty about that union. From the time it originated to the present moment it was a union for good. There were unions in the world that were detrimental, destructive, soul destroying; but this was for the elevation of man, for the conversion of souls, for the glory of God; and therefore they could not attach too much importance to it. He felt that they had need of a larger response to the efforts that were made to establish a basis on a broad basis to secure the bread sympa- pathies of the Christian Church in Widnes; for that was what was wanted. They found a union in sin; in the degradation of human character; in all that was repulsive, • and sad and sickening in the world ;—these were united together. But where was the earnestneee and the 7,01 of the church. If they wished to elevate society' and influ- ence hearts around them right they must lay hold upon the young. They could not do it too soon. Their little minds must be trained, and their thoughts drawn to good and pure things, to that which really benefited and elevated souls. And that was the object of this union—to draw them . heavenward and Christwerd. There was nothing harsh, nothing repulsive, about the Master's command "Feed my lambs." Where was that sentiment brought out more beautifully, more truly, more earnestly, than in the operation of Sabbath schools? There were so many things which engaged the "mighty public" in the present day; but politics and the varied efforts which were being put forth to draw the attention of men to science and philosophy, and so forth, were nothing approaching to the beauty of the Master's sentiment like the operations of Sabbath schools. Those of them who had known something of Sunday schools for many years, who had felt their influence, felt to-day that if they were of any service to society in any form it was due to them. The teachers in Wales- -men and women who devoted their hearts and the best of their lives to the great work of train- ing the young, had something to look upon that would be more glorious than fields of battle, than triumphs made in other departments of effort in the world. The efforts of the humble Sunday school teacher made 'long, long age, had laid the basis of many a triumph in the present day. What maid Lancashire have been had it not been for the Sabbath school ? Look where they would there were triumphs of the Sabbath eohool. It was not to build up shibboleths to zet the sect or party, but to disperse and dispense thoughts that should kindle the hearts of people, educate their lives, and make them gnod men and good women in society. These were the objects of this union, and they must not forget the old adage that " union is strength." He believed the union would attain what it aimed at—the extension, the improvement, and the permanency of what was good and nesful in Sunday school work. (Hear, hear.) Union andl co-operation were the grandest terms of the present day, it I ey were in the right direction ; and there was no reason tis , • v they should not ce-operate, and earnestly .and strenu- • 'Y work to benefit and bless the age in which we live. It s not for themselves only, for they were exeiting an cc upon future ages. The seed they weretreyLntgurtoe 'wetter vere bringing their influence to bear upon th and thus they should do their part in their day, and be able to mess i benefit the world. The resoh was ws carried unanimously, and with accla- me. T. S. SsY.ALES (I.4lCey•Street, Wesleyan) read the rules r adoption. and moved Mei Mr. F. Liwal 'esene (Albert-road Wealeyan) seconded the

motion, making a few observations on the work of the union intended to accomplish. Mr. T. J. PETERS supported their adoption in a few appropriate remarks, and the motion was carried unani- mously. Mr. H. G. SEDDON (Hutchinson-street Primitive Metho- dist chapel) moved that the following persons be selected officers for the union: president, Mr. Benjamin Brown; vice-president, Mr. Thomas Marshall; chairman of commit- tee, 111 r. S. Drought ; treasurer, Mr. F. Lawrinson ; visitor, Mr. Fogg: secretaries, Mr. T. J. Peters and Mr. Joseph Peate.
_ ____. The motion was seconded by the Rev. J. H. CUMMINGS, and carried,
The meeting then terminated.

div.head: MAN ATTACKED BY A MOB AT WIDNES. PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: A MAN ATTACKED BY A MOB AT WIDNES. PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

On Sunday evening a rumour gained currency in Widnes that a man had been murdered with a crew bar on the Old Marsh, and though criminal offences have been not unfre- quently committed in Widnes, considerable excitement was caused. During Monday the tension was relaxed when it became known that the affair was not of so serious a nature. It appears that a man named John Norton had on Sunday night been in a beerhouse on the Old Marsh, Widnes. A mob of about 30 people were waiting at the door for his ap- pearance, and immediately on his emerging from the house he was assailed with bricks and stones. He was felled to the ground and savagely maltreated. A dreadful wound was made in his forehead, his hip was cut, and every part of his body was more or less injured. After exe- cuting their purpose the ruffians made good tbeirescape,and it was not until Monday night that the police succeeded in making any arrests. Norton's injuries are of so serious a nature that he is confined to bed, but the wounds are not likely to have a fat3l termination. On Tuesday morning, at the Widnes Police-court, before Mr. Holbrook GAskell, jun., Peter Quinn, a powder packer, John Lane, a labourer, and Mary Mannion, a single Yeoman, all residing on the Old Marsh, were brought up charged with unlawfully wound- ug, intent to do grievous bodily harm, John Norton, about eight o'clock en Sunday night. Inspector Barnett said it appeared that on Sunday night the injured man Norton was in Mark Wright's public-house, Old Marsh, with a comrade or two. When he came out a mob attacked him. The prisoner Quinn threw a brick at him, and the other two prisoners, along with about 30 more, set upon him, beat him with bricks and kicked him about the face and body. He received a wound on his forehead about two inches long, penetrating to the bone, and which the doctor said was dangerous. In fact the pro- secutor was bruised in some measure all over his body, and Dr. McLennan, who was in attendance upon him, said he was unable to appear that morning. He should consequently ask for a remand.

Annie Keogh, wife of Patrick Joseph Keogh, residing en the Old Marsh, said: I was at home on Sunday night, and I then saw John Norton, whom I know, assaulted. I was standing about 20 yards from my own door, and saw the prisoners with about 20 or SO more people. They kicked Norton, and the prisoner Quinn threw a brick at him and then ran away. Mary Mannion stood ever him with a brick in her hand and struck him on the forehead.

Inspector Barnett : What did Lane do? I did not see him do anything. He was present among the crowd. How long did the row last? About half an hour. What state was the prosecutor in when the mob left hint He was bleeding very much from hie face, and his clothes were all " slutched." His head and lips were cut, and his face was badly bruised. Were his eyes blackened ? No. His cheeks were cut. His wife took him home, where I have siace seen him in bed. He is unable to get up. Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) : Have you any question to ask Quinn—she says she saw you throw a brick! I did do; hut he had an iron bar the length of his arm. Mary Mannion : Did you see ma with a brick? Yes. I saw you strike him. How could you see me if there were 30 people round! Its all a bit of spite. You are swearing false, and you know it. _

Mary Norton, wife of the injured man, living on the Old Marsh, deposed: I saw my husband attacked on Sunday night, and IWM there at the cammencement. It took place about 20 yards from my own door. When my hus- band came from Mark Wright's there were about SO people standing round the door, and they met him. My husband took up a piece of iron when the crowd attacked him, btat he never struck anybody with it. He threw it away when the prisoner Quinn picked the brick up. Quinn sent the brick, and the crowd thcew my husband to the floor. They kicked him on the head, lace, and body. I was in the midst of

the crowd crying out for help, and they never touched me, but they kept "pegging away" at my husband. Quinn kicked him, and Mannion threw a brick. My husband is a little better this morning, but he is bedfast. The doctor says he is not to be moved for a few days. He is being at- tended by Dr. McLennan. Dr. Cooper's assistant dressed the wound on Sunday plight. Quinn: Before I found the brick he (Norton) came with the iron bar and threatened to strike rue. Lane : He started at me first in the taproom, and he-- Mr. Lewin : You had better not say anything now. Inspector Bennett asked for a remand until Friday. There was more in this case than was at present revealed, and other men concerned who had not been apprehended. The prisoners were remanded. Yesterday the prisoners were again brought up at the Widnes Court, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun.—lnspector Barnett asked for a further remand until Wednesday next as there were other persons c, ncerned in the attack on, Norton, who were not yet in custody. He therefore did not wish to go into the case at present. Mr. Gaskell: How is the man going on? Inspector Barnett: He is improving very much. Mr. Gaskell (to prisoners) : You are remanded until Wednesday next.—Bail was refused.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONnAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. DRUNKENNESS.—Edward Ploughman. James Dooley, and Philip McCabe were each charged with being drunk and disorderly at Widnes, on Saturday, and a fine of ss. and costs was imposed in each case. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—John Murphy, a chemical labourer, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly; and also with assaulting P.C. McDonald, whilst in the execution of his duty.—P.C. McDonald said at about 8 o'clock, on Saturday night, the prisoner was drunk and dis- orderly in Lugsdale-road, causing a crowd to assemble. He refused to leave the road, and was consequently taken into custody. He became very violent, kicked witness three times on the leg, and struck him several times on the head with his fist. The assistance of several constables had to be obtained, and the prisoner carried to the police station.— He was remanded to Wednesday. Tim ALLEGED WAREHOUSE ROBBERY. -4.- Elizabeth Glasheen and Bridget Taylor, married women, were charged on remand from Friday, with stealing and receiving, know- ing to have been stolen, a dolly tub, a clothes maiden, and a book case, of the value of 7e. 6d., the property of Ellis Sankey. The goods had been abstracted from a warehouse in Anne-street West, between the 19th and 22nd ult. The particulars of the robbery were reported in the last issue of Me Examiner. The evidence having been repeated, Mr. Beasley, who defended, said there was not a tittle of evi- dence to connect the prisoners with the robbery, and with regard to the receiving, he had a complete answer to that. But was the case to be tried there.—Mr. Gaskell said he thought there was a case for trial.—The prisoners were then formally committed to the Sessions for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn, F. H. Gossage and Holbrook Gaskell, junr.

Mrsetmr.a.svous.—Mary Duneghan was charged with corn- mitting a breach of the peace in Elizabeth-streeet, on the 10th June; and she was bound over in the usual recog- nisances for three months.—Michael Stowey, for being drunk and disorderly in Anne-street West, on the 20th ult., was fined ss. and costs. John Eavers was bound over to keep the peace for committing a Lreach of the pace on the 18th June; and for a similar offence George Whvment was dealt with in a similar manner.—Sarah Kenny, Frank Morgan, and Elizabeth Doyle were eacb bound over to keep the peace for three months for riotous behaviour. A DRUNKEN PUELICAN.—John Horner, landlord of the Ball Inn, Ditton, was charged with being drunk on his own premiss. He did not appear, and he was fined 10s. and Is. 61. costs. TIIRRATENED ASSAULT wyrit TONGS. A respectable looking woman, named Charlotte Chantler, was charged with using threatening language to a young man named John Smith. It was alleged that the defendant, who resides at Ditton, threatened to strike the complainant with a pair of tongs. Defendant stated siva was continually insulted by the complainant; and after hearing the witnesses the Bench dismissed the case.

A YOUNG Danby, clerk to the School Board, asked the Bench to committ a by named John Heys, 10 years of age, son of Sampson Cross, living at/Simms Cross, to an industrial school. The boy's father was a widower, and could not look after the boy, who had taken to sleeping out at night. Every possible means had been tried to get the boy to school, but without effect, and if he were not sent to an industrial school it was probable he would be sent to prison.—The Bench ordered the boy to Le sent to an industrial school until he was 16 years of age. THEFT OF EGGS.—James Conway, a youth, employed as afarm labourer, was charged with stealing nine turkey eggs, the property of John Cartwright, farmer, of Tarbock. About two o'clock on the previous afternoon, the prosecutor saw the prisoner in his plantation, and as he had frequently missed turkey eggs, he searched his pockets, and found the nine turkey eggs produced.—As this was the prisoner's first offence, the Bench fined him is. and costs, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment. QUARRELSOME WOMEN.—Julia Hodgkinson was sum- moned by Eliza Platt for assaulting her on the 24-11 ult. It seems the parties. who are married women, were engaged in the occupation of "swilling" the flags. A disagreement arose, and it was alleged that the defendant struck the com- plainant on the head with a brush. She was about to re- peat the blow, but the complainant raised her brush, and the defendant's was smashed upon it.—A number of witnesses were called, and the defendant was fined ss. and costs, total 22a —Mrs. Hodgkinson had-issued a cross summons against Mrs; Platt, but this was dismissed, as was one also issued ..gamst Julia Hodgkinson for using defamatory language to Grace McGuffic —Mr. 'Beasley represented Mrs. Hodgkin- .n in these cases. ASSAULT ONA WOMAN.—John Gill and Bridget Gill,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 1, 1882. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 1, 1882. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

man and wife, were summoned for having, on the 26th ult., assaulted Mary Ellen Shepherd. The complainant alleged ' that whilst passing the defendants' house door, the male de- fendant made a remark reflecting upon her character. She spoke to him, when he seized her by the shoulder and struck her on the forehead. The female defendant then sent a quantity of warm tea in her face, and going in she returned with a mug. She threw the contents, consisting of soap suds, on the complainant, who was wet to the skin.—The husband was fined 7s. 6d. and costs, and the' wife ss. and costs, or 14 days each. AN INceunous THIEP.—A young man, named Josepb Burtonwood, was brought up in custody charged with steal- ing 35. from the Green Dragon Inn, Whisten, kept by Ann Edwardson. On Saturday morning, about ten o'clock, the prisoner went in the public-house, where he remained more or less during the whole day. At live o'clock he was in the bar with a man named Collins, and the landlady went into the kitchen to have tea. Whilst there she heard the jingling of money and she entered the bar. The prisoner was then leaning over the bar, with his hand in the money drawer. She accused him of stealing, and he banded her 35., which he said was all he had got.—The Superintendent said the prisoner came from Wigan and was a bad character, and the Bench under those circumstances committed him to gaol foy two months with hard labour.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. S B. Chadwick (chairman) and Mr. C. Reynolds. THE CANAL BOATS ACT.—A boat owner named William Adams, who did not appear, was charged with allowing a boat to be used as a dwelling without having the same lettered, marked, and numbered, as requirei by the Canal Boats Act.—Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, gave evidence in support of the charge, and the defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and 16s. 6d. costs.

AN EXPENSIVE STUMBLE.—Patrick Donoghue, an elderly I man, was charged with being drunk.--P.C. Mellor said on the 17th ;nst.' he found the prisoner lying drunk across the footpath in Bridgepstreet.—The defendant: I missed my foot, your reverence, and it is the first time I have been here. —Superintendent Williamson said the defendant was a very quiet man.—The Chairman said he was sorry the defendant had put himself in that position, and he would have to pay a fine of ss. and Ps. 6d. costs. CONTRAVENTION Or THE EDUCATION Ac.—The follow- ing persons were summoned for contravention of the Ele- mentary Education Act :—Edwin Lewis, Spring Gardens, whose child Alfred bad not made any attendances during the past two months; Charlotte Done, Mill Brow, whose child Joseph had not bc•.en present at school during the past two months; John Fisher, Brunswick-street, whose child Robert had made no attendances dnring the past two months; Eliza Maddock, Egerton-street, whose child Arthur had not been at school for two months; Jane Hicks, Cooper- street, whose son Thomas had not attended school once during two months; Joseph Mannering, Briscoe-street, whose child Mary Helen had only been present seven times out of 74; Ellen Rogerson, Dover-street, whose child Eliza Rogerson had only been at school nine times out of 74; Peter Sefton, Zion Place, whose son Peter had only been at school 22 times out of a possible 76; John Antrobus, whose child Jesse had only made four attendances out of a pos- sible 76: and John Filkin (who was arrested unger a war- rant), Percival-lane, whose child Agnes had only been present at school 11 times out of a possible 74.—Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, appeared on behalf of the Board. In the first five cases attendance orders on the parents were made. Mannering'a case was adjourned, and in each of the remaining cases a fine of 5s including costs, was imposed. STEALING A FLAT'S CHIMNEY.—Robert Mulrane, an ostler, possessing only one arm, was charged with stealing an iron funnel, value 155., the property of the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company, Limited.—The funnel was missed from the flat Lymm. of which Thomas Heath is the master, at Weston Poi, on Sunday morning, the 17th instant. It was found on the 23rd by James Weedall, a canal constable, set in the roof of the driver's hut at Weston Point. The prisoner told Sergeant McMichael that he rented the hut, and he was taken into custody. P.S. McMichael charged him with stealing the funnel, and in answer to the charge the prisoner said he did not steal it, but gave a boy sixpence for it; but he knew where the chimney came from, and there was no use in tell- ing any lies about was sent to prison for one month with hard labour.
THIIRSDAL—Before Messrs, S. B. Chadwick, and C. W.
Hatlehurst.

A Row IN TRH "BLUR BALL."—Elimlbeth Ellen Bird, a young woman, was charged under a warrant with having on the Ttl: June, been quarrelsome and disorderly in the Blue Ball Inn, Friar-street. The prisoner, who is a woman of bad character, went in the Inn about twenty minutes to eleven accompanied by another young woman. She was in a state of intoxication, and the landlady, Mrs. Abram, refused to serve her with beer. 'The prisoner then seized two glasses of beer which had been served to other persons, and drank the cofitents. She also made use of filthy expressions to the landlady's assistant, and created a disturbance.—The Bench fined the prisoner £1 and LI costs. A RUNCORN LOAYER.—Thomas Blakemore was charged under a warrant with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in High-street, on the 7th ult.—The defendant pleaded guilty, but stated he was separating two women who were quarrelling, when a man struck him and they had a fight.—Superintendent Williamson said he believed the scene was most disgraceful. He further added that the prisoner was an "idle loafing fellow," who did not care how little he worked so that he could live on the proceeds of other people's labour.—Prisoner: I am working, sir.—The Superintendent: He won't work, your worship ; anything but work.—Mr. Chadwick remarked that the prisoner was any- thing but a stranger at that court, and bound him over to , keep the peace, himself in £lO, and two sureties of £5 each, or in default one month.
SPECIAL MEETING. A special meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held at the Board offices, en Monday afternoon, for the purpose of laying a general district rate, and also to consider some

ciestion in regard to the new sewer. Mr. Carey was voted to the chair, and there were present Messrs. Forster, Flank- burst, T. Handley, Wright, hlidwood, Martley, Johnson, Webster, Kershaw, Shuttleworth, and Allen (clerk), and Dickson (nuisance inspector).
THE MAIN SEWER. The consideration of the main sewer was the first on the paper, and Mr. Kershaw moved that the Board go into committee with that object. _

Mr. MIDWOOD said Ite should like to know the reason before he agreed to such a proposition. He did not believe in this committee work altogether. Mr. KERSHAW replied that it was a legal matter which it would not be to the interests of the ratepayers to discuss openly. The CHAIRMAN also explained that it was not with any desire to keep the public in ignorance of the subject that they wished to discuss it in committee. When it was advisable in the interests of the public that the public should know, they would receive full information; but there were many cases in which it was absolutely impossible to have subjects reported while under discussion. In the present in- stance the Board were in the midst of litigation, and were they to show their "trump cards" to their opponents, they would damage their own case in a great degree. A little further discussion took place in the same strain, when a letter was passed round to each member; and it was then decided to discuss the sewerage question in com- mittee after the rate had been laid.
The estimates of the Hospital and Highway Committees now came under consideration, but no reduction was made is either of these.

Mr. Jointsom asked with reference to an item on the esti- mate of the Finance Committee, whether Mr. Carey had not said the hospital was given to the town. . Mr. CARET replied that the manufacturers purchased the houses for £1,200 and gave them to the town, but there was then the expense of fitting and furnishing which had to be borne by the Board. Mr. KERSHAW referred to the sum paid for salaries, and remarked that the people outside thought Mr. Allen's salary too much. The matter rested thus: whether the Board thought it too much as well as the public. Mr. HANDLEY said he could only say that Mr. Allen was a most efficient official, and fully earned his salary. There were duties which Mr. Allen undertock which formerly cost the Board £5OO a year, so that instead of increasing the expense of the office Mr. Allen, with his additional £lOO, had saved the Board £4OO per annum. They had an instance last March in the renewing of loans amounting to £2OOO, where' had the previous clerk been in office, the ; Board would have been charged about £4OO commission; but Mr. Allen had received no additional payments. He did not think they could ask Mr. Allen to take a less salary than be had at present. Mr. MIDWOOD remarked there was considerable feeling among the ratepayers with regard to Mr. Allen and his salaty. He understood that when Mr. Allen was appointed a great deal of the " law " which the Board had had in pre- vious years would have ceased, but it had not done so. Mr. Allen was undoubtedly a good servant, and they would never get a better. The CHAIRMAN related an instance where Mr. Beasley received £BO for which Mr. Allen received no remuneration at all.
Mr. MIDWOOD thought Mr. Allen might save the Board a lot in regard to law charges; but it was pointed out by several members that Mr. Allen could not undertake the law business.

It was suggested that a vote of confidence in Mr. Allen be passed; and the Chairman observed they had made a good bargain in securing Mr. Allen's services, and that it was sufficiently understood they had confidence in him without passing a formal resolution. Finally the estimates of the Finance Committee were reduced £4O, making a total reduction on all the estimates of £llO. Mr. MIDWOOD moved that a rate of 2s 4d in -the be laid, which he contended would be amply sufficient to meet the expenditure. Mr. KERSHAW seconded the motion. _ _ _

Mr. HANDLEY gave his reasons why a 2s 6cl rate should be laid, remarking that since the estimates were laid bills amounting to £lOOO had been received. The amendment being put was carried by a majority of two votes. A rate of 2s 4 ! in the £ will therefore be laid. The Board then resolved themselves into committee to con- sider the main sewer, having been then sitting from 2 to 5-30 p.m.

div.head: MR. E. K. MUSPRATT AND LIBERAL POLICY.
div.p: MR. E. K. MUSPRATT AND LIBERAL POLICY.

Speaking at a meeting of the Liverpool Liberal Nine Hundred. on Wednesday, Mr. E. R. Muspratt said that there was a time when the English were considered a practical people; and he could remember the time when .they even considered other nations were incapable of exercising Parlia mentary government. When they thought that they had not that practical common sense which the English had, and that therefore Parliamentary government with nations on the Continent was a fallacy. But now the tables were turned, and the Continent the legislatures were able to carry on legislation, while the English Parliament was unable to do so. They had at the present time a Ministry in power who would bear favourable comparison with any ministry that ever governed this country—(loud applause)— not only because they' were Liberals, but because they were eminently practical business men. The Postmaster-General —and he was only a specimen of the rest—had shown that he meant to carry out reforms. He had carried out practi- cal reforms, and the other members of the Government were prepared to do so, but were prevented by the obstructive policy of a number of the Tory party, who were, if not sup- ported, at any rate winked at by their leaders—(hear, hear) —for although Sir Stafford Northcote did not exercise any forms of obstruction, they found that the "Fourth Party " (laughter)—and the leader of the Tory party in the House of Lords were always in unison. (Hear. hear.) A large part of the time et' the House of 'Commons during the last few weeks had been taken up in asking questions. ("Shame.") No doubt the Irish members had asked ques- tions, but they had some reason for doing so, and knew something about the country of which they were speaking; but the large ;lumber of questions with reference to Egypt had been asked by members of the Tory party about a country and about a policy of which they knew nothing. (Hear, hear.) Then they found that they not only asked questions, but if they got an answer not very agreeable to them they made use of the rule' of the House and moved the adjournment of the debate. They had had a singular example of that in the representative for the borough on the other side of the water—(laughter)—who was supposed to represent a busi- ness community. Mr. Maclver moved the adjournment of the House because a minister, in replying to him, said that he thought the question was unpatriotic. Why Mr. Maclver should have been irate at tieing called unpatriotic he could not imagine. The Liberal party were quite accustomed to be called unpatriotic by their opponents—(laughter)—and he (the speaker) had begun to consider that when he was called that he was paid a great compliment. (Renewed laughter.) They knew that the Government desired to carry out several practical reforms which were of special interest to Liverpool as a business community. There were the Bankruptcy Bill, the Patents Bill, the Electric Lighting Bill, all upon questions about which they were eminently interested, end yet how did they End the representatives of this commercial community behaving under those circum- stances? There was a short discussion the other night upon the reduction of the price of telegrams. Mr. Whitley— (laughter)— promised them that when the first occasion arose he w mild sneak; hut he did not upon that occasion. Lord C. J. Hamilton—(" Oh. oh," and." Worse and worse")— who attended a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce. and professed himself desirous of representing a commercial constituency—did not speak on that occasion. (A voice: "ere cetild not.") In fact, he (Mr. Muspratt) did not think they even voted upon the matter. But they knew perfectly well that Mr. Whitley • sat side by side with Mr. Warton— laughter)—and yet these men were returned by the Tory party to represent a business community like Liverpool. If the'Liherale of the city could not succeed in returnine their representatives, they could at any rate give their support to the Government in their endeavour to carry out the measures of reform they desired. (Hear, hear.) The other night there was a debate on the navy estimates somewhere about one or two in the morning, and it only took a tithe of the time occupied by questions at an earlier part of the evening,. He felt convinced that one of the principal reme- dies for this WAR the first rule of procedure, viz , the closure of a dehate—wten. to the evident sense if the Houee end the Speaker, enough had been said, and it was felt the de- bits was only carried on for the purposes of obstruction— bv the simple vote of the majority present. (Applause). Many other nations had adopted similar rules, and the Americans had some such regulation in nearly every legis- lative body in the States. And when it was found that nearly every other nation had such a rule, he thought this nation, now that they had found necessity for it, would be wise in adopting it likewise. (Applause).

ALLEGED LARCENY AT PERE,COT.—Oft Monday, at the Prescot Police Court, before T, Pilkington, Esq., a col. her, named Joseph Burton Wood, living at Whiston, was remanded on a charge of stealing 3s, from the till of the Green Dragon public-house.

div.head: OPENING OF RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: THE OPENING OF RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

A meeting of the Free Library Committee was held at the Commissioners Board-room, on Wednesday, Canon Barclay in the chair. It was reported that William Heyes, Esq., bad presented to the Weary the sum of £lO to be ex- pended in purchasing books, and the secretary, Mr. Brooks, was instructed to convey to him the thanks of the Com- mittee. On the evening of the same day a meeting of dele- gates from the different friendly societies in Runcorn was held in Regent-street school to consider the proposed arrangements for the demonstration on Thursday next. It was unanimously resolved "that 'the delegates present recommend their respective lodges to join in the procession to he formed on the occasion of the opening of the Runcorn Free Public Library by Sir James A. Picton." In addition to the arrangements published last week, we may state that the public meeting will be presided over by the Rev. Canon Barclay, and a series of resolutions will be submitted. Mr, Charles Wigg will move, Mr, John Simpson second, and Dr. Steele support the first resolution, tendering the heartiest acknowledge- ments of the inhabitants of Runcorn to Sir James Picton for the honour conferred upon them by his opening the library. An address will then be delivered by that gentleman. The second resolution set forth "That this meeting believes the increased incentive to the acquisition of knowledge afforded by the opening of the Runcorn Free Public Library, will powerfully stimulate our moral, intellectual, and commercial life and be an inestimable noon to the youth of our popula- tion ;" and will be moved by the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., seconded by the Rev. John Nowell, and supported by Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst. A motion will then be made by Dr. McDougall, acknowledging with gratitute all gifts, dona- tions, and services in connection with tho establishment of the library. Mr. W. Handley will second this, and Mr. P. Briscoe will speak in its support. The last resolution, tendering the thanks of the meeting to all those who have contributed to the success of the day's demonstration, is to be moved by Mr. J. R. Frith, seconded by Mr. G. Rhodes. No labour is being spared to make the ceremony a success, and, if favoured with fine weather, there is no doubt it will be of an imposing character and participated in by thousands of people.

div.head: STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.
div.p: STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers. Market-street, Manchester, writes (June 29) :—During the past week attention has been mainly directed to speculative securities which, influenced by every rumour from Egypt, have accorded many fluctuations, with however a persistent downward movement, arrested a few. times, but too strong to be effectually stopped. Another influence tending to depress markets is the fear of difficul- ties developing at the settlement, and, in view of these, 1- spite very fair announcements as to earnings, many invest- ment stocks have suffered along with the more fickle securi- ties,t hough not generally to the same extent. The settlement to-day has, however, disclosed nothing alarming. Ihe pro- minent channels et operations having absorbed so much at- tention has caused a dearth of business in the other classes of shares reported upon. These show comparatively very few transactions, and, excepting in Bank shares, the balance both of prices realized on dealings and in changes of quota- tions shew a little general weakness in values. BANKS though producing few sales keep firm, prices where lots have changed hands being fully up to best lately marked. INSURANCE SHARES still show a balance of unfavourable change in quotations, but the declines are not so severe as some we have had to note recently. The business done is al- most entirely confined to Lancashires, which have been dose repeatedly at slight fluctuations, the last price obtained being 6, the lowest of the week, and at which price they were also done on Saturday last. Some few quotations have been raised without distinct quotable change. COAL, IRON, &C., AND MlNlNG—Numerically, the move- ments in quotation show an adverse majority, but here also the changes are not near so decided as some we have had to notice during the past few weeks. Very little business has passed herein, a few lots of Ebbw Vales comprising near the whole of the aggregate of transactions. Ebbws had a harden- ing tendency up to yesterday, when they touched 91; but they have receded to-day, and now show a fall as compared with last week's prices. The meeting of this cemaany held here yesterday confirmed the director's report recommending the 59. dividend, and refused the appointment of a small committee to consider a scheme for re-arrangement of capital. I3olckow are neglected, and the £l2 paid are easier. John B. own's now ex-dividend are reckoning dividend. off little higher. Higher 'lndian Glenrock gold, k. Indian Phcenix, *. Lower Tharses Sulphur, Sze., A. Knowles and Sons, k. Bolckows £l2 paid, id. Cammello, k. Nanty, Crlo, and Blaina preferred, l. United States Rolling Stock. ±. Rio Tinto, *. Ebbw Vales, *; and Canadian Copper. rte., .6. COTTON SPINNING AND MANUFACTURING.—Market very inanimate only a few of the foremost concerns showing any activity. Operations seem determined to wait the results to be published at the end of this month, prior to doing fresh business to any extent. CORPORATION STOCKS &C. show no diminution in values; on the contrary further rise is to be noted in Leeds Stock of * and in Bradford Stack of ±. MISCELLANEOUS do net present many features of impor- tance. Very few dealings are reported but where quota- tions are altered, the change is favourable. Barlow and Jones are strong, Rylands and Sons * higher, Hudson Bay (now quoted the dividend and the return of £2 of capital), with one solitary transaction are not quotably altered. RAILWAYS.—Since our last report the market on several ,occasiens has been in a state of semi-panic, caused by the political news regarding Egypt, and prices generally show severe reduction. Brighton A's are foremost in the decline being subjected, as denoted by continuation rates; to heavy bear operations. South Eastern A's too, are distinctly lower. Some of the heavy lines have suffered bjeclosinp.; of Bull accounts ; particularly is this the case with Great Westerns. he news to-day is however considered to some , extent tranquilizing, and a good rally is the result.
ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Befare T. P. E. Tliompson Esq., judge, and W. Tyrer, Esq ,registrar.

. , . EVADING AN EXECUTION.—CharIes Rathbone, market gardener, Farnworth, was sued by Joseph Hatton, butcher, Westfield-street, for £26 58 5d for goods sold and delivered. —Mr. Cook, of the firm of Messrs. Barrow and Cook, appeared for the plaintiff.—Mr. Cook said that an execution had been formerly issued, but it was found that it could not be executed on account of a bill of sale banging over the° defendant's premises. This bill of sale, it was assumed, had been contracted for the purpose of evading the warrant. The defendant, Mr. Cook said, was the owner of seven, cucumber frames, and be would probably be enabled to send to market some £lO or £l2 worth of produce. lie was also making arrangements to build.—A commitment order was made. A PIGEON-FLYING DISPUTE.—A collier named Williatn Marsh, living at St. Helens, sued William Briars, a collier, of the same place, for the sum of £2.—Mr. Swift, solicitor, appeared for the plaintiff, and stated that there had been a flying match with pigeons arranged between the plaintiff , and a man named Walsh, and the defendant was appointed ' stake-holder and referee. The match was flown at Eccles- ton on the 22nd May, and defendant then decided that the plaintiff's pigeon had won, but afterwards refused to pay plaintiff the stakes.—The plaintiff denied that the pigeon bad won.—His Honour said this appeared to be ono of those cases in which an attempt was being made to get clear from paying a just debt, ;Act Qz.derQd an irnme4i4o tIA.Y• mout with Qoits,

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS, The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. J. Ashton. There were present the Revs. J. W. N. Taner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. T. Norman. E. A. Wallington, Jno. Highfield, J. Smith, C. Rigby, H. Stringer, Lowe, Midwood, T. Andrews, W. Tickle, Wm. Whitlow, Jno. Knowles, J. Davies, Jas. Weir, Jos. Baguley, G. S. Haalehurst, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). SUNDAY CLOSING. The CLERK bad received from Manchester a petition, which the Board were asked to sign, asking Government to stop the sale of intoxicating liquor on Sunday, excepting from the prohibition the bona fide travellers. Mr. RIGBY moved and Mr. MIDWOOD seconded a motion that the Chairman sign the petition on behalf of the Board. The motion was passed. THE DRAINAGE OF THE WORKHOUSE. In accordance with a resolution of the Board, the Master r (Mr. Jones) had prepared a plan of a scheme of sewerage for the workhouse which was estimated to cost £194. Mr. RIGBY remarked that these works were required in consequence of the canal and railway stopping the natural fall to the river. The CLERK said there was still the natural fall. Mr. RIGBY thought the matter might be amicably ar- ranged with the canal company without going into an ex- penditure of £2OO. The CLERK: They say we are causing a nuisance. Mr. RIGBY : So we are where it is. I mean to discharge it into the canal in the open. It causes an abominable nuisance in the tunnel. The DEPUTY CLERK: Their grievance is that you have no right to send the sewage from 200 people into the canal.

Mr. RIGHT replied that the canal company had cut the natural fall anti were bound to provide for a sewer. On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. RIGHT, it was decided to hold a meeting of the Board in committee to discuss the scheme. TITB REPRESENTATION OF THE UNION: THE PROPOSED CHANGES RESCINDED. Mr. WM. WHITLOW moved the resolution of which he had given notice which was as follows :—" That the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Board for the amalgama- tion of Norton and Stockham, and of Keckwick and Dares- bury be rescinded." He contended that the townships named paid as large a contribution to the rate as those with larger populations and were entitled to send representatives. He had no objection to giving an additional Guardian to Apple- ton and Weston, but it was, in his opinion, unjust to take one from another township. Answering Mr. Darbvshire. the CLERK said no commu- nication had been received from the Local Government Board in reference to the matter. Mr. RAWy endorsed all that Mr. Whitlow had said, and seconded the motion. He had heard outside that if the townships were amalgamated there would be a contest annually, and consequently a serious expense. Mr. ',Own said he was one of those members who voted for the amalgamation of the townships at the last meeting, but he should now, after mature consideration, vote with Mr. Whitlow (Hear, hear.) He would suggest that they take a guardian from Runcorn. (Laughter.) It seemed the people there did not . care much about the nomination ef Guardians. They were at least very careless, perhaps be- cause they had too many representatives, and they might meet the difficulty by taking one from Runcorn and giving it to Weston. Mr. NORMAN : You are on the wrong horse there. Mr. Lows: Well, Runcorn people don't seem to care. Mr. NORMAN: The Local Government Board will ride you out of this. Mr. BAGDLEY, as representative for Stockham, begged to say a few words on this question. It was true he had not made his appearance at the Board very often' but having no out-relief in Stockham he had not considered it necessary to do so. Other offices appertaining to the government of the township were carried out, and be thought it would :be unfair to take a Guardian from them. Personally he cared little whether he bad the right to sit at the Board or whether the township had the right to be represented directly, but if the Guardians would properly look into the matter they would find they had scarcely fixed on the right township. If another representative must be given to Apple- ton and Weston, there were two other townships whose united populations did not reach the population of either Stockham or Norton. There was one township without a re- presentative at the present time—he alluded to Aston Grange. At the same time he was not one to stand in the way of the general good, to attain which the few ought to give way. The CLERK remarked that he had expressed his willing- ness to sacrifice one township with which he was connected, but some people seemed to think he wished to put more power in his own hands. He rather thought it would be reducing his power. Mr. DAREYSHIRE explained why he voted for the amalga- mation at the last Board meeting. Appleton was certainly in want of another representative. Rev. J. LOCKWOOD thought each township was entitled to representation however small its population might be. Mr. BAGULET said the population of Stockham was not so small as represented by the last census. It had not been so low as it was then for 20 years, and it had now one-third more of a population. The township of Norton was already three miles long, and if Stockham was added it would be increased to four. If they had no paupers in Stockham, there was no telling bow soon they might have. (Laughter.) Rev. J. Loexwoon said he was in correspondence with the census registrar with reference to the populations. It had been under estimated. Mr. Nonsaw remarked that if the Guardians did not do something in the matter, the Local Government Board would do it for them. Mr. RIGBY : Don't you be afraid of that. They do it regularly. The CLERK said Appleton made exactly the same appli- cation 20 years ago, the same objection was made by the Local Government Board, and the same suggestions made as were now being made. Mr. NORMAN suggested that it woald take a majority of two-thirds of the Board to carry the resolution. Mr. RISIBY :No cloture! (Loud Laughter.) A • simple majority. 'the motion was then ptif, when 13 voted for and five against. It was decided to forward the resolution to the Local Government Board and state the majority by which t had been carried.

EXTRA SERVICES. The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said the Financ• Committee had. to report with regard to the extraordinary duties of the Clerk in connection with the settlement and removal of paupers. It had been the custom to recommend the pay- ment to him of two guineas for each case. This year they numbered 16. The number removed from Union was three, ceased to be chargeable six, continued chargeable and re- lief repaid 1, refused to accept a pauper not removed to this Union I. number of paupers whose settlement was inquired into 2. The Clerk had had to travel 475 miles in connection with these matters, and the Finance Committee bad every confidence in recommending the sum of 33 guineas for these services. Mr. Nonstes seconded the motion, which was ended. DAINTY DINNERS AT DUTTON. VER LOWE AGAIN ON "FEEDING." Mr. Lows asked the Clerk what the letter from the Local Government Board said as to the nature of the refreshment to be prepared for Guardians at the House. Were they not to consist of something plain? The CLans:. If you had given me notice to produce the letters they should have been here. But they are not here' Mr. LOWE: I understand the Guardians are having grand dinners.

Mr. RIGBY : No, no. Mr. LOWE : I have heard of such delicacies as quarters of lamb, plum puddings, beef, beer, oranges, and blkne "sang*. (Laughter.) I think we are getting rather grand. Rev. J. LOCKWOOD: For which we all paid. Mr. Lowe said he understood the meat was weighed when placed on the table; and when the dinner was copcluded the scraps were weighed and charged to the ratepayers. That was not what the Local Government Board intended should be. He did not think the ratepayers should pay for scraps. If the Guardians wanted a dinner, let them have it and pay for it. Mr. RIGBY : We had a good dinner, and we paid for it. (Laughter.) Mr. Lowe: I object to the ratepayers paying for the scraps picked off the table. The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said the dinner provided was satisfactory in every respect, and such a one as could be ob- tained in Liverpool or Manchester at the same price. Mr. Lowe's charge was unjust, and he hoped next time the Guardians had a dinner that geetleman would accept an invitation. Mr. Lows: Is it not the practice when the Guardians get their dinner here to weigh the food when placed upon the tablh and when removed? Mr. RIGBY : It is not. A MEMZER said if Mr. Lowe had wandered.up and down those fields ac long as they did, he would have wanted a , dinner. Mr. Wee. WHITLOW: And with a keen appetite by the sewage smell. (Laughter.). Mr. LOWE: It is or was the practice here. The CLERK : Well, we don't know what became of the dinner after we had done• with it. We, made a veryegaod job of it (Laughter.) The DEPUTY CLERK said having heard some rumour of this question he had asked Mr. Jonee,as to the mattere. Mr. Janes purchased the provisions far•the Guardiana! dinner separately, and he divided the cost of the purchase 'among , those who partook of the dinner. Whatever was left went tee the House without paying for. • Mr. LOWE : What, all the °Sher dinners? Have clinnees ' ever been done in, the way I mune lk A MEMBER : That is in times gone by. Mr. NORMAN: I think the better plan wird be to call in Mr. Jones—(Cries of " Nceno.")—and get the information. Mr. Lows :, Call Mr. Jones in. Mr. RIGBY: It is not worth. while. Not a bit of it. The CHAIRMAN : It yon will move a resolution, Mr. Lowe, we will act wan it. Mr. RIGBY : Mr. Chairman, we heel a good dinner,—a good plain dinner. I don't know w'mat Mr. Lowe refers to when he says plain dinner. We bad no ch tmpagne—[Mr. Lows: Beer.]—nor hock. (Laughter.) Nothing hut a good, plain, substantial dinner ;and for my own part I don't care how soon lam invited tee another dinner. (Laugher.) It was very nicely cooked ad dished up too; and credit is due to everybody. If Mr. Lowe had only been here at the dinner he would have been delighted and not said a word about it. (Laughter.)

I don't thick it is right, 20 members A M ! 'gild ratepayers did ot fi:arilfilf:rt list' The discussion then ceased. div.head: 11111 LAYING OF THE RATE: A REDUCTION MADE.
div.p: 11111 LAYING OF THE RATE: A REDUCTION MADE.

Mr. HANDLEY proposed that a rate of 2s. 6d. in the be laid for the next twelve months. The matter was fully gone into at the last Board meeting and nothing had since transpired to shake his opinion that a half-a-crown rate was the proper one to lay. In fact, since the meeting that after- noon he had heard that another bill of 300 bad been re- ceived by the Board. So that even in a half-a-crown rate he was afraid they would beon the wrong side at the end of the year. Mr. FonsTER seconded the motion.

Mr. MmwooD said he understood that meeting was to dis- cuss the details of the estimates, and then if the Board thought advisable to lay a less rate than the one proposed. The CHAIRMAN observed that if Mr. Midwood found the estimates could be reasonably reduced, and the Board agreed with him, he could propose an amendment that the rate should be reduced.
Mr. JoHNsort suggested that the Board consider the estimates in rotation.

The CITAIRMLN pointed out that the estimate of the various Committees had been passed, and they could not again be considered. Mr. KERSHAW said he understood at the last meeting that a special meeting would be called to consider the estimates. Mr. JonNsoN remarked that he on the last occasion ob- jpcted to the estimates being passed because they were not given on the agenda paper. The CHAIRMAN: We had better refer to the minute book. We cannot upset the minute. The CLERK stated the minute read that Mr. Midwood moved and Mr. Wright seconded a motion to call a special meeting of the Board to consider the rate, which was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN said then the meeting was not called to consider the expenditure but the rate. Mr. JointsoN: We don't know of the items of which the rate is made up, and you cannot expect us t vote for them. I for one won't. _ _

The CHAIRMAN : You are under a misapprehension there. All the items have been given with the exception of the interest. The CLurts : The Finance Committee did not show their estimates in the agenda paper. The CHAIRMAN: Then the estimates of the Finance Com- mittee were not passed at the last meeting, and are 1 presume open to us now to discuss. Mr. WEBSTER made the suggestion that in future years each member of the Board should be supplied with copies of the estimate. Mr. JOHNSON said at the last meeting of the Board he ob- jected to the passing of the whole of the estimates. The CHAIRMAN: You could not do anything so unreason- able as that. It had not been usual for each member to re- ceive a detailed estimate of the expenditure, which used to

be brouttht before the Board without notice. Mr. JOHNSON remarked that that was a very loose way of doing business. The CHAIRMAN: I don't think it is for us to re-open this question of the estimates. Mr. JOITNSON: I cannot consider them settled by the Board. Mr. MIDWOOD persisted in his statement that he moved for a special meeting to consider the estimates; and how it could be ruled that the question could not be discussed was .more than he could understand. The CHAIRMAN: It was not understood so, nor is it so on the minute. Mr. MIDWOOD: They put anything on the minute. The CHAIRMAN: If you doubt the ability of Mr. Allen to take down a proposition you should write it. I understood you wished to discuss the rate and not the estimate. Mr. MIDWOOD said the rate could not be properly under- stood without going into the estimates. Mr. HANDLEY thought it would be as well if they took , the estimates. The rate should be laid at once.
Mr. MARTLEY inquired if there was something in the estimates which was objectionable because they had not to be discussed.

The CHAIRMAN said there was not except that he was afraid they might be out of order. Mr. JOHNSON>: I propose that this meeting be adjourned to the next general Board day. The CHAIRMAN: There is no objection to having a friendly talk over the estimates. I don't think we have any right to rescind the resolution of last Board day. It was then decided to discuss the estimates, and that if any alteration was to be made notice must be given at the next Board meeting. _

The estimates of the Health Committee were the first to be considered ; and Mr. KERSHAW, referring to the loss sus- tained by the Board in the working of the market, recom- mended that they at once take steps to let off the market by tender, and thus get rid of a fruitful source of expense. The CHAIRMAN intimated that the qoestion of the market was not at present before the Board ; and asked Mr. Kershaw to confine his remarks to the matter in hand. Mr. KERSHAW : I suppose this is a mere informal meeting, and we may sit down to discuss the subject. Mr. Mtuwoon : I would shut up the market altogether.

The CHAIRMAN: it is no use looking cross about the market. None of the members now on the Beard built it, and we were always against it. Mr. KERSHAW : I don't think so. The CHAIRMAN: I was. I was always against it before I came on the Board. But it is of no use crying over spilled milk.
Mr. DIXON explained that the repairs to the windows of the mrket were required in consequence of the putty having shrank.

- The CHAIRMAN : It was DIA up in it Jerry way. Mr. Midwood- rose to make some remarks. The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Kershaw has not finished yet. Mr. MIDWOOD : He has sat down. The CHAIRMAN : Yes; he has been sitting down whilst speaking. Mr. KERSHAW: Yes, we may it down. We have no need to stand up enless we are so small that we cannot be seen except wg do. (Laughter.) Excuse me, Mr. Midwood. (La ugh ter.) Mr. MARTLEY said it was really necessary that something should be done to the market. He passed a few Saturday's ago when it was raining heavily, and several stall holders asked him to go in. Water was coming in not in one place but all round the building, and if the Board expected to get tolls they must make it water tight. Mr. KERSHAW and Mr. WEBSTER thought £5 would remedy that. Several questions were asked with regard to slaughter- houses. and Mr. DIXON said they had not paid as well as they were expected to do. They were established with the object of preventing the killing of pigs in backyards. When the Real of salaries was reached a discussion arose as to the employment of a man named Massey. Mr. KER- SHAW said the Highway Committee some time ago dispensed with the services of Massey, and the Health Committee had now taken him on, but were still charging his salary through the Highway Committee. The CLERIC explained that the account of Massey's wages was charged to the Highway Committee to avoid having separate checks. It would be inconvenient if the wages were divided between the two committees. Mr. MIDWOOD protested against this method of conduct- ing business, as well as Mr. Kershaw. The committee had discharged this man; and he was now informed that the Health Oimmittee had found him employment. The CHAIRMAN replied that it did not matter to the Com- mittee whether it was Massey or any other man. They simply wished for a man to do certain work, and if this was done satisfactorily this was all that was needed. Massey was only employed occasionally. Mr. KERSHAW remarked that if the Health Committee employed the man they ought to pay him. I The CHAIRMAN: But you only get hold of one half of the story. You have not patience to inquire. Mr. Dickson being responsible far the disinfecting of houses has employed Massey for a short time; the rest he employs, I understand, on his own business. Mr. HIGGINSON explained the work intended to be done, and said he might possibly manage with a less amount than 150.

Mr. MIDWOOD expressed dissatisfaction at the item placed down for slaughter-houses. The CITAIRM&N said if the Board were opposed to it the Committee were quite willing the alterations should stand over. They hai been disappointed at the income which had been realised from the building; but when it was erected there were a greater number of pigs slaughtered in Widnes than at present. Being able to obtain American meat, the butchers did not care to slaughter in Widnes. Answering several questions with regard to the man Massey, the Chair- man-Mid he had been a useful man. The sum spent on dis- infecting during the year was £2O, and there had been £1.9 expended for material-. After further discussion, it was decided to reduce the amounts in the estimate as follows :—Ventilating sowers from £5O to £25; alterations and repairs to markt% £5O to £3O; cleaning, .225 to £10; and slaughter-houses X2O to £lO. These sums amounted to a reduction el 47() QT. tha Committee's estimates.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—Notice to Dairy. JUP men, Cowkeepers, and Purveyors of Milk.—The Dairies, Cowsheds, and Miikshops Order of July, 1879.—Pursuant to the above-mentioned order of the Privy Council, made the Ninth day of July, 1879, under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878. The Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of che Borough of Warrington, being the Local Authority for the said Borough, do HEREBY GIN'S PUBLIC NOTICE that a REGISTER is now open for the registration, under the said order, of all persons from time to time carrying on within the said Borough the trades of Cowkeepers, Dairymen, or Pur- veyors of Milk. The mode of registration is as follows: Every Dairyman, Cowkeeper. and Purveyor of Milk shall make written application to the Town Clerk to be registered, and shall describe in such application his trade, and the situa- tion, number, and dimensions of the buildings and premises in respect of which he applies to be registered. When the appli- cation is filled up in the presctibed manner, it must be forwarded to the Town Clerk, at his Offices in Lyme-street. Warrington, and upon the Town Clerk being satisfied that the requirements of the order and of the notice of the Local Authority have been complied with, he shalt forthw th register the same in the register kept by him for he purpose, and shall transmit to the applicant a certificate of the registration thereof. Forms of application will be supplied free of charge to any applicant, and may be obtained at the office of the Town Clerk. And Notice is also Hereby Given that it is not lawful for any person to carry on in the said Borough the trade of a Cowkeeper, Dairyman. or Purveyor of Milk, unless he is re- gistered as such under the said order.—Dated this 26th day of June, 1882. WM. fly. BROOK, Town Clerk. estrrtoir.—By secs. 60 and 61 of the above-named Act, it is provided that if any person does anything in contravention of the said Act, or of an order of Council, or of a regulation of a i Local Authority, he renders himself liable to a penalty not exceeding Twenty Pounds.

Mr. NEWSOME asked the Clerk if it was not a fact that it took three Guardians to form a quorum on the Visiting Committee. The CL7,:nx : Yes; sir. Mr NEWSOME : Then I see by the book that on Sunday Mr. J. T. Hall had visited by himself. Mr. HALL: I must admit that Mr. Newsome is very kind. He does make some wise remarks sometimes. About visit- , ing the workhouse on Sunday I must explain. The CHAIRMAN There is no explanation at all neces- sary. Mr. HALL: I want to satisfy the learned member for Eccleston. (Laughter.) I am sorry to say he shows that there is some Irish blood knocking about. (Cries of " No, no.") I chanced to meet Dr. Hall going to visit some cases at the werkhouse, and he kindly asked me to walk across with him. I said " With pleasure," and walked across with him, and I find that my name has been put in the book. I was not here above four or five minutes, and it is a monstrous piece of impertinence on the part of Mr. New- s= to mention it. (Cries of "No, no," and "Keep your temper," in the midst of which Mr. Hall threw the. visiting book, which he had in his hand, violently on to the .table.) Mr. BARNACLE: I think that is no business to us at all. Mr. HALL: You know the man, don't you? Mr. CHAMBERS said he thought Mr. 'Newsam had only asked a proper question. Mr. Hall has answered it and the matter is at an end. Mr. HALL: I don't think Mr. Newsam has been in the workhouse once during the wlsole fime he has been on the Committee. This terminated the business.
